Paul tells the Colossians that believers have been circumcised with a circumcision made without hands, by the circumcision of Christ, and buried with him (Colossians 2:11–12). The circumcision of Christ most likely means his death: there the old self under sin was cut away, and everyone joined to him by faith shares in it. Everything the sign pointed to, belonging, cleansing, a place in Abraham’s family (3:29), Titus already had in Christ. To demand the sign now would be to say that Christ’s work had not quite reached him.

Why circumcise Timothy and not Titus? A reader who knows Acts will feel this immediately. Paul later took Timothy and circumcised him (Acts 16:3). How is that not the very thing he refused here? The difference is everything. Timothy’s mother was a Jewish believer (Acts 16:1), so he would probably have been reckoned a Jew by birth who had simply never been marked as one; and nobody was demanding it as a condition of his salvation. Paul did it so that Timothy could get into synagogues and preach. Titus was a Gentile, and the demand was being made as a requirement of acceptance with God. So the rule Paul is working by is not that circumcision is forbidden. It is that anything may be done for the sake of the gospel, and nothing may be added to it. The moment a thing stops being free and starts being necessary, Paul will not move, and the same man who circumcised Timothy would not let anyone touch Titus.

False brothers. Then the sentence turns dark. “False brothers” is pseudadelphoi: they claimed to be Christians but were not. The vocabulary that follows is the vocabulary of espionage: secretly brought in (pareisaktos), the word used of smuggling; slipped in; came to spy out, the word for reconnoitring an enemy position. These were not honest men with a different opinion. They came to gather intelligence on how free the Gentile churches actually were.

To spy out our freedom. Freedom: from the law as a way of justification, and from its ceremonies. Slavery: to the law as a way of standing before God (4:9; 5:1). That is the whole letter in a single phrase. What was on offer looked like a promotion: full membership, the marks of the covenant. It was chains. Anything that makes acceptance with God depend on a performance puts a man on a treadmill he cannot get off, because the performance is never finished and the verdict is never in.

We did not yield. Not for an hour. Compromise never looks like surrender from the inside: it presents itself as a small, reasonable, temporary allowance for the sake of peace.

Preserved for you. And then he says why, and it is the most pastoral sentence in the paragraph. Not so that Paul might win, but for you: a congregation of Gentile converts hundreds of miles away who would never know the meeting had happened. The truth of the gospel is the gospel in its true meaning, free grace, kept from being bent into something else. Paul is not a man who enjoys a fight. He is a man standing in a doorway so that people behind him can stay free, and the freedom of every Gentile believer since, including the freedom of whoever is reading this, came down that corridor. And behind Paul stands the one who bought that freedom: Christ, who set us free (5:1), at the cost of his own life.

What exactly is Christian freedom? It is freedom from the law as a way of earning God’s acceptance, from its curse on our sins, and from the ceremonies that pointed forward to Christ, such as circumcision, the food laws and the sacrificial system. It is not freedom to sin: Paul will say so sharply in 5:13. It is freedom for something: to serve God as sons rather than slaves, gladly, from love. A slave works to avoid punishment; a son works because he belongs to the family. Christian freedom means you never again have to wonder whether today’s obedience was enough to keep you in. You are in, and you obey from there.

In everyday life. Notice the small, reasonable allowances. A rule that began as a helpful habit and has quietly become a test of whether someone is a real Christian. A preference about worship, schooling or Bible translation that you now hold over other believers. Ask of each one: is this free, or have I made it necessary?
verseByVerse.note: Titus was a Greek, uncircumcised — a test case for whether Gentile believers must be circumcised.

verseByVerse.quote: And from those who seemed to be influential (what they were makes no difference to me; God shows no partiality)—those, I say, who seemed influential added nothing to me. On the contrary, when they saw that I had been entrusted with the gospel to the uncircumcised, just as Peter had been entrusted with the gospel to the circumcised (for he who worked through Peter for his apostolic ministry to the circumcised worked also through me for mine to the Gentiles),
verseByVerse.commentary:
Added nothing to me. Two words in Greek, and they end the argument. The Judaizers’ case rested on the claim that Paul’s gospel was incomplete, an abridgement of the full Jerusalem version. So Paul reports the outcome bluntly: the pillars heard his gospel in full and had nothing to add to it. Whatever the Galatians were being told is missing, the men supposedly missing it did not think so.

God shows no partiality. The phrase is close to an Old Testament formula: God does not lift up faces, does not take the important man’s side because he is important (Deuteronomy 10:17; Acts 10:34). Paul turns it on the apostles themselves. Peter had walked with Jesus and Paul had not, and it makes no difference to the truth of the gospel. The same God who is unimpressed by Peter’s record is unimpressed by anyone else’s, which means nobody in the room outranks the truth.

Entrusted. Then the reason they added nothing: they looked at the evidence of what God had plainly been doing in the Gentile world. And the word is entrusted: the language of a steward handed something that belongs to someone else. A man entrusted with a message has no authority to revise it. Paul cannot edit this gospel to please Gentiles and Jerusalem cannot edit it to please Jews, for exactly the same reason. Neither of them owns it.

One Lord behind both commissions. One gospel, two mission fields: Peter mainly to Jews, Paul mainly to Gentiles, not a senior apostle with a junior assistant. Peter was recommissioned by the risen Christ beside the Sea of Galilee (John 21:15–17); Paul was commissioned by the same risen Christ on the Damascus road and sent to open the eyes of the Gentiles (Acts 26:16–18). That is why the gospel to the circumcised and to the uncircumcised is one gospel. It has one owner and one content, the crucified and risen Christ, the same Lord of Jew and Greek alike (Romans 10:12).

He who worked through Peter. Verse 8, in brackets, holds the key to the paragraph: its subject. It is not Peter who worked, and not Paul. The same God energised both ministries; the verb is the one from which we get energy. Which is why the comparison never becomes a competition: two men were used, and one God was working. God is not divided among his servants, spending himself heavily on the impressive ones and thinly on the rest. The whole of him works in each, and so the least of his servants has the same Lord at work in him as the greatest.

What it does not mean. It does not mean there are two gospels, one for Jews and one for Gentiles. Peter would say it himself at the Council: we believe that we will be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they will (Acts 15:11).

Does “God shows no partiality” mean church leaders deserve no respect? No. Paul honours these men; he calls them pillars and accepts their handshake gladly, and elsewhere he tells churches to esteem their leaders very highly in love because of their work (1 Thessalonians 5:12–13). What he refuses is to let their status decide what is true. Respect your pastor, pray for him, follow his teaching gladly when it is faithful to Scripture. But never believe something because of who said it, and never dismiss something because of who said it. The question is always whether it is the gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: and when James and Cephas and John, who seemed to be pillars, perceived the grace that was given to me, they gave the right hand of fellowship to Barnabas and me, that we should go to the Gentiles and they to the circumcised. Only, they asked us to remember the poor, the very thing I was eager to do.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Perceived the grace. The order of this sentence is the point. First they saw the grace; then they extended the hand. The handshake did not confer anything. It acknowledged something God had already done.

The church perceives; it does not manufacture. That is how the church recognises anything. Ordination does not manufacture a minister and a handshake does not manufacture a brother. Where grace is evidently at work, the faithful response is to acknowledge it, and where it is not, no ceremony will supply it.

Pillars. The picture is architectural: the men on whom the weight rests, the leaders of the Jerusalem church (Revelation 3:12). James here is not the apostle John’s brother, who had already been executed by Herod (Acts 12:2), but James the Lord’s brother. Then Peter, and John the son of Zebedee.

The right hand of fellowship. An ancient pledge of good faith: between us this is settled. The word behind fellowship is koinōnia, partnership: a joint stake in the same enterprise, not merely a truce.

A company of forgiven enemies. Consider what happened in that room. The apostle who had been hunting Christians and the apostle who had denied Christ in a courtyard put their hands together over a gospel neither of them had earned. Each owed everything to the same person: Peter restored by the risen Lord after his denials, Paul stopped by him on the way to Damascus. Paul uses this same word for what every believer is called into: the fellowship of God’s Son (1 Corinthians 1:9). Nobody in it had a record worth defending. That is what made it possible.

To the Gentiles. A division of labour, not a division of message, and it was never watertight, since Peter opened the Gentile door in the first place (Acts 10) and Paul went to the synagogue first in almost every town he entered.

Remember the poor. After a meeting about circumcision, the law, and the terms of salvation, the single thing Jerusalem asks is that the poor believers there not be forgotten. Years of Paul’s life went into the collection for the believers in Judea (Romans 15:25–27; 2 Corinthians 8–9).

Not an addition. Paul has just refused to add one item to the gospel, and immediately accepts an obligation to the poor without a murmur, because it is not an addition. Nothing has been placed between a sinner and God. What has been named is what grace does once it has arrived. A church that has understood justification by faith alone and has no interest in the hungry has not understood it (James 2:15–17; 1 John 3:17). It is the gospel of the Lord who became poor for our sake (2 Corinthians 8:9), and he did not wait for us to be worth helping.

Who are the poor I am to remember, and how? First, needy believers, the household of faith, as Paul will say in 6:10; then everyone in need as we have opportunity. Start near: the widow in your congregation, the family where a job has been lost, the asylum seeker who has turned up on Sunday, the student who cannot afford the trip. Give regularly and deliberately, not only when moved. Give through your church so that help is wise and sustained. Give time and friendship as well as money, because the poor are usually lonely as well as short. And remember the persecuted and impoverished church abroad. Do it gladly; Paul was eager, not pressured.

In everyday life. When you see grace at work in another Christian, especially one from a different background, church or tradition, perceive it and say so: give him the right hand, in words if not in a handshake.
verseByVerse.note: Pillars held up a building; these three were the leaders of the Jerusalem church. The poor were the believers in Judea.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At Antioch Peter had been eating freely with Gentile believers, but when men came from James he drew back for fear of the circumcision party, and the other Jewish believers, even Barnabas, followed. Paul saw that they were not walking in step with the truth of the gospel, and he challenged Peter in front of them all.
verseByVerse.theology:
The gospel governs the feet, not only the confession

Peter’s failure was not in his doctrine. He had defended the acceptance of Gentiles and won the argument (Acts 11). What verse 14 exposes is a gap between a belief truly held and a life not walking in line with it, which is what Paul means by hypocrisy here, not the pretence of a faith one does not have. The gospel must govern table habits and the pull of social pressure, not only statements of faith.

Scripture also records, without embarrassment, an apostle publicly corrected by another apostle on a matter of the gospel: whatever authority the Jerusalem leaders had, it was never authority over the message.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Peter’s withdrawal at Antioch came from fear, not conviction: verse 12 says he feared the circumcision party. It is the snare Paul named at 1:10, the wish to please people, and it carried the other Jewish believers and Barnabas with it (v. 13).

Now: Two things here reach a reader directly: the room in which he is a slightly different Christian, and the question of when a leader should be corrected in public. Paul’s case met every condition at once (public conduct, the gospel at stake, others carried away, a rebuke spoken to Peter’s face), and the friendship survived it (2 Peter 3:15–16).

verseByVerse.quote: But when Cephas came to Antioch, I opposed him to his face, because he stood condemned. For before certain men came from James, he was eating with the Gentiles; but when they came he drew back and separated himself, fearing the circumcision party.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I opposed him to his face. The scene changes to Antioch in Syria, the first great Gentile church (Acts 11:19–26), and the man just called a pillar is about to be called wrong. Face to face, and in front of everybody (v. 14), not behind his back.

In the flow. Verses 1–10 showed the Jerusalem leaders agreeing with Paul; verses 11–14 show that agreement tested, and failing in the most unlikely man. Paul did not get his gospel from Peter, because he could correct Peter by it.

Because he stood condemned. A courtroom word: not that Paul condemned him, but that he stood already condemned, by the contradiction between what he believed and what he was doing. Paul did not pass the sentence. He read it out.

Eating with the Gentiles. A shared table in that world meant shared life, mutual acceptance, family, and in the church it may well have included the Lord’s Supper. For a Jew to sit down to a Gentile meal was to declare that the wall had come down, and Peter had been doing it, meal after meal.

He drew back. Both verbs are gradual; the tense pictures him withdrawing bit by bit. He drew back, a word used of troops pulling back from a position. He separated himself, aphorizō, the word from which the name Pharisee may come. Nobody announced a policy. He simply began sitting elsewhere, and everyone knew what it meant.

Fearing the circumcision party. It was not conviction. Peter had not changed his mind about anything; he changed his seat because of who was watching. It is the fear of man (Proverbs 29:25), the same weakness that once led Peter to deny Jesus.

How was this possible? This is the man who had the vision on the rooftop and heard the voice saying, what God has made clean, do not call common; who walked into Cornelius’s house and watched the Spirit fall on Gentiles; who defended the whole thing to the Jerusalem church and won the argument (Acts 10–11). He was not under-informed. He was the leading expert in the room on precisely this point. Which is the lesson, and it is a hard one. Knowing a truth and having settled it publicly does not immunise a man against abandoning it when the wrong people walk in. The mechanism had not changed in nearly twenty years: not doubt, not argument, but the sudden weight of a watching face. Fear of man is not a beginner’s sin that maturity leaves behind.

A table the Lord had opened. Peter was not only stepping back from his own vision. He was stepping back from his Lord. Mark, whose Gospel the early church connected with Peter’s preaching, records Jesus teaching that what goes into a person from outside cannot defile him: thus he declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19). So when Peter moved his plate away from Gentile believers, he was putting back a wall that Christ himself had taken down. The question was whether Christ’s cleansing was enough to make a Gentile fit company.

Certain men from James. The phrase has been used to blame James, and probably should not be. The Jerusalem church later wrote to Antioch about men who had gone out from them, although we gave them no instructions (Acts 15:24). They may have claimed James’s authority without his approval. What is certain is the effect: their arrival was enough.

Where Christians differ: Peter’s authority. The Roman Catholic Church teaches that Peter was the head of the apostles and the first pope, with a primacy passed to his successors, including infallibility in defining doctrine. Roman Catholic teaching limits that infallibility to formal definitions, not conduct; but the point here is wider. This commentary’s view: Peter was a great apostle and leader. But here Paul publicly rebukes him for a serious error affecting the gospel. Peter was neither infallible in practice nor above correction by another apostle. The gospel judges Peter, not Peter the gospel, and that is true of every church leader since. The authority of the church rests on the apostolic teaching recorded in Scripture, not on the succession of one office (Ephesians 2:20).

Is it wrong to adapt to the people I am with? Not in itself. Paul said he became as a Jew to Jews and as one outside the law to those outside the law, so that he might win them (1 Corinthians 9:20–22). Adapting your customs, your food, your manner, for the sake of love and the gospel is Christlike. What Peter did was different in two ways. His motive was fear, not love. And his action told fellow believers that they were not fully acceptable unless they changed. The question to ask is: am I adapting to serve these people, or to protect myself? And does my adapting tell any brother or sister in Christ that they are second-class?

For worship. There is one man in all of Scripture who never once changed his table because of who was watching. He ate with tax collectors in front of the Pharisees and with Pharisees in front of the tax collectors, because he lived before the face of his Father. And when Peter failed again, that same Lord did not cast him off; he sent him a brother to tell him the truth. The Lord who restored Peter by a charcoal fire restored him again at Antioch, and he is patient still with every one of us who has changed seats.
verseByVerse.note: Antioch in Syria was the first great Gentile church. Eating together was the test: strict Jews would not share a table with Gentiles.

verseByVerse.quote: And the rest of the Jews acted hypocritically along with him, so that even Barnabas was led astray by their hypocrisy. But when I saw that their conduct was not in step with the truth of the gospel, I said to Cephas before them all, “If you, though a Jew, live like a Gentile and not like a Jew, how can you force the Gentiles to live like Jews?”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Acted hypocritically. The damage spreads in a single verse. The word is synypokrinomai, to play the actor together, from the theatre. Paul is not accusing these men of secret unbelief. They were acting: behaving in a way their convictions did not support because the audience had changed.

Even Barnabas. The son of encouragement (Acts 4:36), who had stood up for Paul when the Jerusalem church was afraid of him, fetched him from Tarsus, and travelled the first missionary journey at his side defending Gentile believers (Acts 11:22–26; 13–14). If one man in Antioch could be counted on, it was Barnabas, and he was carried away too. That detail shows how strong the current was. Nobody has recorded a single word of persuasion in this passage. It took a few significant people sitting at a different table, and the whole church moved.

Not in step. The verb is orthopodeō, apparently to walk straight (orthos, straight, and pous, foot). Paul does not say their doctrine was wrong; every man at those tables would have signed the same confession. Their feet were wrong. The gospel is something to be walked in, and it can be denied by a seating plan as effectively as by a sermon. In Christ Jesus there is neither Jew nor Greek (3:28). His death had made the Gentile believer clean, and his Spirit had made him a son. To leave that man eating alone was to say, without a word, that Christ had not been quite enough to bring him in. The table at Antioch was always meant to be a picture of something bigger: the marriage supper of the Lamb, where people from every tribe and language and nation will sit down together, and no one will ask anyone else to become something first. The one who spreads that table paid for every seat, and he does not move anyone to a lower one.

I said to Cephas before them all. Public sin with public effect required public correction (1 Timothy 5:20). Peter had been living freely, not keeping the Jewish food laws, so he plainly did not believe they still bound him. Yet by withdrawing he was telling Gentile believers that to have full fellowship with us, you must become Jews. That denied the gospel. And pressure does not have to be spoken to be applied.

Should a Christian confront leaders publicly? Usually not, and Scripture is careful about it. The Lord’s instruction for sin between brothers is to go privately first, and only widen the circle if there is no repentance (Matthew 18:15–17). Paul himself tells Timothy not to admit a charge against an elder except on the evidence of two or three witnesses. But the same passage adds the other half: as for those who persist in sin, rebuke them in the presence of all (1 Timothy 5:19–20). Four things line up here, and they rarely all line up. The conduct was public, so a private word could not undo it. The matter was the gospel itself, not a preference or a personality. Others were already being swept away, Barnabas among them. And Paul said it to his face, in the room, at cost to himself, not about him, afterwards, to somebody else. That last one is the test most often failed. A great deal of what calls itself courage in the church is a message sent to a third party, or a post written about a man who will never be in the room. Paul’s way is harder and kinder: he said it where Peter could answer.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul relished confronting Peter, and it did not end the friendship. Years later Peter, writing his last letter, mentioned our beloved brother Paul, and the things in his letters that are hard to understand (2 Peter 3:15–16). Two men who both knew what it was to be forgiven could survive being told the truth.

What are the separate tables today? Rarely food laws. More often it is the church where the professionals sit together and the cleaners sit together, the congregation that welcomes newcomers who look like the existing members, the fellowship that is warm to the respectable and cool to the man who has come out of prison or the woman with a messy history. Wherever believers make others feel that full acceptance requires them to become like us, culturally, socially, in class or race, the Antioch problem is back. The gospel says that whoever is in Christ belongs at the table, and the table is the Lord’s, not ours.

What if I am the one who has been rebuked? Do what Peter evidently did: listen, and do not defend yourself first. Ask whether the rebuke is true, even if it was delivered badly. If it is, own it plainly before God and before those affected, without excuses, and change course. Faithful are the wounds of a friend (Proverbs 27:6). A believer who can receive correction is a believer who is resting on Christ’s righteousness rather than his own, because he has nothing to protect.
verseByVerse.note: Barnabas had been Paul’s partner on the first journey.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul now states the gospel plainly. Even Jews by birth are justified only through faith in Christ. That does not make Christ a promoter of sin; going back to the law as the way to God is what makes a person a transgressor. Through the law Paul died to the law so that he might live to God, crucified with Christ and now living by faith in the Son of God who loved him. To make righteousness come by the law would mean Christ died for nothing.
verseByVerse.theology:
The article by which the church stands or falls

Protestant theology came to call justification by faith the article by which the church stands or falls, a summary of Luther’s own conviction, and vv. 15–21 are the classic passage for it. Justification is a declaration of our standing before God, not an infusion of goodness, though a changed life always follows. It is by grace alone, through faith alone, in Christ alone, and these stand or fall together.

Either way the phrase in v. 16 is read (faith in Christ, or his faithfulness, discussed at that verse), faith is not a work that earns the verdict but the empty hand that receives it.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Jewish believers had every religious advantage and still came the same way as the Gentiles they were now refusing to eat with (v. 15). And verse 18 lands directly on Antioch, where stones were going back into a wall that had been pulled down.

Now: The person who comes to faith from a respectable life and the person who comes from obvious wreckage stand on the same ground, with the same righteousness, which is Christ’s. The respectability counts for as little in the verdict as the wreckage.

verseByVerse.quote: We ourselves are Jews by birth and not Gentile sinners; yet we know that a person is not justified by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ, so we also have believed in Christ Jesus, in order to be justified by faith in Christ and not by works of the law, because by works of the law no one will be justified.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The centre of the letter. Here is the letter’s own centre of gravity: Paul says it three times inside one verse, because everything else stands on it. He is probably still addressing Peter, or expanding on what he said to him, and the words become a statement of the gospel for every reader.

In the flow. Every later argument in Galatians is this verse unfolded: Abraham (3:6), the curse Christ bore (3:13), the law as guardian (3:24), sons not slaves (4:7), and the life of the Spirit (chapters 5 and 6).

Jews by birth. Gentiles were regarded as sinners because they were outside the law, and Paul may be quoting the Jewish attitude. Take the most advantaged religious people on earth: the covenant, the Scriptures, the temple, a lifetime of training. And they too believed in Christ Jesus. If the law could have justified anybody, it would have justified them. The irreligious man is not too far gone to come by faith, and the religious man is not too good to need to.

Not justified. The word to get clear is justified (dikaioō), a courtroom word. To justify is not to make someone good; it is to declare someone to be in the right: acquitted, accepted. A judge who justifies a defendant does not improve him. He pronounces a verdict, and the man walks out of the court with a status he did not have when he walked in.

A verdict, not a treatment. Many people instinctively think of salvation in medical terms: God as a physician gradually curing us, with heaven at the end if the treatment works. Justification is the judge’s verdict, given whole, in a moment, at the beginning rather than the end. God does also heal the sinner he acquits, for a lifetime. But he does not acquit him because the healing is going well.

What “justified” means, and what it does not. It is more than not guilty: it is accepted as righteous, the opposite of being condemned (Romans 8:33–34). It does not mean God pretends we are good when we are not. He declares us righteous because the righteousness of Christ is counted to us (Romans 4:5–6; 2 Corinthians 5:21; Philippians 3:9). Our sins were counted to him at the cross; his obedience is counted to us. The Judge of all the earth has a verdict to give on every human life, and he has given it in advance for everyone who trusts his Son: righteous. Not because he was deceived about us, nor because he lowered his standard, but because his own Son met the standard in our place and bore the sentence we had earned (Romans 3:26). There is no higher court and no appeal against it, and the one who sits on the bench is our Father.

By works of the law. Works of the law means, first, deeds done in obedience to the law of Moses, and particularly the visible markers that separated Jew from Gentile: circumcision, the food rules, the holy days, the exact issues at Antioch. But Paul’s conclusion is wider than the markers, and the last clause shows it.

No one will be justified. From Psalm 143:2: enter not into judgment with your servant, for no one living is righteous before you. Not the Gentile without the law, and not the Pharisee who kept it better than his peers, because no one keeps it perfectly (3:10; Romans 3:20). Even David begs not to be brought into court. The reason is not that the law is a bad thing; it is holy. The reason is that the law is a mirror, and a mirror has never washed a face.

But through faith in Jesus Christ. Faith receives Christ and his righteousness, and it justifies not because it is strong but because he is. A weak faith in a strong Saviour is as fully justified as a strong faith, because the righteousness it receives is his, not its own.

Where Christians differ: what are works of the law? Some scholars of the New Perspective on Paul, such as E. P. Sanders, James Dunn and N. T. Wright, argue that works of the law mean mainly the boundary markers that separated Jews from Gentiles: circumcision, food laws and the Sabbath. So justification is mainly about who belongs to God’s people, not how a sinner is made right with God. This commentary’s view: works of the law certainly include those boundary markers, as the Antioch incident shows; the New Perspective is right about the occasion. But Paul’s argument goes deeper: no one is justified by the law because no one keeps the whole law (3:10–12; 5:3). Justification is God’s legal declaration that a sinner is righteous, on the ground of Christ’s righteousness, received by faith alone (Romans 4:4–8). It certainly has consequences for who belongs together at the table. But it is first about how a guilty person can stand before a holy God (the Westminster Confession 11.1; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 11.1).

Where Christians differ: declared righteous or made righteous? The Roman Catholic Church teaches (Council of Trent, 1547) that justification is a process in which God pours grace into the soul and makes the person inwardly righteous; it grows through the sacraments and good works, can be lost by mortal sin, and is restored by penance. On that view a person is accepted by God as far as he has been made righteous. The Reformers taught that justification is God’s once-for-all legal verdict, received by faith alone, on the ground of Christ’s righteousness alone, and that sanctification, the lifelong work of making us holy, always follows it but is distinct from it. This commentary’s view: the Reformation view is right. Paul’s word is a law-court word: God justifies the ungodly (Romans 4:5), which cannot mean he finds them already godly. Justification is complete the moment a person believes (Romans 5:1; 8:1), and so it cannot grow or be lost. Works matter greatly, but as the fruit of justification, not its ground (Ephesians 2:8–10; Westminster 11.1–2; 1689 11.1–2). If our acceptance depended on how far we had been made righteous, no one could ever be sure of it, and the cross would be only a beginning; but Christ died for no purpose if righteousness comes by anything we do (v. 21).

Where Christians differ: faith in Christ, or the faithfulness of Christ? The Greek phrase pistis Christou, used twice in this verse, can be read as faith in Christ (our trust in him) or as the faith or faithfulness of Christ (his own faithful obedience to the Father, even to the cross). Some recent scholars prefer the second, and say Paul means we are justified by Christ’s faithfulness. This commentary’s view: faith in Christ is the better reading. In this very verse Paul adds, “we also have believed in Christ Jesus,” which shows plainly that our believing is in view. Both truths are biblical: we are saved by Christ’s faithful obedience (Romans 5:19), and we receive it by trusting him. But here Paul’s point is that the way to receive righteousness is believing, not doing. Either way the doing is his; the receiving is ours.

Do Paul and James contradict each other? James says a person is justified by works and not by faith alone (James 2:24). No, they do not contradict. Paul asks how a guilty sinner is declared righteous before God, and answers: by faith, apart from works. James asks how a claim to faith is shown to be real, and answers that faith without works is dead (James 2:17). Paul opposes works as the ground of acceptance; James opposes a faith that is only words. Paul agrees that true faith works: faith working through love (5:6). We are justified by faith alone, but the faith that justifies is never alone.

What it does not mean. It does not mean faith is a work that earns justification. Faith is the empty hand that receives Christ: not what we are justified for, but how we receive the one for whose sake we are justified.

If I am justified, why do I still feel guilty? Because feelings lag behind facts, and because you still sin, and a tender conscience notices. Real conviction of a specific sin is the Spirit’s kindness, calling you to confess it and be cleansed (1 John 1:9). But a general cloud of condemnation that hangs over you after you have confessed is not from God, because there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1). When that cloud comes, do not argue with it from your record. Argue from his. Say to your conscience: the verdict was given at the cross, on the ground of what Christ did, and it does not move with my moods.

In everyday life. The verdict on you is not waiting on Friday’s performance (Romans 3:20–24). Begin each day by remembering it, and then obey from it, not towards it.

parallels.desc: no one living is righteous before you

verseByVerse.quote: But if, in our endeavor to be justified in Christ, we too were found to be sinners, is Christ then a servant of sin? Certainly not!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Found to be sinners. Paul stops to answer the objection this doctrine has always attracted. Jewish believers who came to Christ stopped keeping the food laws and started eating with Gentiles. By the law’s reckoning they became sinners in the process, sinners like the Gentiles.

Is Christ then a servant of sin? So Christ has taken observant men and made them law-breakers. Is he then a servant of sin: not merely tolerating it but actively promoting it, running errands for it? Does Christ encourage sin by freeing people from the law? It was the common objection to justification by faith (Romans 6:1).

Certainly not! The Greek is mē genoito, the phrase Paul reaches for when a suggestion is not to be weighed but thrown out of the room: may it never be. Justification by faith leads to holiness, not licence (5:13–25).

An insult to a friend. To call Christ a servant of sin is to slander the one who took the whole weight of sin into his own body and went into the dark under it. Paul reacts the way anyone reacts when someone slanders a friend who is not there to answer. Christ is not the servant of sin. He is its executioner. He came to destroy the works of the devil (1 John 3:8), and he did it by letting sin do its worst to him, and rising out from under it.

A strange compliment. Paul faced the same objection in Romans: are we to continue in sin that grace may abound? (Romans 6:1). If a preacher has never once been accused of making grace too free, it is worth asking whether he has actually preached it.

Grace changes the person, not only the paperwork. Paul’s answer is not a retreat into rule-keeping. Grace does not leave a sinner where it found him and merely change his paperwork. It puts him to death and raises him, which is why Paul’s answer ends at a cross, I have been crucified with Christ (2:20), rather than at a code of conduct.

Then why do Christians still sin, and does that make grace a failure? Christians still sin because sanctification, God’s work of making a justified person holy, is lifelong; the old desires are defeated but not yet removed, and the war goes on until we see Christ (5:17; 1 John 3:2). That is not grace failing. It is grace still at work. The difference between a Christian and an unbeliever is not that one sins and the other does not, but that the Christian has a new master, hates his sin, fights it, confesses it, and is slowly changed. If you are using grace as an excuse to keep a sin you love, do not comfort yourself with this verse; it says certainly not. If you are grieving your sin and running to Christ with it, grace has not failed you. It has hold of you.

In everyday life. When you notice yourself thinking, it does not matter, I am forgiven anyway, stop and look at who forgave you and what it cost him. Then ask him for strength to obey in the very thing you were about to excuse; his Spirit lives in you for exactly this (5:16).

verseByVerse.quote: For if I rebuild what I tore down, I prove myself to be a transgressor. For through the law I died to the law, so that I might live to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If I rebuild what I tore down. Imagine a man who has pulled down a building he judged unsound, and then goes back and puts every stone up again. He has publicly declared that the demolition was the crime.

What Paul tore down. It was the whole structure of acceptance by performance: the life of chapter 1, advancing beyond his peers, building a righteousness of his own. And this is the answer to the man who says grace makes sinners: the transgression is not in leaving the law behind as a way of righteousness but in going back to it. And there is a direct application to Antioch: Peter had been living in the freedom of the gospel and had begun laying stones back in place, one meal at a time.

Through the law I died to the law. Through the law: not by escaping it; the law itself was the instrument of his death to the law. In Christ, who bore the law’s curse, Paul died to the law’s claims (Romans 7:4).

How can the law make me die to the law? This is one of Paul’s most compressed sentences, so it helps to take it in steps. First, the law demands perfect obedience and pronounces death on every transgressor (3:10). Second, Paul was a transgressor, so the law’s sentence on him was death. Third, Christ took that sentence for him: he was born under the law (4:4) and died under its curse in his people’s place (3:13). Fourth, Paul was united to Christ by faith, so when Christ died, Paul died with him (v. 20). So the law did carry out its sentence on Paul: in Christ, he died. And a dead man is free from the law’s claim; the law has nothing more to say to someone whose sentence has been fully carried out (Romans 7:1–4, where Paul uses the picture of a marriage ended by death). That is why it was through the law: the law itself demanded the death by which he was set free from it. There is a second strand too: the law, by exposing his sin, drove him to stop trusting it and to flee to Christ (3:24; Romans 7:9–10).

How the law kills. The law came to a man doing rather well and kept pressing until it had him. Paul tells us which commandment found him out: you shall not covet, a law about the desire and not only the deed (Romans 7:7–11). Jesus read the whole law the same way: not just murder, but anger (Matthew 5:21–28). So the law did precisely what God gave it to do. It killed him, so that he could stop trying to live by it.

The last kindness of a schoolmaster. Nobody comes to Christ while his own account still looks solvent. The ache underneath religious striving, the sense that it is never enough, that the standard keeps moving, is not a malfunction. It is the law doing its work, the last kindness of a guardian who intends to hand the pupil over to someone else (3:24).

What it does not mean. Dying to the law does not mean becoming lawless. Paul died to the law as a way of being right with God, and as a master that condemns him; he did not die to God’s will. He is now under the law of Christ (1 Corinthians 9:21), and the Spirit leads him to fulfil the law’s righteous requirement in love (5:14; Romans 8:4).

So that I might live to God. The demolition was not to leave a man in the rubble, but to get him out from under a life spent proving himself, and into a life lived toward God. The law could not make him live for God; Christ does. The law’s sentence on us was death, and God did not cancel the sentence. He carried it out, on his Son, and counted us as having died in him. Christ honoured every demand of the law, in his life and in his death, so that sinners could be set free from it without the law being dishonoured at all.

Do Christians still need to keep the Ten Commandments? Not as a way of being accepted by God, and not under the law’s curse. But the moral will of God that the commandments express has not changed, because it flows from God’s own character. Jesus deepened the commandments rather than abolishing them (Matthew 5:17–48), and the apostles repeat their substance to Christians (Romans 13:8–10; Ephesians 6:1–3). So the believer reads the moral law as the shape of a life of love, the path his Father has marked out for children who are already his. Christians differ on how the fourth commandment applies today, and on how much of the old covenant law carries over; but no Christian is free to steal, lie, covet or commit adultery. The ceremonial laws that pointed to Christ, such as circumcision and the food laws, are fulfilled in him and no longer bind.

In everyday life. Notice the stones you keep laying back in place: the private rules by which you measure whether God is pleased with you this week. Put them down, and live towards God today, gladly, as a man let out of prison lives towards the friend who paid his fine.

verseByVerse.quote: I have been crucified with Christ. It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me. And the life I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I have been crucified with Christ. The summit of the letter begins with a funeral. The tense is the perfect, a thing done in the past whose results stand permanently in the present. Not I try to crucify myself. It happened. When Christ died, Paul died, because Christ died as a representative, the way Adam acted for a race, so that what happened to him happened to everyone joined to him. His old self, under the law’s condemnation, died (Romans 6:6).

Crucified. Paul could have said he died with Christ; he says he was crucified, which is what you do to a criminal in public. The old self, the one with the record and the rising reputation in Judaism, did not retire honourably. It was executed.

Christ who lives in me. This does not mean Paul has been erased, personality and all. The next clause says the life I now live: there is plainly still an I doing the living. And the man who wrote this letter is unmistakably himself on every page, angry, tender and affectionate by turns. Grace killed what he was living for and left him more himself than before. What died was the self that had to be somebody. Christ now lives in Paul by his Spirit (Romans 8:9–10; Colossians 1:27), turning his will towards God and growing in him love, joy, peace and patience (5:22–23). This is real power: the Spirit who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in him (Romans 8:11).

In the flesh. Here “the flesh” means ordinary bodily, earthly life, not the sinful nature of 5:16–24: a stomach, a temper and a tentmaking business. This is Monday he is describing.

By faith in the Son of God. Faith is not just the door into the Christian life; it is the way of living it. Paul does not say he lives by a sensation of Christ’s presence, but by trusting a person he cannot see, on days when nothing is felt at all. The indwelling is a fact about where Christ is, not a report on how the believer is doing.

Who loved me and gave himself for me. And then Paul’s grammar goes suddenly singular. A chapter of councils, delegations and mission fields ends with one man saying me twice. The cross is wide enough for the world and narrow enough to have a single name written on it. This is the same Paul who had been dragging women out of houses to prison (Acts 8:3). Luther urged his readers to read the words me and for me with great vehemence, and to take them as spoken of themselves.

What “crucified with Christ” does not mean. It is not a special experience that advanced Christians reach, nor a feeling to be worked up, nor a command (crucify yourself!). It is true of every believer by union with Christ (Romans 6:3–6). It does not mean Paul no longer struggles with sin (5:17). It means Christ has replaced self as the centre, the source of his life, and the object of his trust.

How do I live by faith on an ordinary day? By turning, again and again, from yourself to Christ. In the morning, before the list, remind yourself who you are in him: crucified with him, raised with him, loved by him. When temptation comes, say no on the strength of the fact that the old self who loved that sin was put to death. When you fail, go straight back to the one who loved you and gave himself for you, without waiting to feel better first. When you have to do something hard, ask him for the strength, and expect him to give it, because he lives in you. None of this needs a feeling. It needs only the habit of looking at him.

Can I say “for me” if I am not sure I am chosen? Yes. You do not need to look into God’s secret decree before you come to Christ; no one can. The gospel invites every sinner who hears it to trust Christ, and promises that whoever comes to him will never be cast out (John 6:37). Christ did die for his people in particular, and his death secured their salvation; but you discover that you are one of them not by peering into heaven but by coming to him. This is what Reformed Christians call definite or particular atonement: the belief that the cross was aimed at saving a particular people and actually accomplished it (John 10:11, 15; Ephesians 5:25). Many faithful Christians believe instead that Christ died for all in the same way; both gladly offer him to everyone, and neither asks you to settle the question before you come. If you trust Christ, you may say, without presumption, the Son of God loved me and gave himself for me. Paul’s me is the word of every believer.

For worship. The Son of God loved this particular man, with this particular record, while that record was still being written. And he did not send help; he gave himself, the only gift that costs the giver everything. He had the Father’s glory and set it down. He had legions and did not call them. He went to a public execution for people who were his enemies at the time, and he would not be talked out of it (Ephesians 5:2; 1 John 3:16). Eternity will not be long enough to get to the end of a love like that.

verseByVerse.quote: I do not nullify the grace of God, for if righteousness were through the law, then Christ died for no purpose.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I do not nullify the grace of God. “Nullify” is atheteō, to set aside, cancel: the term for treating a legal instrument as void. It is probably a charge thrown back where it came from. Paul is accused of treating God’s law as counting for nothing; he answers that it is the other side who are annulling something, and it is grace.

In the flow. This verse closes the defence that began in 1:11. Chapter 2 ends at the cross and chapter 3 begins there (3:1), because the cross is the one thing a gospel of law-keeping has no real need of.

If righteousness were through the law. Suppose there is any route to being right with God that runs through human obedience, even a small one, even as a supplement to grace. Then God had a way of saving people that did not require the death of his Son, and Calvary was not a rescue but an appalling waste. A Father would have watched his Son die in the dark for something that could have been managed another way.

For no purpose. The phrase is dōrean: for nothing, in vain. It is the same word Paul uses elsewhere for freely, as a gift (Romans 3:24), and the play is bitter. Either righteousness is given freely, or Christ died freely, for nothing.

Why Paul’s temper is not disproportionate. The Judaizers thought they were adding a little rigour to a message that had gone soft. But you cannot say Christ plus my performance without saying, underneath it, that his performance was insufficient, and the cross does not survive being called a supplement. Every addition to grace is an insult to the cross.

Does this mean sincere, good people of other religions are lost? Paul’s logic answers it. If righteousness could come through the law of Moses, given by God himself, then Christ died for nothing; how much more if it could come through any other path. The cross was necessary because there is no other way to God, and so salvation is through conscious faith in Christ alone (John 14:6; Acts 4:12). That is not arrogance on the Christian’s part; we are saved the same way, as beggars. Some Christians hope that God may save people through Christ without their ever knowing his name; Scripture gives no such promise to rest on, which is why the church sends missionaries, and every soul is safe in the hands of a Judge who will do what is right (Genesis 18:25). It is a reason for urgency and compassion. The people you love who trust in their own goodness need to hear about the one who died because their goodness could never be enough.

What if I keep feeling I must earn God’s favour? Most Christians do; the instinct to pay our way runs deep. Treat the feeling as a temptation, not a revelation. When it comes, answer it with this verse: if I could earn it, Christ died for nothing, and he did not die for nothing. Thank God out loud for what Christ has already done. Then go and obey, not to earn, but because you are loved; and when the obedience goes badly, do not let that reopen the question. The question was closed at the cross.

For worship. Had there been another way, the Son of God would have taken it; he asked in the garden, three times, and his sweat became like great drops of blood falling down to the ground (Matthew 26:39–44; Luke 22:44, a verse missing from some early manuscripts). There was not. He did not die for no purpose. He died for sinners, and it is finished, and there is nothing to add to it (Hebrews 10:11–14).

2.text: <sup>1</sup>Then after fourteen years I went up again to Jerusalem with Barnabas, taking Titus along with me.<sup>2</sup>I went up because of a revelation and set before them (though privately before those who seemed influential) the gospel that I proclaim among the Gentiles, in order to make sure I was not running or had not run in vain.<sup>3</sup>But even Titus, who was with me, was not forced to be circumcised, though he was a Greek.<sup>4</sup>Yet because of false brothers secretly brought in—who slipped in to spy out our freedom that we have in Christ Jesus, so that they might bring us into slavery—<sup>5</sup>to them we did not yield in submission even for a moment, so that the truth of the gospel might be preserved for you.<sup>6</sup>And from those who seemed to be influential (what they were makes no difference to me; God shows no partiality)—those, I say, who seemed influential added nothing to me.<sup>7</sup>On the contrary, when they saw that I had been entrusted with the gospel to the uncircumcised, just as Peter had been entrusted with the gospel to the circumcised<sup>8</sup>(for he who worked through Peter for his apostolic ministry to the circumcised worked also through me for mine to the Gentiles),<sup>9</sup>and when James and Cephas and John, who seemed to be pillars, perceived the grace that was given to me, they gave the right hand of fellowship to Barnabas and me, that we should go to the Gentiles and they to the circumcised.<sup>10</sup>Only, they asked us to remember the poor, the very thing I was eager to do.<sup>11</sup>But when Cephas came to Antioch, I opposed him to his face, because he stood condemned.<sup>12</sup>For before certain men came from James, he was eating with the Gentiles; but when they came he drew back and separated himself, fearing the circumcision party.<sup>13</sup>And the rest of the Jews acted hypocritically along with him, so that even Barnabas was led astray by their hypocrisy.<sup>14</sup>But when I saw that their conduct was not in step with the truth of the gospel, I said to Cephas before them all, “If you, though a Jew, live like a Gentile and not like a Jew, how can you force the Gentiles to live like Jews?”<sup>15</sup>We ourselves are Jews by birth and not Gentile sinners;<sup>16</sup>yet we know that a person is not justified by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ, so we also have believed in Christ Jesus, in order to be justified by faith in Christ and not by works of the law, because by works of the law no one will be justified.<sup>17</sup>But if, in our endeavor to be justified in Christ, we too were found to be sinners, is Christ then a servant of sin? Certainly not!<sup>18</sup>For if I rebuild what I tore down, I prove myself to be a transgressor.<sup>19</sup>For through the law I died to the law, so that I might live to God.<sup>20</sup>I have been crucified with Christ. It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me. And the life I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me.<sup>21</sup>I do not nullify the grace of God, for if righteousness were through the law, then Christ died for no purpose.

3.title: The Promise and the Law: Abraham, Faith, and the Curse
3.overview:
Chapter 3 is the heart of Paul’s argument in Galatians: God has always justified people by faith, not by the law. Paul argues first from the Galatians’ own experience: they received the Spirit by hearing with faith, not by keeping the law. He argues from Abraham, who believed God and was counted righteous, so that all who believe are his children.

He argues from the law itself, which curses everyone who fails to keep it, and then comes to the centre of the chapter: Christ redeemed us from that curse by becoming a curse for us (v. 13), so that the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles. The law came centuries after the promise and cannot cancel it; it was added for a time, to expose sin and to guard God’s people until Christ came. Now all who believe are sons of God, clothed with Christ, one in him, and heirs of the promise.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul turns from defending his apostleship to the Galatians themselves, and instead of an argument he asks about their own experience: did they receive the Spirit by keeping the law, or by hearing the gospel and believing it (v. 2)? To begin by the Spirit and then try to finish by human effort is folly (v. 3), and God is still at work among them on the same terms (v. 5).

The question runs straight on into Abraham (v. 6), who believed God and was counted righteous (Genesis 15:6). So it is those of faith who are Abraham’s sons (v. 7). Scripture announced the gospel to Abraham in advance, and every believer is blessed along with him (vv. 8–9).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Spirit Is Received by Faith

Paul’s appeal in vv. 2 and 5 is not to religious feeling but to a fact: how God gave them his Spirit. The Spirit unites us to Christ, and that union is received by faith alone; here Paul argues it from their own experience. If the Spirit came through hearing the gospel and not through works of the law, then law-keeping was never the channel, and no later addition can make it one.

Verse 3 shows that the Christian life does not have two stages, beginning by grace and advancing by performance. The same Spirit, received in the same way, is at work from first to last. And vv. 6–9 show that this is not new: Abraham was counted righteous by faith in Genesis 15, years before circumcision was given in Genesis 17. Justification by faith is how God has always dealt with sinners.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Judaizers were not asking the Galatians to abandon Christ. They were offering completion: take the mark, keep the calendar, and become full sons of Abraham. Paul makes them look at their own conversion, when they had nothing in their hands and God gave them his Spirit, and then he takes Abraham, the Judaizers’ own best example, and shows that he too was justified by faith.

Now: Few believers decide to be justified by works; the drift of v. 3 is quieter. Over the years our empty hands fill with good things, a habit of prayer, a place on the serving rota, a reputation, and our confidence slowly moves from Christ to them. The cure is in vv. 6–9: there is one way in, by faith in God’s promise, and the newest believer stands in it beside Abraham himself.

verseByVerse.quote: O foolish Galatians! Who has bewitched you? It was before your eyes that Jesus Christ was publicly portrayed as crucified.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Galatians 3 is Paul’s great argument that God has always justified people by faith, not by the law. He argues from the Galatians’ own experience of the Spirit (vv. 1–5), from Abraham (vv. 6–9), from the law’s curse that Christ bore (vv. 10–14), and from history: the promise came 430 years before the law and cannot be cancelled by it (vv. 15–18). The law was a guardian until Christ came (vv. 19–25); now all believers are God’s children, one in Christ, and heirs of the promise (vv. 26–29).

O foolish Galatians! The letter has already left out the usual thanksgiving; now it drops the courtesy altogether. The word is anoētoi: not stupid, but without understanding, people with a perfectly good brain who have stopped using it on the one subject where everything is at stake. Paul is not insulting their intelligence. He is saying they have stopped thinking about what they already know.

Who has bewitched you? The verb is baskainō, from the world of the evil eye: the malign look that was thought to wither a crop or sicken a child. Like the rest of the ancient world, Galatia was full of magic and superstition, and Paul’s readers knew the idea well. Paul does not believe in the evil eye, and he is not saying a spell was cast. He is reaching for the only category that fits what he is looking at: something has come over these people that ordinary argument does not explain. They have not been out-reasoned. They have been charmed. The false teaching worked like a spell, fascinating them away from the truth. And see where he puts the eye. Something has looked at them and done them harm, and yet what was set before their eyes was Jesus Christ crucified: two sights competing for the same congregation, and whichever one you keep looking at is the one that will shape you.

Publicly portrayed as crucified. The word is prographō: posted up, placarded, written large in a public place, like a governor’s ruling in the marketplace. That is Paul’s picture of his own preaching. He had not offered them a religious option. He had put up a public notice in their town, and it said: the Son of God was executed, and it was for you.

Before your eyes. None of the Galatians had been at Golgotha. Neither had Paul. But preaching that does its work does not merely inform people about the cross; it sets the cross in front of them until a listener in a Galatian market town could shut his eyes and see a man on a Roman beam dying in his place.

In the flow. Paul closed chapter 2 with if righteousness were through the law, then Christ died for no purpose (2:21). Verse 1 picks up the word crucified and turns it on the readers. Paul has told his own story; now he argues from theirs (3:1–5), and then from Abraham and the law (3:6–4:7).

How do I keep Christ crucified before my eyes? By putting yourself, deliberately and often, where the cross is set before you. Sit under preaching that is full of Christ and his cross, not only of advice. Come to the Lord’s Supper as the moment the Lord himself places his death in front of you (1 Corinthians 11:26). Read the Gospel accounts of the crucifixion slowly, more than once a year. Sing hymns that dwell on it. And when your conscience accuses you, train yourself to answer it by looking there first, not at your week. The cross does not fade because it changes. It fades because we stop looking.

For worship. God did not leave the Galatians to guess what he is like. He put it on a placard in their town, and the placard was his own Son, dying for enemies. Every spell that dazzles us away from it is a cheap light beside a crucified Lord, and the God who painted that picture before our eyes is still the one who opens them to see it.
verseByVerse.note: “Bewitched” pictures someone under a spell or the evil eye. “Publicly portrayed” uses the word for a public notice posted for all to read.

verseByVerse.quote: Let me ask you only this: Did you receive the Spirit by works of the law or by hearing with faith?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let me ask you only this. Paul has a whole letter of arguments ready, and before he uses any of them he asks one question. If they answer it honestly, the programme of the Judaizers, the teachers who insisted that Gentile believers be circumcised and keep the law of Moses, collapses.

Did you receive the Spirit by works of the law or by hearing with faith? The question is not about theology. It is about their own biography. He does not ask them what they believe now, because that is exactly what is in dispute and is being renegotiated weekly by men with impressive credentials. He asks them what happened to them then. That is not up for negotiation. It is a matter of record, and every one of them was there. And the Spirit is the decisive mark of belonging to God: anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him (Romans 8:9). So if they have the Spirit, they already belong.

What had happened. They knew perfectly well. Paul had walked into their towns, a travel-worn stranger, and announced a crucified and risen Jew as Lord of the world. Some believed, and God gave them himself: sins forgiven, a new hunger for God, love for people they had despised, and in some cases manifest power. Most of them were uncircumcised pagans who had never kept a Sabbath. They heard and believed, and God moved in. When God gave them his greatest gift, what was in their hands? Nothing. That is what God is like. He gives the best first, and he gives it to the empty-handed.

Hearing with faith. The phrase is akoē pisteōs, deliberately loose in Greek: the hearing that consists of faith, or the message that is heard and produces faith (Romans 10:17). Paul may well intend both: a message announced, and a heart that stops arguing and takes it. Even the taking is worked in us by the Spirit we are receiving.

A gift poured out by the risen Son. Why should hearing be enough? Because the Spirit was not a reward for listening well; he was the gift Christ had won. Christ became a curse for us so that we might receive the promised Spirit through faith (3:13–14), and the exalted Jesus received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit and poured him out (Acts 2:33). When the Galatians believed, the crucified and risen Lord was reaching down to them, sharing with the empty-handed what he had bought with his own blood.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the Spirit is received in a second experience after faith. They received him when they believed. There is no Christian without the Spirit, and no later stage at which a believer is given him for the first time.

How do I know I have received the Spirit? Not mainly by an unusual experience, though God may give one, but by what the Spirit does. He makes you trust Christ and call God Father (4:6; Romans 8:15–16). He makes Christ precious to you and the Bible alive to you. He gives you a new hatred of your sin and a new desire to please God. He grows love, joy, peace and the rest of his fruit, slowly and often unnoticed (5:22–23). He draws you to other believers. If you believe in Jesus and want to follow him, however weakly, the Spirit is already at work in you, because no one can say Jesus is Lord except by the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:3).

verseByVerse.quote: Are you so foolish? Having begun by the Spirit, are you now being perfected by the flesh? Did you suffer so many things in vain—if indeed it was in vain?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Are you so foolish? He asks it a second time, repeated in amazement, and this time he supplies the content of the folly. It is the sentence in this letter that ordinary Christians most need to hear: having begun by the Spirit, are you now being perfected by the flesh?

Begun and perfected. Begun is enarxamenoi and perfected is epiteleō, to complete, a matched pair that could be used of a sacrifice, begun and then brought to completion. Nobody in Galatia was proposing to abandon the Spirit. The false teachers said: faith is the start, but circumcision and law-keeping complete you. Paul says: you began with the Spirit of God himself at work in you, and you now propose to finish with a knife and a calendar.

What “flesh” means here. Not first lust or temper. Circumcision is a cut in literal flesh; the whole programme of the Judaizers lands on the body. So the flesh here is the realm of what a human being can do, mark, keep and show: religious achievement, visible, measurable, and yours. He is warning them off religion as self-effort.

How it happens to us. That is why this verse finds the reader who is doing nothing obviously wrong. Almost no Christian consciously decides to be justified by works. You come to Christ with empty hands and are received with joy. Then, over a few years, the hands slowly fill: a devotional habit, a serving rota, a reputation for reliability. None of it is bad; all of it may be the Spirit’s own fruit. But somewhere the ground of your confidence migrates from the finished work of Christ to the evidence of your progress, and you never notice the day it moved.

Perfected by a single offering. The Galatians were being offered completion. But by a single offering Christ has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified (Hebrews 10:14). The finishing the false teachers were selling had already been done on a cross, and the Spirit’s work is to make us, day by day, more like the one in whom we are already complete (Colossians 2:10). To reach for the flesh to finish what Christ has finished is to step back from him. We did not begin ourselves, and we will not finish ourselves, and that is not our humiliation. It is our rest.

Did you suffer so many things in vain? Then verse 4, and the tone changes. The verb paschō can mean suffer or simply experience. These people had paid for their faith. If, as many think, these churches included the towns of Acts 13–14, they had watched Paul stoned at Lystra and dragged out of the city for dead, and had taken their own share of it; Paul and Barnabas told them that through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God (Acts 14:2, 5, 19–22). Or Paul may mean the many blessings they had experienced. Either way, would they throw it away? He is asking whether all of that was for nothing.

If indeed it was in vain. And then he cannot finish the sentence. The great polemicist, mid-thunder, breaks off and will not pronounce them lost. He raises the possibility because they need to feel the danger, and then refuses to close his hand on it: furious with them and unable to bear losing them, and the two are not in tension (2 Corinthians 2:4; Galatians 4:19).

Where Christians differ: sanctification by effort? Some think justification is by faith, but sanctification is by our own effort and rule-keeping. Justification is the Judge’s verdict, given once and never revised; sanctification is the slow, real change by which the Spirit makes the justified person holy in practice. This commentary’s view: sanctification, like justification, is a work of the Spirit received by faith. It involves real effort and obedience (Philippians 2:12–13), but effort that depends on the Spirit, not on the flesh. Christians grow not by adding laws but by walking in the Spirit (5:16, 25).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians make no effort. It means the effort is Spirit-empowered faith, not self-reliant striving. Paul worked harder than anyone, and said in the same breath that it was not he, but the grace of God that was with him (1 Corinthians 15:10).

Then what do I actually do to grow? Use the means God has given, and use them as a needy child, not as a contractor. Read and hear his word, because the Spirit grows faith through it. Pray, because prayer is the confession that you cannot do it alone. Come to the Lord’s Supper and the fellowship of the church. Obey in the specific thing in front of you, asking for strength as you do it. Put sin to death by the Spirit (Romans 8:13): name it, flee it, cut off what feeds it. The difference between Spirit and flesh is not whether you make an effort, but what you lean on while you make it, and who gets the credit when it works.

In everyday life. Take your worst week: the one where you prayed nothing, snapped at everyone, and went to church because it was easier than explaining why you had not. Was God as pleased with you in Christ on that Sunday as on your best? The gospel answers yes, because on both Sundays you stood in Christ and not in your week. If something in you flinches at that answer, you have started finishing by the flesh what was begun by the Spirit, and the way back is the way you began: empty hands, and Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: Does he who supplies the Spirit to you and works miracles among you do so by works of the law, or by hearing with faith— just as Abraham “believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness”?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Does he who supplies the Spirit. The last of Paul’s questions moves from their past into their present: epichorēgōn, going on supplying, and works miracles among you is present too (Acts 14:3, 8–10). Whatever the Judaizers were saying about the Galatians’ deficient standing, the evidence was in the room while the argument was going on.

Supplies. Chorēgeō began in the theatre: the chorēgos was the wealthy citizen who paid for a chorus for the civic festival, at his own expense. By Paul’s day it simply meant to supply generously, and the old picture still suits it. God is not paying wages. He is underwriting the whole thing, because he chose to.

Do so by works of the law, or by hearing with faith? The same question as verse 2, and the answer is just as obvious: by faith. And the question does not end there. It runs straight on into verse 6: or by hearing with faith, just as Abraham believed God? Abraham is not a new topic. He is the last clause of the question, and the question is still a question when his name arrives.

Just as Abraham believed God. The quotation is Genesis 15:6, and Paul chose his ground with care. The false teachers appealed to Abraham, who was circumcised (Genesis 17). Paul appeals to Abraham too: before he was circumcised, he was counted righteous by faith (Romans 4:9–11). What happened in Galatia last year and what happened to Abraham are the same transaction: God spoke, a man believed him, and God credited it to him as righteousness.

Counted. The verb is a bookkeeping term: logizomai, to credit, to post an entry to an account. A childless old man under a sky full of stars took God at his word, and God wrote righteous in the ledger against his name: in full, that night, before circumcision, before Moriah. This is imputation.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Abraham’s faith was so admirable that God accepted it in place of the righteousness he lacked; that would put the ground of acceptance back inside the man. Faith is the empty hand that receives a righteousness belonging to another (Romans 4:3–5; Philippians 3:9).

Written for us also. The words it was counted to him were written for our sake also, who believe in him who raised Jesus from the dead (Romans 4:23–25). And the entry God writes is no fiction. He can write righteous against a sinner’s name without falsifying the books because the debt was posted to Christ: for our sake God made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God (2 Corinthians 5:21).

Where Christians differ: do miracles continue? They were the signs that accompanied the first preaching of the gospel in Galatia; Luke says that at Iconium the Lord bore witness to the word of his grace, granting signs and wonders to be done by their hands (Acts 14:3). Paul’s point is not that miracles are normal, but that God gave the Spirit and his powers to people who believed, not to people who kept the law. Continuationists, Christians who believe all the gifts of the apostolic age continue today, take the present tense here as evidence that such works go on in every church, and many of them are careful, faithful readers of Scripture. This commentary’s view: the more likely reading is that these signs belonged to the apostolic founding of the churches, the signs of a true apostle (2 Corinthians 12:12; Hebrews 2:3–4), and have ceased in that form; the Spirit himself, received by faith, remains, and God still answers prayer, heals and acts in his providence as he pleases. Brothers who see it differently are to be loved as brothers.

Do Paul and James disagree about Abraham? James quotes the same verse about Abraham and says he was justified by works when he offered up his son Isaac (James 2:21–23). Genesis 15 gives the verdict; Genesis 22, many years later, shows the faith was real. James speaks of faith shown to be real, Paul of faith counted before God. There is one Abraham, with one faith: the faith that received God’s verdict under the stars was the same faith that climbed Moriah.

Is my faith strong enough to be counted? It is not the strength of your faith that saves you, but the strength of the one you trust. Abraham’s faith was real but not flawless; between Genesis 15 and 22 he lied about his wife and tried to force the promise through Hagar. A drowning man who grabs a rope with a trembling hand is pulled out just as surely as one with a firm grip, because the rope does the saving. If you are trusting Christ, even with doubts and fears, God counts his righteousness to you in full. Ask him to strengthen your faith, as the father did who said, I believe; help my unbelief (Mark 9:24).

parallels.desc: he believed the LORD, and he counted it to him as righteousness

verseByVerse.quote: Know then that it is those of faith who are the sons of Abraham. And the Scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, preached the gospel beforehand to Abraham, saying, “In you shall all the nations be blessed.” So then, those who are of faith are blessed along with Abraham, the man of faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those of faith. In a first-century synagogue this conclusion is a bombshell. To be a son of Abraham was a legal identity, traced by blood and marked in the body, and a Gentile could enter only by becoming, in effect, a Jew. That was exactly the offer the Judaizers were making, and from the inside it looked generous.

Faith, not blood. Paul cuts the ground out from under it in a single sentence. Abraham’s true children are those who share his faith (Romans 4:11–12, 16). Jesus said the same to men who boasted of their descent: if you were Abraham’s children, you would be doing the works Abraham did (John 8:39). Descent alone never made a man Abraham’s son, or Ishmael and Esau would have been in.

The Scripture, foreseeing. Scripture foresaw and Scripture preached: what Scripture says, God says. God planned from the start to justify Gentiles who simply believed him, on the ground of what his Son would do (Romans 3:24–26). So whoever opens his Bible is not reading about a God who once spoke. He is being spoken to.

Preached the gospel beforehand to Abraham. The verb is proeuangelizomai: to announce the gospel in advance. Paul is claiming that when God said to a childless man from Mesopotamia, in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed (Genesis 12:3; 18:18), the gospel was already being announced: the actual gospel, the one Paul preaches, in its seed form. The gospel is not new; it is the fulfilment of God’s oldest promise. God had the Gentiles in view from the first time he spoke to Abraham.

The blessing has a name. How would a blessing reach every family on earth through one old man from Ur? Through his offspring. Peter quoted the same promise in the temple and told his hearers what it meant: God, having raised up his servant, sent him to you first, to bless you by turning every one of you from your wickedness (Acts 3:25–26). The blessing of Abraham is Jesus, crucified and raised, turning sinners back to God. The Galatians were not slipping into Abraham’s family by a side door.

Inside out. So the Judaizers had the story inside out. They treated Gentile inclusion as a late concession, to be granted only on Jewish terms. Paul says it was the point from the beginning: the family existed so that the blessing could reach everyone else.

Blessed along with Abraham. Not after him, at a lower grade. “Man of faith” translates pistos, believing. An Anatolian farmer who believed a travelling preacher stands in the same blessing as the patriarch, on the same footing.

Where Christians differ: Israel and the church. Dispensationalists, who read the Bible as a series of distinct eras, distinguish sharply between Israel and the church as two peoples with separate promises; many of them are devoted students of Scripture and warm friends of the Jewish people. This commentary’s view: Paul teaches that all who have faith, Jew or Gentile, are Abraham’s children and heirs of the promise (v. 29). There is one people of God across history, united by faith in the promised offspring, Christ. This is covenant theology’s insight: the one covenant of grace, administered in different ways, runs from Abraham to the church (the Westminster Confession 7.5–6). God has not cast off the Jewish people (Romans 11:1–2, 23), but they are saved within the one people, not alongside it.

Has the church then replaced Israel? Not in the sense the question usually means. Paul is not saying that the Jewish people have no future, but that Abraham’s true family has always been defined by faith, not blood.
