Gentiles who believe are added to that family; Jews who believe are its natural members; and unbelieving Jews can be grafted back in (Romans 11:23). The family was never replaced. It was enlarged to its intended size.

Do Jewish people today need to believe in Jesus? Yes, and to say so is not hostility but love. Paul, a Jew, wept over his own people and prayed that they would be saved (Romans 9:1–3; 10:1). Since Abraham’s true children are those of faith, and the promise was always to his offspring, Christ, there is no way to Abraham’s blessing that bypasses Abraham’s Seed. Christians should therefore love Jewish people, reject every form of antisemitism as a sin against the people from whom Christ came, and share the gospel with them gladly, humbly, and first (Romans 1:16).

For worship. Abraham has been a believer for four thousand years and is blessed by faith. You believed last March and are blessed by faith. There is one queue, and everybody in it got in the same way. And at its head stands the God who looked at a childless man under the stars and saw already the farmers of Galatia and the city-dwellers of every continent, and promised to bless them all through one Seed. He has been keeping that promise ever since, one believer at a time, and he will not stop until every nation has come in.

parallels.desc: in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–14 — The Righteous Shall Live by Faith
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Having made his case from Abraham, Paul now makes it from the law. Verse 10 says something unexpected: it is those who rely on the law, the serious and observant, who are under a curse, because the law demands that everyone do all that it requires (Deuteronomy 27:26), and no one does. Verses 11–12 set Habakkuk 2:4 beside the law’s own principle (Leviticus 18:5): the law’s offer of life was real, but no sinner can meet its terms.

Then v. 13, the summit of the chapter: Christ bought us out from the law’s curse by becoming a curse in our place. Verse 14 gives the purpose twice: so that the blessing of Abraham might reach the Gentiles, and so that we might receive the promised Spirit through faith, which brings the chapter back to the question of v. 2.
verseByVerse.theology:
Penal Substitution: The Curse Exchanged

Verse 13 says plainly that Christ bore in our place the penalty due to sinners, the law’s curse. The curse of vv. 10–12 fell on him, so that the blessing of v. 14 could come to those who had no claim to it. He did not only suffer with us; he suffered instead of us, bearing what was ours.

This does not mean the Father stopped loving the Son; Jesus said the opposite (John 10:17). The sentence was real, and so was the Father’s delight in his obedient Son in that same hour.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Judaizers offered the law as a supplement to faith. Verses 10–12 show that the law cannot be a supplement: as a way to God it accepts only perfect obedience, and no one has given it. Verse 13 names the one way out, and v. 14 explains how a Gentile with no covenant and no ancestry ends up with the Spirit of God.

Now: Some readers come to v. 10 already afraid that God is disappointed with them. Read it exactly. The curse falls on relying on the law, the very thing we use to cover our failure, and v. 13 says what became of it: the sentence was carried out, and not on you.

verseByVerse.quote: For all who rely on works of the law are under a curse; for it is written, “Cursed be everyone who does not abide by all things written in the Book of the Law, and do them.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
All who rely on works of the law. Paul has proved his case from Abraham; now he proves it from the law itself. He does not say that those who break the law are under a curse, but that those who rely on it are: the serious, observant ones, whose standing with God depends on law-keeping. The very people who thought the law was their shelter are standing under the one thing it guarantees for sinners. In Scripture a curse is not a spell or a run of bad luck but the opposite of God’s blessing: his sentence of judgment on the sinner, shutting him out from God’s favour (Deuteronomy 28:15; Matthew 25:41).

For it is written. The proof comes from the law’s own closing ceremony. In Deuteronomy 27 Israel is drawn up on two mountains, Ebal and Gerizim, with the covenant read aloud between them, and the last of twelve curses is the one Paul takes (Deuteronomy 27:26). At the end of every curse the whole nation answered Amen, ratifying the terms themselves.

Four words. Everyone: no exemptions. All things: the whole code, not a representative selection. Abide by: continuously, not in a good season. And do them: performance, not agreement; you can admire a command all your life without once obeying it. And the unstated premise of the argument is the one every reader knows: no one does all things.

A seamless garment. The law is not a pass mark but a seamless garment. Whoever keeps the whole law but fails in one point has become guilty of all of it (James 2:10). The law is not a list of separate regulations; it is the expression of one Person’s will. To break any of it is to have said no to him.

A road and a cliff. So the choice is not between an easier and a harder road to God, but between a road and a cliff. Whoever takes his stand on law-keeping has entered a system with only two verdicts, flawless obedience and curse, and he has already failed, which is why the religion of the law-keeper is so often anxious under its composure.

An altar on the mountain of curse. Moses told Israel to build an altar and offer burnt offerings on Mount Ebal, the very mountain where the tribes stood for the curse (Deuteronomy 27:4–7, 13). The sacrifice stood where the curse fell. Even on the day Israel said Amen to its own condemnation, God was pointing to an offering made in their place. The substance came when the one man who abode by all things, who could say I always do the things that are pleasing to him (John 8:29), went outside the city wall to take the law’s curse on himself. God did not pretend the terms were softer than they were, and he did not let the Amen of Ebal fall to the ground. The God who is too holy to cancel his own law is the God who loves sinners too much to leave them under it, and at the cross both are seen at once: his justice satisfied to the last letter, and his mercy flowing out through the very place it was satisfied.

Is God disappointed with me? This is where a certain kind of reader needs to be met honestly, because he is reading with his stomach tight. He is not one of the Judaizers, the teachers who made law-keeping a condition of acceptance. He has simply never been able to shake the sense that God is disappointed with him, and this verse looks like proof. If you are that reader, look at exactly what Paul says and what he does not. He does not say that people who sin are cursed with no way out; if he did, there would be no hope for anyone in this letter or out of it. He says that people who rely on law-keeping are cursed, because they have chosen a standard that will certainly convict them. The curse is not aimed at your failure so much as at the thing you were trying to use to cover your failure. And the curse did not stay where it was aimed: Christ redeemed us from it by becoming a curse for us (3:13).

Were the Israelites of the Old Testament all under this curse? Not those who trusted God. Old Testament believers were saved the same way Abraham was: by faith in God’s promise, looking forward to the Redeemer. The law itself provided sacrifices for sin, pointing to Christ, and the psalms are full of people who knew they could not stand on their own record and cast themselves on God’s mercy (Psalm 32:1–2; 130:3–4). What Paul condemns is relying on the law as the ground of acceptance, which the faithful in Israel never did. David, Isaiah and Daniel were not law-climbers; they were forgiven sinners who loved God’s law because they had first received his mercy.

In everyday life. Most of us stand on our record more often than we think: when you feel you deserve an answer to prayer because you have been faithful, or that God owes you a smoother life because of your service. Those small reliances on works lead to anxiety or resentment. You do not have to stand on your own record: Christ abode by all things written for you and took the curse you earned, so his obedience is counted as yours (Romans 5:19), and your imperfect service is accepted for his sake, not weighed as wages.

parallels.desc: cursed be anyone who does not confirm the words of this law

verseByVerse.quote: Now it is evident that no one is justified before God by the law, for “The righteous shall live by faith.” But the law is not of faith, rather “The one who does them shall live by them.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Evident. Two quotations from the Old Testament, and between them Paul settles how anyone has ever been right with God. Evident is dēlon, plain, already established. Before God: in his sight, by his standard.

For “The righteous shall live by faith.” The proof is Habakkuk 2:4 (also Romans 1:17; Hebrews 10:38). Habakkuk had been watching the Babylonians come, and the answer he was given was not an explanation but a way to survive: the righteous man will live, keep his footing when everything visible is against him, by faith. Luther took it from Paul; by his own account it was the verse that opened the gospel to him.

The one who does them. The quotation is Leviticus 18:5. As a way to righteousness, the law’s principle is: do and live. Faith’s principle is: believe and live. Since no one does them perfectly, life by the law is impossible.

How can Paul set Moses against Habakkuk? It can look as if Paul is pitting one Old Testament verse against another. He is not. In Leviticus 18:5, God speaks to a people he has already redeemed from Egypt: keep my laws and you will enjoy life with me in the land. For them, obedience was the grateful way of life of the redeemed, and the sacrifices were provided for their failures. But the false teachers were using the law as a ladder to climb up to God: do these things and you will be accepted. Paul takes them at their word. If you make the law the ground of your acceptance, then Leviticus 18:5 states the terms: you must do them, all of them (v. 10), to live by them. No sinner can meet those terms. Habakkuk 2:4 states the other way, the only way open to sinners: the righteous live by trusting God. Christ is the one person who met the terms of Leviticus 18:5, and he did it for us (4:4–5; Romans 10:4–5).

A sound contract offered to a bankrupt. The law really does promise life to whoever keeps it, and there is nothing defective about it: it is holy and righteous and good (Romans 7:12). The defect is in the material it has to work with. The law was weakened by the flesh (Romans 8:3), like a perfectly sound contract offered to a bankrupt.

Two kinds of sentence. Do and live puts the weight on the doer; live by faith puts it on the one believed. They are two answers to one question, who is responsible for my standing before God, and the second answer cancels the first.

The coming one. The prophet was told to wait for the vision: it will surely come (Habakkuk 2:3). Hebrews reads that waiting as waiting for Christ: yet a little while, and the coming one will come and will not delay; but my righteous one shall live by faith (Hebrews 10:37–38). Faith was never trust in trust. The righteous live by faith because the Righteous One has come.

What does living by faith look like when life is hard? It looks like Habakkuk. He did not get an explanation of why the Babylonians were coming; he got a promise, and a God to trust. By the end of his book the fig tree has not blossomed, the fields have failed and the stalls are empty, and he says he will still rejoice in the LORD and take joy in the God of his salvation (Habakkuk 3:17–18). Living by faith does not mean pretending things are fine. It means telling God honestly that they are not, and then deciding to trust what he has said about himself over what your circumstances are saying. The righteous do not live by understanding. They live by faith.

For worship. Leviticus 18:5 was never revoked. Someone had to do the things and live by them, and someone did. There has been exactly one man on this earth who could stand under the law’s own terms and claim its promise honestly. He earned the life. And then he went to a place where the law had nothing but a curse to give, and he took the curse instead, and left the life to us.

parallels.desc: the righteous shall live by his faith
by doing them a person shall live

verseByVerse.quote: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us—for it is written, “Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree”—
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law. Everything in the chapter has been climbing to this sentence. Redeemed is exagorazō, a market-place word: to buy out, as a slave could be bought out of slavery, with a real price paid to secure a real release.

From the curse of the law. Not from the law as God’s good will, but from its curse, the penalty it pronounces on lawbreakers: death and God’s wrath.

By becoming a curse for us. Then the mechanism, and it is deliberately shocking. Not by pitying us or showing how much God cares: he became the thing itself. “For us” is hyper hēmōn, on our behalf, in our place. This is penal substitution: Christ bore in our place the penalty God’s law pronounces on our sin, so that it will never be laid on us (Isaiah 53:5–6; 2 Corinthians 5:21; 1 Peter 2:24).

Hanged on a tree. The proof text is one that no Jew could hear without flinching (Deuteronomy 21:23). In Deuteronomy 21 hanging is not the method of execution. A man is put to death, and then his body is hung on a tree as a public sign of what he was, and taken down by nightfall, because a hanged man is cursed by God. The tree announced the verdict of heaven to everyone walking past.

Saul before a cross. For a Pharisee this text was the closing argument against Jesus of Nazareth: God had published his verdict on a beam outside the city wall. A crucified Messiah was a stumbling block to Jews (1 Corinthians 1:23). On the Damascus road the argument went inside out. Saul had been right that the tree published a curse. He had been wrong about only one thing: whose. For us. The two smallest words in the sentence are the whole gospel. He was cursed, and not for anything he had done.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christ was personally guilty or that God stopped loving his Son. Jesus said the opposite: for this reason the Father loves me, because I lay down my life (John 10:17). The Son was never more precious to the Father than in the hour he was bearing our sentence, and the sentence was real, and both of those are true at once.

Why did it have to be a cross? Because God meant the manner of Christ’s death to say what it was. Any death would have shown that he died; only a death on a tree could show, in the law’s own language, that he died under the curse. The authorities who handed him over may well have wanted him crucified to show that God had rejected him, and the Romans wanted it to shame him; God used both to publish the truth they did not intend: that the curse of God was falling on this man for sinners. The shame was not an accident around the edges of the atonement. It was part of the price, and Jesus despised it for the joy set before him (Hebrews 12:2).

Is this fair, that an innocent man should be punished for the guilty? It would be unjust if a judge seized an unwilling bystander. But that is not what happened. The Son came willingly, as one with the Father in purpose. He is himself the Judge who was wronged, choosing to bear the penalty of those who wronged him. And he is our representative, united to us as our head, as Adam was, so that what he did counts for those who are his. God is not punishing a third party. He is, in his Son, taking the cost of our sin on himself. That is not injustice. It is the highest justice joined to the deepest love (Romans 3:25–26).

In everyday life. When your past sins come back to accuse you, do not answer by listing your recent improvements. Name the sin, and then say: that curse fell on him, outside the city wall, and it will not fall on me.

For worship. The Son of God walked into the courtroom, took the sentence before it reached us, and carried it out of the city on his own back. The tree that was designed to publish the curse of God has become the place where the curse of God ran out.
verseByVerse.note: Under the law, the body of an executed criminal hung on a tree was under God’s curse.

parallels.desc: a hanged man is cursed by God

verseByVerse.quote: so that in Christ Jesus the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles, so that we might receive the promised Spirit through faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The blessing of Abraham. Now the purpose clause, given twice: so that, so that. The cross was a rescue for something. First, the blessing promised to Abraham, justification and life, now flows to the nations (v. 8). That promise has been travelling since Genesis 12, and here it arrives, in a Galatian town, in the hands of people whose grandparents worshipped Zeus.

In Christ Jesus. Not because God relaxed the terms. The Judaizers wanted Gentiles brought in through the door marked become a Jew; God brought them in through a door marked be in Christ, and it is the only door there has ever been. Nothing was cheapened to let the nations in. The full weight of the law’s sentence fell, and it fell on his Son, so that a man in Iconium with no covenant, no ancestry and no merit could be given the Spirit of the living God. God met the terms in Christ, and paid for everyone who never could.

Closing the circle. Second, the Spirit. Paul began the chapter by asking how they got the Spirit (v. 2); he now says the cross is why they got him, and that he is received through faith.

The promised Spirit. The Spirit is not a bonus for advanced believers. He is the promise: God himself coming to live in Gentile bodies, as Ezekiel (Ezekiel 36:27) and Joel (Joel 2:28) foretold. The Galatians had it, and they were being told they lacked something.

Am I missing a deeper blessing? The most common form of Christian discouragement is not doubt about doctrine; it is the settled suspicion that you have somehow received a lesser version of the Christian faith than other people have: that there is a fuller thing, a deeper blessing, a level of God’s favour that others reached and you did not. Verse 14 forecloses it. The blessing of Abraham and the promised Spirit are not two prizes handed out at different levels of attainment. They are one gift, purchased at one cross, received by one faith, and if you are in Christ you have them. You may grow in enjoying what you have; you will never be given more of a standing than you already possess.

How do I depend on the Spirit day by day? Begin each day by acknowledging him: you live in me, and I need you today. Before you read Scripture, ask him to open it. Before a hard conversation, ask him for the right words and a gentle heart. When temptation comes, ask him for strength in the moment, and then act, trusting that he is giving it. When you fail, do not grieve him further by hiding; confess and return. Depending on the Spirit is not a feeling you wait for. It is a posture of asking, trusting and obeying, all day long.

parallels.desc: I will pour my Spirit upon your offspring

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul turns from the cross to an illustration from everyday law, and calls the Galatians brothers again. Once a covenant or will has been ratified, no one can add a clause to it (v. 15), and the Judaizers’ demand was exactly that, an amendment to God’s promise. The promise was made to Abraham’s offspring, singular, who is Christ (v. 16), the one person toward whom the line of promise always narrowed.

The law came 430 years after the promise and cannot cancel it (v. 17). And the inheritance cannot come both by law and by promise (v. 18): God gave it to Abraham freely, and it stands given.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Promise Comes First and Cannot Fail

God’s unconditional oath to bless all nations through Abraham’s offspring came before the law of Moses and does not depend on it. The covenant of grace, God’s one plan to save sinners by grace through faith in the promised Christ, runs through the whole Bible, and the law given at Sinai served it for a season without changing its terms.

Verse 16 shows why the promise cannot fail. God made it with the one heir who would not break it, and everyone else inherits by being in him. And in v. 18 the verb is a perfect tense: God has given it, and it stands given. A promise that rests on the character of the one who swore it is a different kind of possession from anything that depends on the one who receives it.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Judaizers argued, in effect, that the law of Moses changed the conditions of the earlier promise to Abraham. Verses 15 and 17 show that this is impossible, and v. 18 shows what it would cost: not an improved promise but no promise at all.

Now: Because the inheritance rests on God’s promise and not on our performance, a believer who fails can run to his Father instead of hiding from him, and get up again as one whose house is already his.

verseByVerse.quote: To give a human example, brothers: even with a man-made covenant, no one annuls it or adds to it once it has been ratified. Now the promises were made to Abraham and to his offspring. It does not say, “And to offsprings,” referring to many, but referring to one, “And to your offspring,” who is Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To give a human example, brothers. He has just been at Golgotha; now he takes them to a lawyer’s office. And he calls them brothers, the anger letting a warm word through, as at 1:11.

In the flow. A careful opponent has a reply ready: granted that Abraham was justified by faith, did God not give the law later, at Sinai, and does the later word not set the terms now? Verses 15–18 answer it: a promise God has sworn cannot be amended by something that came afterwards. That raises the next question: then why was the law given at all (3:19)?

A man-made covenant. The word is diathēkē, which covers both a covenant and a last will and testament. Once a will is legally confirmed, nobody can come along later and insert a clause. If that is true of a document drawn up by men, how much more of an agreement God has sworn to?

An amendment is a different document. The Judaizers were not proposing to tear up the promise to Abraham, only an amendment: the promise, plus a condition. Paul says anyone attempting it is not adding to God’s covenant but writing a different one.

Who is Christ. God’s promises to Abraham are repeated again and again (Genesis 12:7; 13:15; 17:8; 22:18). Paul observes that God said to your offspring, singular, and concludes that the promise was made to one person, who is Christ. To a modern reader that looks like a trick, since offspring (literally seed) is a collective noun, and Genesis 15:5 promised descendants as numerous as the stars. But in verse 29 Paul himself uses the same word collectively: you are Abraham’s offspring, of a whole church. A man does not build an argument on a word’s singularity and then use it of a crowd unless he knows exactly what the word does.

The promise always narrowed. So what is the argument? The promise to Abraham always narrowed. Ishmael was a son of Abraham and was not the line of promise: through Isaac shall your offspring be named (Genesis 21:12). Esau was passed over. The line runs to Judah, then to David’s house, and at every fork it gets narrower. The singular lets Paul say what the history was always saying: this promise had one destination, and it was a person (Genesis 22:17–18). God made his covenant with one man who would not break it, and everyone else gets in by being in him. Paul is reading the Old Testament the way the risen Christ taught his disciples to read it on the Emmaus road (Luke 24:27).

Do all the promises of the Old Testament apply to me? All the covenant promises of God find their yes in Christ (2 Corinthians 1:20), and if you are in Christ you share in them: forgiveness, God as your God, his presence, his Spirit, his faithfulness, an everlasting inheritance. But read each promise in its setting. Some were given to particular people for particular situations, such as a specific word to a king or to the exiles in Babylon, and they show God’s character rather than guaranteeing you the same outcome. The safe way is to ask: what does this promise show about God, and how is it fulfilled in Christ? Then you can claim it through him without twisting it.

In everyday life. If the promise was made to Christ, then it cannot fail, because its heir cannot fail. When you doubt whether God will keep his word to you, stop looking at your own reliability and look at his Son’s. The promise rests on the one to whom it was made, and you are in him.
verseByVerse.note: “Offspring” (literally “seed”) is a singular noun that can refer to one descendant or many.

parallels.desc: in your offspring shall all the nations be blessed

verseByVerse.quote: This is what I mean: the law, which came 430 years afterward, does not annul a covenant previously ratified by God, so as to make the promise void. For if the inheritance comes by the law, it no longer comes by promise; but God gave it to Abraham by a promise.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The law, which came 430 years afterward. Now Paul puts a date on it. The promise is the older document by four centuries, and in any court the later paper cannot cancel the earlier one.

The 430 years. Exodus 12:40 says Israel lived in Egypt 430 years. But the Greek Old Testament that Paul’s readers used, and the Samaritan text, read in Egypt and in Canaan, 430 years from the patriarchs to the exodus in total, and Paul uses the text his churches had in their hands. Nothing in his argument depends on the exact figure: the promise came first.

If the inheritance comes by the law. Verse 18 is the cleanest either-or in the letter. An inheritance is given; a wage is earned. A promise is something one party swears and the other receives; a law is something one party demands and the other performs. Make my performance a condition and you have not enriched the promise; you have dissolved it.

The father and the tidy room. A father tells his son that the house will be his; it is written, signed, witnessed. Later the father says: and keep your room tidy. If tidiness is how a son who has been given a house behaves in it, nothing has changed. But if tidiness is now the condition of inheriting, the son has a contract, and he will spend the rest of his life measuring the floor, and he will never once be sure.

Obeying God, or securing God. That is the difference between a Christian who obeys God and a Christian who is trying to secure God. The behaviour can look identical. The difference is invisible until something goes wrong: one of them fails and runs to his Father, and the other fails and hides, because the failure has just moved his inheritance.

Gave it by a promise. The verb is charizomai, to give freely, from the same root as grace. And it is a perfect tense: God has given, and it stands given. The deed was signed before Sinai, by someone who does not revise (Romans 4:13–16; Hebrews 6:17–18). Through Egypt and the wilderness, through judges and kings and exile, through every generation that failed to keep the law, the promise stood untouched, because it had never rested on them.

A will that needed a death. Diathēkē also means a will, and a will takes effect only at death. That is why Christ is the mediator of a new covenant, so that those who are called may receive the promised eternal inheritance, since a death has occurred (Hebrews 9:15–17). The inheritance promised to Abraham comes to us through the death of the Son, and we are fellow heirs with him (Romans 8:17).

Can I lose my inheritance? Not if it rests on God’s promise, and that is exactly Paul’s point. An inheritance that depended on your performance could be forfeited any day. One given by promise depends on the faithfulness of the one who promised, and God does not break his word. That is why Scripture can speak of an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled and unfading, kept in heaven for you, by God’s power guarding you through faith (1 Peter 1:4–5). True believers persevere, not because they hold on so tightly, but because they are held. If you are worried that you have lost it, the worry itself shows you care; bring it to Christ, and rest on what he has promised.
verseByVerse.note: Exodus gives 430 years for Israel’s stay in Egypt; Paul uses the figure for the long gap between the promise and the law.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–25 — The Purpose of the Law
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
If the law cannot justify or give life, why did God give it (v. 19)? Paul gives three answers. It was added because of transgressions, to name and expose sin. It was given until the offspring, Christ, should come, so it had an end written into it. And it came through angels and a human go-between, Moses, while the promise came from God directly.

A mediator stands between two parties, and Sinai was a two-sided covenant, while God alone made the promise to Abraham (v. 20). The law is not against the promise (v. 21); it was simply never able to give life. Scripture shut everyone up under sin so that the promise might be given to those who believe (v. 22). The law was a guardian until the boy came of age (vv. 23–24), and now that faith has come, believers are no longer under a guardian (v. 25).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Law as Guardian: Real, Strict, Temporary

The covenant of grace is one across both Testaments, and the law of Moses had a distinct job within it. Verses 19 and 24 show that the law was truly from God, truly binding in its time, and truly serving the promise, but it was given for a stage and not for the end. Its ending as the framework of God’s people is not God changing his mind; it is God completing his plan.

God’s moral will has not been repealed (5:14). And v. 22 shows that the law’s severity was a mercy: every exit was closed so that the one open door would be taken.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Judaizers wanted the guardian brought back after the child had come of age. Paul answers that the guardian was appointed for a term that has ended (vv. 19, 25), and that the promise never depended on two signatures (v. 20).

Now: Many believers are adults in Christ and still live as if under supervision, expecting the stick and surprised by kindness. Verses 21–25 tell them that the guardian has done his work: they are sons, and may go to their Father as sons.

verseByVerse.quote: Why then the law? It was added because of transgressions, until the offspring should come to whom the promise had been made, and it was put in place through angels by an intermediary.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why then the law? Paul has been so severe about the law that the obvious objection now has to be faced, and he faces it head on. If it cannot justify, cannot give life, and cannot amend the promise, why did God give it at all? Was Sinai a mistake? The answer is three phrases, and each one puts the law in its place without insulting it.

It was added because of transgressions. Added is the first demotion: an addition is not the foundation. And because of transgressions means this: sin was in the world long before Sinai, but a transgression is a stepping over, the deliberate breaking of God’s known law, and you cannot step over a line that has not been drawn. The law drew the line. It turned the vague human sense that something is wrong with us into specific counts, written on stone by the finger of God (Exodus 31:18). Paul would not have known what it is to covet if the law had not said, you shall not covet (Romans 7:7; 5:20). The law makes sin visible, restrains it, and shows our need of a Saviour.

The diagnosis, not the medicine. That is one of the kindest things God could have done. A man who feels vaguely unwell will put off the appointment for years; a man handed a diagnosis with a name on it goes that afternoon. The law does not cause the disease and it cannot cure it, and anyone who mistakes the chart for the medicine will die holding it. But without it we would have gone on managing our symptoms and calling ourselves basically decent people. The diagnosis was given so that the cure would be wanted, and the cure is the Lord himself.

Until the offspring should come. The second demotion. The law, as the governing covenant, came with an end written into it: not a failure but a term, which ran until the Offspring arrived, Christ (v. 16). Everything in the law was waiting for him: its sacrifices for the Lamb of God, its priesthood for a priest who lives for ever, its tabernacle for the Word who became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14, 29; Hebrews 7:24–25). Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes (Romans 10:4): its goal, and so its term.

Through angels by an intermediary. The third demotion, and the sharpest. Scripture describes Sinai as attended by angelic hosts (Deuteronomy 33:2), and both Stephen and Hebrews take it for granted that the law was delivered by angels (Acts 7:53; Hebrews 2:2). Then Moses stood between the LORD and the people, because the people were afraid (Deuteronomy 5:5; Exodus 20:19), and their fear was fitting: sinners cannot stand near a holy God without someone between. Count the links: God, angels, Moses, Israel. Now count the links in the promise: God, Abraham. The law came down a staircase. The promise was handed over directly, by a God who needed no one between himself and the man he was speaking to. And when the Offspring arrived, God himself had come down the whole staircase to stand among us.

Where Christians differ: the uses of the law. Some say the law has no role for Christians at all; others make it the centre of the Christian life. This commentary’s view: the Reformers identified three uses of the law. First, it shows sin and drives sinners to Christ (the use Paul focuses on here). Second, it restrains evil in society. Third, it guides believers in how to please God (often called the third use of the law), as the moral law summarised in the Ten Commandments (Romans 13:8–10). The ceremonial and civil laws of Israel (its sacrifices and purity rules, and its national laws) were fulfilled and ended in Christ, but the moral law remains the rule of life, not as a covenant of works, that is, a way of earning life by obedience, but as the will of our Father (the Westminster Confession 19.5–6; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 19.5–6).

Why would God give a law he knew no one could keep? Because its main purpose was never to be the road by which we earn our way to him. It was given to a people he had already redeemed, as the shape of a holy life, with sacrifices built in for their failures. And it was given to show all of us, with total clarity, what we are and what we need. A law that sinners could keep perfectly would have flattered us and left us without Christ. A law we cannot keep strips away every excuse and sends us to the one who kept it for us. God was not setting a trap. He was drawing a map, and every road on it ends at the cross.

In everyday life. Read one of the Ten Commandments slowly this week, the way Jesus read them in the Sermon on the Mount: not only the deed but the desire. Let it show you where you stand. Then go to Christ with what it has shown you, and thank him that he kept it all.
verseByVerse.note: Jewish tradition held that angels were present at the giving of the law; Moses was the intermediary.

parallels.desc: I stood between the LORD and you

verseByVerse.quote: Now an intermediary implies more than one, but God is one.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now an intermediary implies more than one. This is famously one of the most compressed sentences in the letter, but the direction of the thought is not really in doubt, because Paul has just been counting links in a chain. A mediator stands between parties, each with obligations. So the very presence of Moses tells you what kind of arrangement Sinai was: a two-sided covenant with conditions, with a man in the middle holding the terms. Everything depended on both parties keeping their word, and the people had barely received it before there was a golden calf at the foot of the mountain (Exodus 19:8; 32:1–6).

But God is one. When God came to Abraham there was no second party and no man in the middle. Abraham did not negotiate; he was asleep. God put him into a deep sleep and then passed alone between the pieces of the sacrifice: a smoking fire pot and a flaming torch walking the aisle of blood by themselves (Genesis 15:12, 17). In such a ceremony those who made the covenant walked between the pieces and invoked the fate of the animals on whoever broke faith (Jeremiah 34:18–20). God walked it alone, binding only himself, while Abraham lay a witness and not a party.

Two signatures or one. So the contrast is between an agreement that can fail because it has two signatures on it, and a promise that cannot fail because it has one, and the one who signed it is God, who does not have a bad year.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christ is not a mediator. Christ is the one mediator between God and men (1 Timothy 2:5), and he is himself God. Moses stood between two parties as a third man. Christ stands between God and us as one who is both, so that in him the promise rests on God alone and is brought to us by one of us.

What is a mediator, and why do I need one? A mediator is someone who stands between two parties to bring them together. We need one because there is a real distance between a holy God and sinners: not of miles but of guilt. Moses could carry God’s words to the people, but he could not take away their sin; he once offered to be blotted out for them, and God would not accept it (Exodus 32:32–33). Christ is the mediator Moses could not be. He does not only carry messages; he offers himself, and he always lives to intercede for those who draw near to God through him (Hebrews 7:25). You need no other go-between, no priest, saint or ritual. You come to the Father through the Son.

For worship. God swore the whole covenant by himself, knowing every century of unfaithfulness that was coming, and what it would cost him to keep his own oath when the other side had broken theirs. He walked between the pieces alone under the night sky, and when the time came his Son walked out to a hill alone, and kept it. If we are faithless, he remains faithful, for he cannot deny himself (2 Timothy 2:13).

verseByVerse.quote: Is the law then contrary to the promises of God? Certainly not! For if a law had been given that could give life, then righteousness would indeed be by the law. But the Scripture imprisoned everything under sin, so that the promise by faith in Jesus Christ might be given to those who believe.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Is the law then contrary to the promises of God? Certainly not! Paul has demoted the law three times in two verses, and he knows how it sounds, so he asks the question his opponents would shout. And the answer is mē genoito, the strongest negative he owns, which he keeps for conclusions he finds unthinkable. The law and the promise both came from the same God and both serve the same purpose in his one plan. They are not rivals. They are a diagnosis and a cure, and only a fool sets those against each other.

A law that could give life. If any legal code could make a dead man live, God would have used it. The law was never given that job. It can command but not empower (Romans 8:3). A speed limit has never once made a reckless man careful. It tells him what careful looks like and records the fact that he is not.

The true measure of our condition. If we were merely misinformed, instruction would be enough; if we were merely weak, encouragement would be enough. We were dead in trespasses and sins (Ephesians 2:1), and nothing you say to a corpse improves it. We needed resurrection.

What the law could not do. What the law could not do, God did by sending his own Son (Romans 8:3). The law could describe life; Christ is the life (John 14:6). A Person has raised the dead, and he speaks to the dead still: the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live (John 5:25).

Imprisoned everything under sin. The verb is synkleiō: shut up together, locked in with no other door, the word Luke uses for a shoal of fish enclosed in a net (Luke 5:6). And the object is not only everyone but everything (Romans 3:9–20; 11:32). To be under sin is more than to have sinned now and then: it is to live under sin’s guilt, which condemns us, and under its power, which rules us. And it is Scripture that did the locking: our confinement is not a verdict we can appeal to a higher authority.

So that the promise. The imprisonment is a mercy. As long as a man believes there is another way out, he will keep trying doors: being respectable, useful, sincere, spiritual. God locked every one of them so that we would finally turn round and see the one door that stands open, and it has a person’s name on it. The jailer and the deliverer are the same God, and he never meant the prison to be the end of the story: he himself became the door (John 10:9), and he holds it open still to everyone who believes.

Does “everything under sin” include the good people I know? Yes, and that includes you and me. Some people are kinder, more honest and more generous than others, and God is pleased with real kindness wherever it is found. But no one has loved God with all his heart, and no one has kept the law, and a good life lived for oneself is still a life lived apart from God. The verse is not saying everyone is as bad as he could be. It is saying everyone is shut in the same prison, the respectable and the disreputable alike, and needs the same way out. That is humbling, and it is also the great leveller: the nicest person you know and the worst person you know are invited to Christ on exactly the same terms.

In everyday life. If the harder you try the worse the accounting gets, do not read that as God’s absence. It may well be his kindness: he is closing the exits so that you will turn round to Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: Now before faith came, we were held captive under the law, imprisoned until the coming faith would be revealed. So then, the law was our guardian until Christ came, in order that we might be justified by faith. But now that faith has come, we are no longer under a guardian,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now before faith came. Abraham had faith, and so did Habakkuk. Paul means the era of faith: the age that opened when Christ came, so that faith in Christ is now the open, announced way in. The Old Testament believer was looking down a corridor at a door he could not yet see. We are standing in the room.

Held captive. Phroureō, to guard, as a garrison guards a city. Israel was guarded by the law, but only for a time: custody, not a life sentence.

Our guardian. The law was our paidagōgos. Older English versions said schoolmaster, which is misleading. A paidagōgos was a household slave, often stern, who had charge of the boy from about six until he came of age. He walked him to school and home, kept him off the wrong streets, checked his manners, and had a stick and authority to use it. He was not there to educate the boy, but to get him to the one who would.

Three things about the guardian. They answer the Judaizers. The paidagōgos was genuinely appointed: the boy who resented him was resenting his father’s arrangement. He was genuinely strict. And he was genuinely temporary: nobody was under a paidagōgos at thirty, and even his strictness was aimed at the moment he would hand the boy over.

Walked to the door of Christ. Where was the guardian taking the boy? To a Person. Moses wrote of him (John 5:46; Luke 24:44). The lamb at Passover, the blood on the mercy seat, the priests who died and had to be replaced, the curse on the one who failed, were walking the boy toward Christ. And the one he is handed over to is no harsher guardian with longer lists. It is the Son himself: Come to me, all who labour and are heavy laden, and learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart (Matthew 11:28–29).

In the flow. Paul finishes his answer to why then the law? (3:19): it had a time limit. Paul says we were held captive, speaking as a Jew; in the next verse he turns to you, all of you, Jew and Gentile together (3:26). He takes up the guardian picture again at 4:1–7.

No longer under a guardian. The son has come of age, and the Judaizers were telling the grown man that if he really wanted to please his father, he should send for the old slave again and ask to be walked to school. Everything strict and narrow in the old arrangement was the Father’s care for children too young for the house; everything open and free in the new is the same Father’s joy in sons come of age. He has never been anything but a father.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers may live as they please. God’s moral will has not been repealed; Paul will spend two chapters telling these people how to live (5:14). What has ended is the law as the framework of the relationship, the guardianship under which God’s people lived as minors, with its ceremonies. Christians are under the law of Christ (1 Corinthians 9:21). Nor were Old Testament believers second-class: they were children in the same family, in the care their age required.

How do I stop living like a child under supervision? Many believers are technically adults in Christ and emotionally still under the guardian: still measuring the day’s performance, still expecting the stick, still surprised by kindness. Start by believing what your Father has said, that you are his son or daughter, not his employee or his ward on probation. Talk to him as a child talks to a loving father, plainly and often. When you obey, do it because you want to please him, not to keep him from punishing you. When you fail, go to him, not away. And let the Spirit’s cry of Abba, Father (4:6) become your own. It takes time to unlearn the guardian, but the guardian has been dismissed.
verseByVerse.note: The “guardian” (paidagogos) was a household slave who supervised a child, took him to school and kept him in line until he came of age.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter ends with what believers now are. Through faith every believer is a son of God in Christ Jesus, clothed with Christ (vv. 26–27). The divisions that ruled the ancient world, Jew and Greek, slave and free, male and female, no longer decide anyone’s standing before God (v. 28), and all who belong to Christ are Abraham’s offspring and heirs of the promise (v. 29).
verseByVerse.theology:
Union with Christ, and the Unity It Creates

Verses 26–27 give the ground of everything Paul has argued: the believer’s standing is not a quality in himself but a place. He is in Christ, clothed with Christ, and so shares the standing of the Son.

Verse 28 shows that the gospel does not only change individuals; it makes a community in which race, class and sex no longer decide anyone’s worth or access to God. Christians who honour Scripture differ on what the verse means for roles in church and home; this commentary holds that Paul speaks here of standing before God, and of roles elsewhere. Both sides agree on what the verse plainly says: there is no hierarchy of worth at the cross, and no smaller share in the inheritance (v. 29).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A strict Jew would not enter a Gentile house; a large part of a city’s population were slaves; and a man’s testimony counted in court where a woman’s often did not. Verse 28 says those three walls do not run through the church, because everyone in it is wearing the same garment (v. 27), and v. 29 tells Gentile believers that they are full heirs, not associate members.

Now: Every congregation has people who have quietly concluded that they are second rank. Verse 28 tells them that Christ has no larger portion for anyone in the building than the one he has given them.

verseByVerse.quote: for in Christ Jesus you are all sons of God, through faith. For as many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All sons of God. Now we are told what the boy has become. Not a graduate. A son. You: the uncircumcised, told they were not yet full members. All: no tiers. Sons: adult sons with full rights of inheritance (4:5–7). Through faith: not through the knife. And governing everything, in Christ Jesus: the sonship is ours because we are in the Son.

Sons, not only children. Paul writes huioi, sons, deliberately, because in that world sons inherited and daughters generally did not. The word is about legal status, the standing of the heir. So a woman reading verse 26 is being told that she holds the inheritance rights of a son in the household of God. Far from excluding her, this is the most generous word in the sentence.

Baptized into Christ. In the New Testament faith and baptism belonged together: people believed and were baptised at once (Acts 8:12; 16:31–33), so Paul can speak of baptism as the moment they were joined to Christ (Romans 6:3–4). What actually unites a person to Christ is the Spirit, received through faith (v. 14; 1 Corinthians 12:13); baptism is the outward picture and public confession of it, as we might say “she gave her hand in marriage” and mean the whole covenant of marriage.

Have put on Christ. “Put on” is endyō, the ordinary word for dressing. In the Roman world a boy who came of age laid aside the child’s toga with its purple border and put on the plain white toga virilis, the garment of a man. Paul has just dismissed the guardian; now he hands out the adult garment, and the garment is Christ himself: his righteousness covering us (Romans 13:14; Isaiah 61:10).

What the Father sees. What the Father sees when he looks at a believer is not first a person making progress. It is his Son’s own righteousness worn as clothing, covering everything the man is ashamed of. That is why assurance is possible for people who know themselves well: the clothing does not fluctuate with the wearer. Much of life is spent dressing to be approved, by others and by God. The one garment that makes us acceptable to God has already been put on us.

Where Christians differ: does baptism save? Some take this verse to mean that water baptism itself unites a person to Christ and regenerates them; Roman Catholic, Lutheran and some other Christians read it this way. This commentary’s view: Paul has just said we are sons through faith (v. 26), and the whole chapter has insisted that everything comes through faith (vv. 2, 14, 26) and nothing by an outward rite performed on the body. Baptism is the sign of union with Christ, which is received by faith. It is not the cause of union. Those who are baptised with faith truly put on Christ; baptism without faith does not save (1 Peter 3:21; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 29.1; the Westminster Confession 28.5). This commentary holds believer’s baptism: the sign follows the faith it signifies, which is exactly the order in this verse: sons through faith (v. 26), then baptised into Christ (v. 27). Christians who baptise infants see baptism as the sign of the covenant given, like circumcision, to believers’ children (Colossians 2:11–12); they are our brothers, and both sides confess what this verse indisputably says: what clothes a sinner before God is Christ, received by faith.

I was baptised as an infant. Should I be baptised now? On the view this commentary holds, baptism is for those who have believed, so a believer who was baptised only as an infant has not yet received believer’s baptism and should ask for it, gladly, as an act of obedience and public confession. It is not a rejection of your parents’ love or prayers, which were real gifts. Talk it through with your pastor and read the New Testament passages on baptism for yourself. And hold your view with charity: many faithful Christians and churches, including the Westminster tradition, sincerely believe infant baptism is right. Do not make the disagreement a wall between you and them. You are clothed with the same Christ.

In everyday life. There is no better-dressed Christian in your congregation than you. The most disciplined believer you know is wearing exactly what you are wearing, and neither of you made it or paid for it.

For worship. The eternal Son put on our flesh so that we could put on him, and at the cross the soldiers cast lots for his tunic (John 19:23–24). He hung there stripped, so that sinners could stand before the Father dressed. No one in the great multitude before his throne will be wearing anything they made: they have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb (Revelation 7:14).

verseByVerse.quote: There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free, there is no male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Neither Jew nor Greek. Those three pairs were the load-bearing walls of the ancient world. Jew and Greek was the great religious and ethnic divide; slave and free the great social one, and a large part of a city like Corinth was property; male and female determined whose testimony counted in court. A Jewish morning prayer recorded in later rabbinic sources thanked God for not making the man praying a Gentile, a slave, or a woman. Paul says that in Christ those three walls do not run through the room.

No male and female. The first two pairs are neither, nor. The third changes: no male and female, the wording of Genesis 1:27 in the Greek Old Testament. Paul has reached back to creation: even the deepest distinction God made in humanity does not determine your standing in Christ.

All one in Christ Jesus. One is heis, one person: not identical, but one body. What is being levelled? Paul has not changed the subject: who is a son of Abraham, who is justified, who inherits. On that ground the three walls are gone entirely. One Christ, one righteousness, one inheritance, and every believer holds all of it. Christ has no larger portion for anyone in the building than the one he has already given you. At the foot of the cross there is no hierarchy of worth, and in the inheritance there is no smaller share.

Difference remains; difference as worth has gone. Paul goes on being a Jew; Onesimus goes on being a slave in Roman law while Paul works on Philemon to receive him as a brother; men and women go on being men and women. What has gone is difference as a measure of worth and as a condition of access to God.

Where Christians differ: does this verse abolish gender roles? Egalitarians use this verse to argue that all distinctions of role between men and women in the church and home are abolished in Christ; they see the verse as the principle and the restrictions elsewhere as temporary concessions to Paul’s culture. This commentary’s view: the context is about who is justified and who is an heir of Abraham: all believers equally, regardless of race, class or sex. It is about status before God, not roles in the church. The distinctions themselves are not abolished: Jews remain Jews, men remain men. Paul elsewhere teaches distinct roles for men and women in the home and church (1 Corinthians 11:3; Ephesians 5:22–33; 1 Timothy 2:12), grounded in creation, not culture. Slavery is no parallel: Paul gave instructions to slaves while sowing the seeds of their freedom, urging slaves to take freedom when they could and condemning slave-traders (1 Corinthians 7:21; 1 Timothy 1:10; Philemon 16), but he never grounded slavery in creation. Equal in worth, distinct in calling: the complementarian view. And headship in Scripture is the self-giving love of Christ for his church, never domination; any abuse of a wife or of any person is a grave sin that the church must never tolerate or cover. Many faithful Christians read this verse the egalitarian way out of a real concern for the dignity of women, a concern the verse itself shares; this commentary honours them as brothers and sisters while holding the view above.

Does this verse condemn racism and snobbery in the church? Yes, plainly. If Christ has given the same standing to every believer, then any church that treats some believers as lesser because of their race, nationality, class, education or sex is denying in practice what this verse says. That was Peter’s sin at Antioch (2:11–14). It can look like separate congregations divided by colour where there is no language reason, leaders always drawn from one social group, a cool welcome for the poor or the foreigner, jokes at someone’s background. Repent of it where you see it in yourself, and gently challenge it where you see it in your church. The one table of the Lord is meant to look like the one family he has made.

In everyday life. Every congregation contains people who have quietly concluded that they are the second rank: the woman talked past in every church she has attended, the man whose accent or prison record marks him out. Seek one of them out this Sunday, as Christ sought you, and listen.

verseByVerse.quote: And if you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to promise.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If you are Christ’s. The whole chapter comes to rest here. The promise was made to the Offspring, and the Offspring is Christ (v. 16). So everything depends on one question: are you his? Now Paul uses offspring in its collective sense: in Christ, all believers are Abraham’s seed.

Not by lowering the requirements. Paul does not say you have qualified, or God has been generous with the entry requirements. Every one of them was met by one man, and you are in him. God narrowed the promise through Isaac and Jacob and Judah and David until it came down to one, and that one carried the curse of the broken law out of the city on his own back so that the promise could be paid to everyone who had no claim on it. Nothing was waived, and nothing failed.

Heirs according to promise. An heir has been given a standing, and the estate follows from the standing. He does not earn it, and does not receive it because he has been useful, but because of who he is in the family (Romans 8:16–17; Ephesians 1:11).

What is actually inherited? Scripture does not leave it vague, and the vagueness of much Christian talk about the future is a loss, not a piety. Heirs of everything God promised Abraham: righteousness, the Spirit, the world to come (Romans 4:13). God himself as your portion, which is the substance of every promise (Genesis 15:1). A body that does not fail, raised imperishable (1 Corinthians 15:42–44). A world put right and handed over, the meek inheriting the earth (Matthew 5:5; Romans 8:17–21). A face to see, the thing Moses asked for and was not given (1 John 3:2; Revelation 22:4). And real service in a real kingdom (Luke 19:17). That is what stands to the account of every Galatian who believed Paul’s preaching, and it is what stands to yours.

Where Christians differ: the land and Israel’s future. Are the promises of land and nation to Israel now void? Paul says that all who are Christ’s are Abraham’s heirs, so the promises are fulfilled in Christ and shared by everyone in him, Jew and Gentile alike, which is not a rejection of the Jewish people (Romans 11:1). Some Christians hold that the land and nation promises remain for ethnic Israel, with a future earthly fulfilment. Many Reformed Christians hold that the promise was always larger than a strip of land: Abraham would be heir of the world (Romans 4:13), the renewed creation. (See the note on Israel and the church at 3:7–9.)

If I am an heir, why does my life feel so poor? Because you are an heir before the reading of the will. Paul will say in the next chapter that an heir, while he is a child, may look no different from a slave (4:1). The estate is real but mostly unseen, and you are living in a world that contradicts it: illness, loss, loneliness, a body that is wearing out. That is the normal Christian condition, not a sign that you have missed out. The inheritance is kept for you, not yet handed over (1 Peter 1:4). Meanwhile you have the down payment: the Spirit himself, the guarantee of what is to come (Ephesians 1:14). Live on the deposit, and look forward to the estate.

3.text: <sup>1</sup>O foolish Galatians! Who has bewitched you? It was before your eyes that Jesus Christ was publicly portrayed as crucified.<sup>2</sup>Let me ask you only this: Did you receive the Spirit by works of the law or by hearing with faith?<sup>3</sup>Are you so foolish? Having begun by the Spirit, are you now being perfected by the flesh?<sup>4</sup>Did you suffer so many things in vain—if indeed it was in vain?<sup>5</sup>Does he who supplies the Spirit to you and works miracles among you do so by works of the law, or by hearing with faith—<sup>6</sup>just as Abraham “believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness”?<sup>7</sup>Know then that it is those of faith who are the sons of Abraham.<sup>8</sup>And the Scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, preached the gospel beforehand to Abraham, saying, “In you shall all the nations be blessed.”<sup>9</sup>So then, those who are of faith are blessed along with Abraham, the man of faith.<sup>10</sup>For all who rely on works of the law are under a curse; for it is written, “Cursed be everyone who does not abide by all things written in the Book of the Law, and do them.”<sup>11</sup>Now it is evident that no one is justified before God by the law, for “The righteous shall live by faith.”<sup>12</sup>But the law is not of faith, rather “The one who does them shall live by them.”<sup>13</sup>Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us—for it is written, “Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree”—<sup>14</sup>so that in Christ Jesus the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles, so that we might receive the promised Spirit through faith.<sup>15</sup>To give a human example, brothers: even with a man-made covenant, no one annuls it or adds to it once it has been ratified.<sup>16</sup>Now the promises were made to Abraham and to his offspring. It does not say, “And to offsprings,” referring to many, but referring to one, “And to your offspring,” who is Christ.<sup>17</sup>This is what I mean: the law, which came 430 years afterward, does not annul a covenant previously ratified by God, so as to make the promise void.<sup>18</sup>For if the inheritance comes by the law, it no longer comes by promise; but God gave it to Abraham by a promise.<sup>19</sup>Why then the law? It was added because of transgressions, until the offspring should come to whom the promise had been made, and it was put in place through angels by an intermediary.<sup>20</sup>Now an intermediary implies more than one, but God is one.<sup>21</sup>Is the law then contrary to the promises of God? Certainly not! For if a law had been given that could give life, then righteousness would indeed be by the law.<sup>22</sup>But the Scripture imprisoned everything under sin, so that the promise by faith in Jesus Christ might be given to those who believe.<sup>23</sup>Now before faith came, we were held captive under the law, imprisoned until the coming faith would be revealed.<sup>24</sup>So then, the law was our guardian until Christ came, in order that we might be justified by faith.<sup>25</sup>But now that faith has come, we are no longer under a guardian,<sup>26</sup>for in Christ Jesus you are all sons of God, through faith.<sup>27</sup>For as many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ.<sup>28</sup>There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free, there is no male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus.<sup>29</sup>And if you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to promise.

4.title: Sons and Heirs: From Slavery to Sonship
4.overview:
Chapter 4 carries the argument of chapter 3 to its goal. The law was a guardian for children; now Paul shows what God gives instead: full sonship, the Spirit of his Son, and the cry of Abba, Father, in the heart of every adopted child. The contrast is between two ways of living before God: the slave who must perform, and the son who belongs.

An heir under age owns everything and controls nothing until the time his father has set. So it was with God’s people under the law, until the fullness of time, when God sent his Son to redeem them and give them adoption, and sent the Spirit of his Son into their hearts (vv. 1–7).

Paul then pleads with the Galatians (vv. 8–20). He recalls how they welcomed him when he came to them sick, and he is in labour again until Christ is formed in them. Finally he reads the story of Hagar and Sarah (vv. 21–31): the two covenants produce two kinds of children, and believers are children of the free woman, the children of promise, heirs of the Jerusalem above.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: An heir who is still a child is no better off than a slave until the time his father has set (vv. 1–2). So we too were enslaved to the elementary principles of the world (v. 3). But at the time God had set, he sent his Son to redeem those under the law and to adopt them as sons (vv. 4–5), and he sent the Spirit of his Son into their hearts (v. 6). So they are no longer slaves but sons, and heirs through God (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology:
Adoption, and the Sending of the Son and the Spirit

In vv. 4–6 the Father sends the Son, and the Father sends the Spirit of the Son. The two sendings are distinct and belong together: the Son wins redemption and adoption for us, outside us, as a settled legal fact, and the Spirit brings them home within, so that the adopted child knows the Father and calls on him.

Adoption (huiothesia) is stated more clearly in this chapter than almost anywhere, and it goes beyond forgiveness. What changes is not the son’s conduct but his family. Verse 7 sums it up: no longer, son, heir, through God. J. I. Packer called adoption the highest privilege the gospel offers.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Galatians already had everything vv. 4–7 describe: the Spirit, the cry of Abba, the inheritance. The Judaizers were offering them a route to a standing they already held, and vv. 1–3 show what they would be going back to: the nursery, the guardians and a calendar.

Now: Verse 6 answers the believer who does not feel like a son: the Spirit is sent because you are one, so the feeling follows the status and never causes it.

verseByVerse.quote: I mean that the heir, as long as he is a child, is no different from a slave, though he is the owner of everything, but he is under guardians and managers until the date set by his father.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Galatians 4 continues the argument that believers are God’s free sons, not slaves under the law. An heir who is a child is no better off than a slave until the day his father has set; in the fullness of time God sent his Son to redeem those under the law and give them adoption, and sent the Spirit of his Son crying Abba, Father (vv. 1–7). How can the Galatians turn back to slavery (vv. 8–11)? Paul appeals to them tenderly, in labour until Christ is formed in them (vv. 12–20), and reads Abraham’s two sons as two covenants, slavery under Sinai and freedom by promise (vv. 21–31).

I mean that the heir, as long as he is a child. Chapter 3 ended with the guardian dismissed. Now Paul runs the same picture from inside the household. The child is nēpios: a minor, a son not yet of legal age.

No different from a slave. In law he is the owner: the deeds are in his name. And it makes no practical difference, because he is seven. He cannot sell a field or give an order that anyone has to obey. Watch him through the day and you could not tell him from the boy who carries the water.

Ownership and enjoyment. Were the believers before Christ saved? Yes: genuinely, by faith, looking forward to the Christ we look back on. Then why speak of bondage? Because ownership and enjoyment are two different things. Abraham was promised that he would be heir of the world (Romans 4:13), and he died having bought only a burial plot for his wife (Genesis 23). He owned everything and held almost nothing, and he was content to wait for the city whose designer and builder is God (Hebrews 11:10).

But he is under guardians and managers. The epitropoi had authority over the boy’s person; the oikonomoi ran the property. Both were servants, both had more practical power over the estate than its owner did, and both held it only for a time.

Until the date set by his father. The arrangements varied in the ancient world, but in every version the boy did not choose the day, and the guardians did not choose the day. The father named it. God set the time for his people’s coming of age, and the date he wrote in the will was the coming of Christ (v. 4). He is not a landlord letting rooms to tenants on good behaviour. He is a Father who drew up the will before the child was born, set the day, kept the estate through centuries of guardians, and never once forgot the name on the deeds.

The Owner in the form of a slave. The picture of an owner of everything who looks no different from a slave has one perfect instance: the Son. He was in the form of God, the appointed heir of all things, and he took the form of a servant (Philippians 2:6–7; Hebrews 1:2), so ordinary to his neighbours that they asked, Is not this the carpenter’s son? (Matthew 13:55). The Lord of the estate entered the condition of the minors so that minors could come of age in him (4:4–5).

Is God unkind to keep anyone in that position? No more than a father is unkind to his seven-year-old. The guardians were not a punishment; they were a protection, the way a loving father secures an estate for a son too young to manage it. The law kept Israel, fenced her, taught her, and kept the line of promise intact until the Christ was born. And in this picture the heir is never in danger of losing the estate. His position is restricted; his inheritance is secure. Every rule that hemmed him in was a sign that something very large had been reserved for him.

In everyday life. Much Christian frustration is about timing: the prayer unanswered for eleven years, the change in yourself you keep asking for, the season that will not lift. Verse 2 does not promise that the date is soon. It says there is one, that it is not arbitrary, and that it was fixed by a Father, not by the guardians who seem to be running your life.

What does living as a son who has come of age actually look like? It looks like freedom of access rather than a rulebook for every step. A minor needs a rule for everything because he does not yet know his father’s mind; a grown son has his father’s Spirit and his father’s word, and he obeys from the inside. So you pray boldly, without first proving you deserve a hearing. You confess sin quickly, because a son does not hide from his father. You read God’s commands as the family’s way of life, not as an entrance exam. And you stop treating other believers’ consciences as your guardians: you are answerable to the Father himself.

verseByVerse.quote: In the same way we also, when we were children, were enslaved to the elementary principles of the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the same way we also, when we were children. Paul puts the whole human race inside the picture. That we includes the Pharisee in the same sentence as men who grew up sacrificing to Cybele. Before Christ, Jew and Gentile alike were minors.

The elementary principles of the world. The phrase is ta stoicheia tou kosmou, one of the genuinely disputed phrases in Paul. Stoicheia means things in a row: the letters of the alphabet, the ABCs, the basic building blocks of anything. Some take it that way here: the elementary stage of religion, the rudiments of rules and rituals, and to go back to them is to be an adult sounding out letters. Others hear something darker, since Paul says enslaved: the spiritual powers thought to stand behind the elements, the heavenly bodies and their calendars (Colossians 2:8, 20). On that reading, going back to law-keeping is a return to territory that has an occupant.

Whichever reading. Most readers today combine the two, and Paul’s argument does not depend on the choice. Two things are certain: the Gentiles were under the stoicheia before they knew God (vv. 8–9), and the Judaizers’ programme would put the Galatians back under them. Paul has just filed the Mosaic law and the pagan festival calendar in the same drawer.

Not according to Christ. In Colossians Paul sets the same phrase against one name: according to the elemental spirits of the world, and not according to Christ (Colossians 2:8). Christ is their conqueror: at the cross he disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame (Colossians 2:15). The Galatians were choosing between masters Christ has already defeated and the Christ who defeated them. None of those masters ever once set a single slave free. Only one Master has ever come into the market to buy his slaves out of it. He is not one more element of the world. He is the one by whom the world was made, and the one in whom all its elements hold together.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the law of Moses and paganism are the same; the law is holy, and the commandment holy and righteous and good (Romans 7:12). But as ways of approaching God apart from Christ, both enslave. Take any good and God-given thing, the Sabbath, the sacraments, a doctrinal system, a discipline of prayer, and make it the thing that secures your standing with God, and it will do to you exactly what an idol does. It will demand, it will never say enough, and you will serve it.

Disappointment or dread. This catches good practices rather than bad ones. Take the most valued religious habit in your life, and imagine dropping it for a fortnight, not through rebellion but through illness. Is what rises in you disappointment, or dread? Disappointment is a son who has missed his father’s company. Dread is a slave who has missed a quota. The habit is identical; the relationship is not.

So should I drop my routines if they have become a burden? No. The answer to a habit that has become a quota is not to abandon the habit but to change its ground. Keep reading your Bible, keep praying, keep gathering with the church: these are the ordinary means by which God feeds his children. What has to go is the idea that they hold up your acceptance. Before you open your Bible tomorrow, say to God plainly that you are already accepted in Christ and you have come to hear your Father, not to earn his attention. Then, on the day you miss it, do not punish yourself with extra. Come back the next morning as a son comes back to the table. The routine stays; the slavery goes.
verseByVerse.note: The “elementary principles” may mean the basic rules of religion, or the spiritual powers people believed ruled the world.

verseByVerse.quote: But when the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son, born of woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when the fullness of time had come. Everything before has been minority, guardians, waiting; and then God moves. The phrase is to plērōma tou chronou: the vessel full to the brim, not a minute early and not a minute late, the moment God had set (v. 2; Mark 1:15; Ephesians 1:10).

Why then? Some of the answer is visible even from here. There were Roman roads running across much of the known world, and a Roman peace that made it possible to walk them. There was one language a Galatian, a Roman and an Alexandrian could all read. There were Jewish synagogues scattered through every major city, the Scriptures in Greek, and Gentile God-fearers already attached to them, so that Paul had a hearing prepared in each town he entered. And among many in that world, confidence in the old gods had worn thin, and a spiritual hunger was growing in its place. Take one of those away and the gospel travels differently. But the deeper answer is in the sentence itself: it was the date set by his father. History was not waiting for conditions to be right. It was waiting for a Father to say now, and the conditions were the Father’s preparations.

God sent forth his Son. The verb is exapostellō, to send out from: from the Father’s side. God sent one who was already his Son, already there to be sent. The Son did not begin at Bethlehem; he came from somewhere. The Son of God became the son of Mary so that the sons of Adam could become the sons of God.

Born of woman. A Hebrew way of saying human, mortal, of our stock: man who is born of a woman is few of days and full of trouble (Job 14:1). He was carried and delivered and fed at a human breast, truly human, with every weakness of our flesh except its sin.

Did Paul know of the virgin birth? A question is often raised about this phrase, and it should be answered rather than left hanging. Paul says born of woman, not born of a virgin, and it is sometimes argued from this that he knew nothing of it. But that is more weight than the sentence will carry. Paul is not writing about how Jesus was conceived; he is writing about which side of the counter he stood on, and every clause in the verse is chosen to press him further into our situation, not out of it. His wording is at least consistent with the virgin birth: born of a woman, with no human father named. And Luke, who travelled with Paul, records the annunciation in detail (Luke 1:26–38).

Born under the law. He took his place inside the very jurisdiction that had every one of us condemned: circumcised on the eighth day, presented in the temple with the poor family’s offering of two birds (Luke 2:21–24, 41–42), and he kept every clause of the code that was killing us, for us.

Why did Jesus need to keep the law, if he was going to die for us anyway? Because we needed two things, not one. We needed our guilt taken away, and we needed a righteousness we did not have. His death bore the curse we had earned (3:13); his life of perfect obedience supplied the record we had failed to produce. Theologians call these his passive and active obedience, but the point is simple: God does not merely wipe your slate clean and leave it blank. He writes his Son’s life on it. When the Father looks at a believer, he sees a whole lifetime, some thirty years and more, of perfect love for God and neighbour, and credits them to you (Romans 5:19; 2 Corinthians 5:21). That is why every year of the hidden life at Nazareth was for you as much as the cross.

To redeem. The purpose comes in two halves. The first is exagorasē, the slave-market word of 3:13: to buy out. The price was himself.

Adoption as sons. And then something more than release. Huiothesia, placing as a son, is a Roman legal term. A man without a suitable heir would take a young man, often an adult, into his own family by a formal act before witnesses. From that day the adopted son bore the new father’s name and inherited on the same footing as any natural son, and in some forms his old debts were extinguished.
