God’s adoption goes further: Roman law allowed a father later to release a son; God never does (John 10:28–29).

Adoption and the new birth. The new birth makes a person a child of God by an inward act: a heart made alive, so that he begins to want what he never wanted (John 1:12–13). Adoption is an outward, legal act: a standing conferred, a name given, an inheritance settled. It is also distinct from justification: we are not only declared righteous in the court, we are welcomed into the family, given the Father’s name, his care, his discipline and his inheritance. On a day when the inward evidence is hard to find, the outward act stands exactly where it stood, because it was never yours to perform.

More than a rescue. Redemption alone would have been extraordinary: the slave bought out of the market and set at liberty at the gate. God did not stop at the gate. He gave him his own name and walked him into the house as a son with the same inheritance as the firstborn. That is not a rescue. That is a family.

Does sons leave out daughters? No. Paul uses sons because in the ancient world it was sons who inherited, and he wants every believer to know they have the heir’s full standing. He has just said there is neither male nor female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus (3:28). So a Christian woman is a son in exactly this sense: not lesser, not a dependant on someone else’s portion, but an heir in her own right. Elsewhere the Lord says it outright: you shall be sons and daughters to me (2 Corinthians 6:18).

In everyday life. Anyone who has adopted knows that the paperwork matters: the day the court signs, the child’s name is changed and no one can take it back. When you are tempted to think your standing with God rises and falls with your week, remember that your adoption was settled by the Son’s blood, not by your behaviour, and receive your Father’s correction without fearing that it means rejection (Hebrews 12:5–11).

verseByVerse.quote: And because you are sons, God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, “Abba! Father!” So you are no longer a slave, but a son, and if a son, then an heir through God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because you are sons. The order of the first four words settles many anxious questions. Not: cry Abba hard enough and you will become a son. The sonship comes first, established by the Son’s redemption in verse 5; the Spirit is sent because of it. The felt experience is the consequence of the status, never the cause. So when the feeling is absent, and for many believers it is absent for long stretches, in illness, in depression, in grief, in plain tiredness, nothing has happened to the sonship. A son asleep in his bed is as much his father’s son as a son laughing at his table.

Two sendings. God sent his Son (v. 4); God has sent the Spirit of his Son (v. 6), the same verb twice. The Son was sent into the world to do something for us; the Spirit into our hearts to do something in us. Salvation is not a transaction between God and a stranger. It is the whole Godhead, Father, Son and Spirit, bringing a family home.

The Spirit of his Son. He is named as the Son’s own Spirit, because what he brings into the believer’s heart is the Son’s relationship to the Father. You are brought inside his. You come to God the way Jesus came to him: as a child who expects to be heard. Jesus taught his disciples to begin with the word he used himself, Father (Luke 11:2), and the Spirit makes that word true in your mouth.

Crying, “Abba! Father!” It is often said that Abba is baby-talk, a toddler’s Daddy. It is not; grown men used it of their fathers all their lives. Abba is the Aramaic word for father used within the family: warm, domestic, not the reverent circumlocution of the synagogue, but the word a son would use turning round in the doorway. And the verb, krazō, is not a whisper. It is a loud, heartfelt cry, the cry of a child who knows he will be heard. The Son who could say Abba by right, from all eternity, shares that word with people who had no right to it at all, and the Spirit puts it in their mouths so that their poorest prayers arrive at the throne in the accent of the Son.

Who is doing the crying? Paul says here that the Spirit cries, and in Romans he says we cry, the Spirit himself bearing witness with our spirit that we are children of God (Romans 8:15–16). Both are true, and together they are enormous comfort: the prayer of a Christian is the Spirit of God praying in him. So the man who says he cannot pray, who gets three words in and dries up, who feels nothing, who is ashamed of how thin it sounds, is describing the outside of something. The cry that reaches the Father is the Son’s Spirit, and he is not thin.

So should I call God Daddy? You may speak to him with the warmth and directness of a child, and you should. But Abba is not a licence for casualness. Jesus said Abba in the garden (Mark 14:36), in the hour when, Luke tells us, his sweat became like great drops of blood (Luke 22:44, a verse missing from some early manuscripts), and in the same breath he said, not what I will, but what you will. The word holds intimacy and reverence together, as a good son’s love for a good father does. So come close, come often, come without rehearsing; and remember who it is you are calling Father. The nearness is astonishing precisely because he is so great.

No longer a slave. In verse 7 Paul narrows from you plural to the singular: he wants each believer to hear it personally. No longer: slavery is now your history rather than your condition. Son: the status, given. Heir: believers are heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ (Romans 8:17), and through God, not by the law.

In the flow. With verse 7 the argument that began at 3:1 reaches its goal. Paul opened by asking how the Galatians received the Spirit (3:2); now he tells them who that Spirit is. And from here the letter turns from argument to appeal: how can you go back to slavery (4:8–9)?

What exactly do I inherit? First and greatest, God himself: the LORD is my portion (Lamentations 3:24), and eternal life is to know him (John 17:3). Then everything that is Christ’s, because you are a fellow heir with him: the new heavens and new earth, the meek inheriting the earth (Matthew 5:5), an inheritance imperishable, undefiled and unfading, kept in heaven for you (1 Peter 1:4). You have a share of it now, in the Spirit, who is the guarantee or down payment of the rest (Ephesians 1:14). And it cannot be lost, because it is not kept by you. It is kept for you, and you are kept for it.

What if I do not feel any of this? Then you are in the company of many of God’s dearest children. The Spirit’s witness is not always a feeling of warmth. Often it is quieter: you cannot stop coming back to Christ; you hate your sin and want to be holy; when you are in trouble, the word that rises to your lips is still Father. Those are the Spirit’s work. Feelings come and go with sleep, health and circumstance; your adoption does not. Rest on the promise, keep praying the word Father even when it feels dry, and let the feeling follow when God gives it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God is our Father in the same way he is Christ’s. Christ is the eternal Son by nature; we are sons by adoption and grace. Jesus kept the distinction carefully: I am ascending to my Father and your Father (John 20:17), not our Father as though the two were the same. But in Christ, we share his place, and the Father loves us with the love with which he has loved him (John 17:23).

In everyday life. Begin your praying with the word Abba, Father, and stay on it for a moment before you ask for anything. And when you are tempted to slink back to God like a hired servant, rehearsing why he should let you in, remember the prodigal: he had his speech ready, and his father never let him finish it (Luke 15:18–24).
verseByVerse.note: “Abba” is the Aramaic word for “father,” used within the family.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before they knew God, the Galatians were enslaved to beings that are not gods. Now that they are known by God, how can they turn back to slavery by observing days and seasons (vv. 8–10)? Paul fears his labour was wasted (v. 11). He recalls how they welcomed him, sick as he was (vv. 12–15), and asks whether he has become their enemy by telling the truth (v. 16). The rival teachers court them for their own ends (vv. 17–18), while Paul is in labour again until Christ is formed in them (vv. 19–20).
verseByVerse.theology:
Two Kinds of Bondage, and the Goal of Ministry

When Paul sets the Judaizers’ calendar beside the pagan one the Galatians had left (vv. 8–10), he is speaking of what it does, not saying the two are morally the same: any God-given thing made the ground of our acceptance will behave like an idol. Moralism is not a minor error but a rival gospel, and it produces its own bondage.

Verse 9 contains one of Paul’s plainest statements of election, given in passing as a pastoral correction. To be known by God is for God to set his love on a person and claim him (Jeremiah 1:5). And v. 19 gives the goal of all ministry: not attendance, giving or doctrinal precision, but Christ formed in his people, taking shape from within like a child in the womb.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Galatians had loved Paul extravagantly (vv. 14–15) and had cooled by v. 16, and vv. 17–18 explain why: the Judaizers courted them and flattered them, then held the door a few inches short of open. Paul wanted not their loyalty to him but Christ formed in them (vv. 19–20).

Now: Verse 10 raises the question of Christmas, Easter and Sunday, and Paul answers it himself in Romans 14:5–6: what he attacks here is not the observance but the ground. Verses 17–18 describe spiritual manipulation with uncomfortable accuracy, and v. 13 belongs to the reader whose plans have been rerouted by illness.

verseByVerse.quote: Formerly, when you did not know God, you were enslaved to those that by nature are not gods. But now that you have come to know God, or rather to be known by God, how can you turn back again to the weak and worthless elementary principles of the world, whose slaves you want to be once more?
verseByVerse.commentary:
By nature are not gods. Paul turns the argument on the Galatians’ own past. Galatia was crowded with religion: the mother goddess with her ecstatic priests, the imperial cult, the household shrines. The Galatians had been intensely religious and enslaved at the same time, to beings who did not exist as gods (1 Corinthians 8:4–5), and it had still owned them. A career, a reputation, a body, a bank balance, the approval of a parent: each can be served with the same anxious devotion, demanding more and never saying enough, and each of them too is by nature not a god.

Are idols nothing, or demons? Both, in different senses. The gods the idols represent do not exist as gods; they are by nature not gods. But Paul says elsewhere that what pagans sacrifice they offer to demons and not to God (1 Corinthians 10:20). Behind the empty idol stand real spiritual powers who use the worship of nothing to enslave people (compare v. 3). So an idol is a lie with a liar behind it.

Or rather to be known by God. Paul begins a sentence and corrects himself in the middle of it. The first way of saying it puts the Galatians in the active seat, as though the decisive event were their discovery. Yes, they know God now, and it is the sweetest thing about them. But the verb belongs to God. They were known: sought, chosen and drawn, before they had turned a single thought toward him.

Known means loved. In Scripture, for God to know a person is for God to set his love on him and claim him: before I formed you in the womb I knew you (Jeremiah 1:5); you only have I known of all the families of the earth (Amos 3:2); if anyone loves God, he is known by God (1 Corinthians 8:3). Some read known by God as meaning only that God foresaw their faith, but that turns Paul’s correction upside down: they came to know God because God first knew them. This is election, God’s free choice to set his love on his people before they chose him (Ephesians 1:4), introduced not as a seminar topic but as a pastoral correction on the way past.

Known by the Shepherd. I know my own and my own know me, Jesus said, and I lay down my life for the sheep (John 10:14–15). To be known by God is to be one of those for whom the Shepherd died. It is the opposite of the most terrible sentence he will ever speak to anyone: I never knew you (Matthew 7:23).

Where the doctrine earns its keep. If your Christian life began with you, it can be ended by you, and every wobble is a threat to it. If it began with God knowing you, then the thing underneath your faith is not your grip. So ask the assurance question the right way round: not, do I know God well enough, but, does God know me? And the evidence that he does is that you are asking at all.

Weak and worthless. Weak (asthenēs): they cannot deliver what they demand. Worthless (ptōchos): literally beggarly, with nothing in the account. Going back to the law as a system of righteousness is as much slavery as going back to idols, and both leave a man begging from a pauper.

Whose slaves you want to be once more? Why would freed slaves want to go back? Paul will not let them describe this as being pressured. Somewhere in them, they wanted it. That is the strangest fact about religious bondage: a system that tells you exactly what to do and exactly where you stand is restful in a way that grace, at first, is not. Grace gives you nothing to hold. Slavery hands you a list. Israel in the wilderness, not long out of Egypt, was already remembering the cucumbers and the melons and forgetting the whips (Numbers 11:5).

Why would anyone want to go back? Because slavery feels safe and freedom feels exposed. Under a list, you always know where you stand, and you can measure yourself against other people. Under grace, you stand where Christ has put you, and you have nothing to bring and nothing to boast about. For proud hearts that is hard. It is also the only place where rest is real. If you notice in yourself a longing for a system that would tell you precisely how good you are, treat that longing as Paul treats it: not as a sign of seriousness, but as the old slave in you reaching for his chains.

For worship. He knew us first. While the Galatians were still carrying offerings to statues that could not see them, the living God had set his love on them and was sending a sick missionary up the road to find them. He found us among the idols, called us by name, and has written that name where no beggarly power can erase it.

parallels.desc: no gods, but the work of men’s hands

verseByVerse.quote: You observe days and months and seasons and years! I am afraid I may have labored over you in vain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You observe days! The exclamation mark carries the whole weight. A Jew raised on that calendar is looking at Gentile converts keeping it, and he can hardly speak. The verb, paratēreō, means to observe with anxious care.

The whole year. The four terms most likely map onto the Jewish year: Sabbaths, new moons, the festivals, and the sabbatical years (Colossians 2:16). Not a stray superstition, but the God-given calendar of the Old Testament, kept as a requirement for righteousness on the advice of men who told them their faith was insufficient without it.

The ground, not the observance. Paul is attacking not the observance in itself but the ground. The Galatians were taking on the calendar as the thing that would complete their standing with God. The same act can be worship or slavery depending on what it is being asked to do. Writing to Rome, Paul allows both practices in the same congregation, each fully convinced in his own mind and neither despising the other (Romans 14:5–6), provided neither is made a way of earning standing with God.

Watching the clock after the hour has struck. The whole calendar of Israel had been counting toward the fullness of time (4:4). To go back to watching it as the ground of acceptance is to keep staring at the clock after the guest you were waiting for has arrived and is sitting at your table.

Where Christians differ: holy days. Some say this verse forbids Christians from keeping any special days, including Sunday, Christmas or Easter. Others insist on strict keeping of the Jewish seventh-day Sabbath. And many Reformed Christians, following the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession, hold that the fourth commandment still binds as the Christian Sabbath, now kept on the Lord’s Day, so that Paul here condemns only the Jewish ceremonial days (Westminster 21.7–8; 1689 22.7–8); they are serious, godly brothers, and their reading deserves respect. This commentary’s view: Paul condemns observing days as a requirement for being right with God, as part of the old covenant law. The Old Testament Sabbath was a shadow fulfilled in Christ (Colossians 2:16–17), who is himself our rest (Matthew 11:28; Hebrews 4:9–10). Gathering on the Lord’s Day, the day of resurrection, is not a return to the law, but a privilege of the new covenant (Acts 20:7; Revelation 1:10): Christians gladly set it apart for worship, fellowship and rest, out of joy and wisdom rather than as a binding law with rules about work, and no one may bind another’s conscience about it (Romans 14:5). Christians may also remember events like Christ’s birth and resurrection, as long as these are not made a means of righteousness or bound on others’ consciences.

So should I keep Sunday differently from other days? Yes, gladly, but as a gift, not a test. The Lord’s Day is the day Christ rose, and his people have gathered on it since the first Easter. Make it the day you meet with the church, hear the word, share the Lord’s Supper, and rest from ordinary work as far as your calling allows. Many find a quieter Sunday a great blessing to the soul. But do not make your way of keeping it the measure of other Christians, and do not imagine that a well-kept Sunday puts God in your debt. It is a feast with your Father, not a payment to him.

Everybody has a calendar. Sunday attendance, the daily reading before work, the fast in Lent, family devotions: all good, and all potentially either. A Christian who has missed church through flu and feels sorrow is worshipping. A Christian who has missed it and feels exposed is observing days, and the cure is not to try harder next Sunday but to hear again that Christ has done it all.

I am afraid I may have labored over you in vain. Then the mood drops. The man who has been issuing anathemas admits to being frightened. He does not say they are lost, and the restraint is deliberate. He has given these towns a great deal: if they are the churches of Acts 14, the stoning at Lystra and the long roads walked twice over (Acts 14:19–23). He can see all of it going.

Does Paul fear that the Galatians are lost? He fears for them; he does not pronounce on them. Some of those in the churches may never have been truly converted, and Paul knows that a church can contain both. But he writes to them as his little children (v. 19), and his fear is the anguish of a father. Warnings like this are one of the means God uses to keep his people from falling away (compare 5:4): the true child hears the warning and runs back, and in running back proves that God’s hold on him was real. Those whom God has truly known he will keep (John 10:28–29), and he keeps them partly by letters like this one.

For worship. All the days and seasons of the old calendar were sketches of one Person: the Sabbath of the rest he gives, the Passover of the Lamb he is, the Day of Atonement of the blood he shed once for all. When the substance has come, the shadows bow to him, and his people gather on the morning of his rising to celebrate that the work is finished, and that the One who rested in the tomb on the Sabbath rose on the first day to make all things new.

verseByVerse.quote: Brothers, I entreat you, become as I am, for I also have become as you are. You did me no wrong.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Brothers, I entreat you. The tone changes completely: brothers, family. Entreat, deomai, is the verb for begging, the word of a man who has run out of arguments and is simply asking.

Become as I am. More specific than a general appeal to imitate Paul. Paul was a Jew of impeccable pedigree, circumcised the eighth day, a Pharisee (Philippians 3:5). He had every marker the Judaizers were selling, by birth, and he had laid them down, living among Gentiles as a Gentile (1 Corinthians 9:21). So the appeal is: I gave up my law-keeping to stand where you stand, on Christ alone. Do not walk into the room I walked out of. Paul became as the Galatians were, but he was only following his Lord a long way behind. The Son of God set aside the glory of heaven and became as we are, flesh and blood, under the law, numbered with the transgressors, so that we might become as he is: sons, free, beloved, heirs.

What it cost him. Writing to Philippi, Paul listed everything he had laid down and said he counted it all as loss, as rubbish, because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ (Philippians 3:7–8). The word is what you throw out. A man who has Christ needs no other ground to stand on: he wants only to be found in him, not having a righteousness of his own that comes from the law (Philippians 3:9).

What are you holding on to? Which puts a question to anyone reading who has never had to give anything up for Christ. Not a guilty question: some believers are simply spared it. But most of us are carrying something we have never once considered laying down: a family standing, a competence we are known for, a record of respectability, a theological rigour that has become an identity. None of those is wrong to have. Every one of them is fatal to hold on to as the thing that makes you acceptable, and the way to find out which you are doing is to ask what it would take from you if it were gone.

You did me no wrong. When he was with them, they treated him well. People who are furious usually have a personal injury somewhere, and Paul forecloses it: this is not a personal quarrel, and he wants that off the table so it cannot be used to explain away what he is saying. Christ did us no wrong, and we did him every wrong, and he still came down to stand where we stood.

The weapon he laid down. Anyone who has to say a hard thing to someone they love is tempted to let the personal hurt do the work, because a wound wins arguments. Paul clears his own grievance out of the way so that they have nothing to react to except the truth.

How do I raise a hard truth without making it about me? Separate the issue from your feelings before you speak. Ask yourself honestly whether you are hurt, and if you are, deal with that before God first, so that it does not leak into the conversation. Then speak about the thing itself, the teaching, the behaviour, the danger, in plain words. Say, as Paul does, that you are not nursing a grievance, and mean it. Make clear that you love the person and want their good. And if they are hurt by what you say, do not reach for your own hurt to win the exchange. Let the truth carry its own weight.

verseByVerse.quote: You know it was because of a bodily ailment that I preached the gospel to you at first, and though my condition was a trial to you, you did not scorn or despise me, but received me as an angel of God, as Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A bodily ailment. Paul takes them back to the day he arrived. The gospel came to Galatia because Paul was ill. It seems he had not planned to preach there, or not then; something happened to his body that stopped or diverted him, and in that condition he preached, and churches were born.

What was the ailment? We do not know, and the honest answer is better than a confident one. Some have suggested malaria caught in the coastal lowlands, which would drive a man up onto the Anatolian plateau where these towns are. Some suggest a disease of the eyes, on the strength of the gouged-out eyes in verse 15 and the large letters of 6:11. Others have thought of the thorn in the flesh of 2 Corinthians 12. Paul does not say, and every generation of sick Christians has been the richer for his silence, because it means no one can be told that their particular affliction is not the kind God uses.

Not the obstacle but the mechanism. The illness was the occasion of the mission, though Paul could only have seen it afterwards. Joseph in the pit, Jeremiah in the cistern, John on Patmos, Paul in chains writing the prison letters: God’s habit of building his church out of interrupted plans is nearly the rule.

And though my condition was a trial to you. Whatever it was, it was hard to look at. In that culture some saw illness as a sign of demonic attack or divine displeasure, and a visibly sick preacher announcing the favour of God was an awkward package.

You did not scorn or despise me. The second verb, from ekptyō, means literally you did not spit out. Meeting a visibly diseased person, you might spit, to ward off the contagion and the evil eye assumed to be behind it. Hold that beside 3:1, where Paul asked who had bewitched them. The Galatians had once refused to treat a sick preacher as a man under a curse. Now someone has looked at them and they are enchanted.

As an angel of God. They treated a sick, unimpressive stranger as God’s messenger, even as Christ Jesus; and in the only sense that matters, he was. Whoever receives you receives me, Jesus said (Matthew 10:40).

Does God really use sickness for good, or is that just something people say? He really does, though not always in ways we can see at the time, and never by making the sickness itself good. Illness is part of the curse, and Christ came to undo it. But God, who rules all things, bends even the curse to serve his children (Romans 8:28). Here the evidence is a whole province of churches. In your case it may be a doctor who hears the gospel, a nurse who watches you trust God, a friendship that would never have happened, or simply a deepening of your own faith that nothing else could have worked. You are allowed to pray for healing, and you should. You are also allowed to believe that the months you thought were wasted are not.

How should I treat a sick or weak Christian, or a weak preacher? As the Galatians first treated Paul. Do not measure a messenger by his health, polish or charm. Visit the sick, sit with the disabled, listen to the preacher who stammers, and receive Christ’s word through them. Many churches quietly honour the strong and forget the weak, and in doing so they miss the very people through whom God most often works (1 Corinthians 1:27; 12:22).

For worship. The gospel arrived in Galatia carried by a sick man, and it arrived in the world carried by a crucified one: a man of sorrows and acquainted with grief, one from whom men hide their faces (Isaiah 53:3). The world spat on him, literally, and he bore it. Our God has always loved to put his treasure in jars of clay, so that the surpassing power belongs to him and not to us (2 Corinthians 4:7).
verseByVerse.note: We do not know what the illness was; some think it affected his eyes.

verseByVerse.quote: What then has become of your blessedness? For I testify to you that, if possible, you would have gouged out your eyes and given them to me. Have I then become your enemy by telling you the truth?
verseByVerse.commentary:
What then has become of your blessedness? The word is makarismos, from the same root as the Beatitudes’ blessed: the state of being congratulated, the joy and happiness of people who know they have been given everything. Paul is not asking where their doctrine went. He is asking where their joy went, and he asks it as a man who remembers what they were like.

Legalism changes the atmosphere first. Legalism does not usually announce itself by error first, but by a change of atmosphere. The doctrine is still broadly right, the meetings still happen, and the gladness has gone out of the room, replaced by an earnest, watchful, slightly anxious carefulness that everyone mistakes for seriousness. If you want to know whether a church has drifted, do not start with its confession. Start with whether anyone in it looks relieved.

The blessing David spoke of. In Romans Paul writes that David speaks of the blessing of the one to whom God counts righteousness apart from works: blessed are those whose lawless deeds are forgiven (Romans 4:6–7). That was the Galatians’ blessedness: the joy of being forgiven, and it lasts exactly as long as Christ’s work is the ground you stand on. Add law to Christ and forgiveness feels conditional again.

Gouged out your eyes. It may be a proverb for giving away what you value most, or a hint that his ailment affected his eyes. Either way, there was nothing they would not have given him.

Have I then become your enemy by telling you the truth? And then verse 16, a lonely sentence. The word for telling the truth is alētheuōn: truthing, dealing truthfully. It is the same word Paul uses in Ephesians when he tells the church to speak the truth in love (Ephesians 4:15). And consider the position he is now in. He has not changed. He has said the same thing he always said. What has changed is what they are willing to hear, and the effect is that the man who loves them most is now filed as the opposition. Truth-tellers are often treated as enemies.

Two things held together. Being treated as the enemy is not proof that you were wrong: Paul is right and unwelcome at the same time. Nor is it proof that you were right: some men are treated as enemies because they told the truth, and some because they enjoyed telling it. The test is what Paul does next: he does not withdraw or harden, and within three verses he is calling them my little children. Truth-telling that has stopped hurting the one who does it has usually stopped being love (2 Corinthians 2:4). The truest Friend who ever lived told the truth and was made an enemy for it. He came to his own, and his own people did not receive him (John 1:11). And he did not withdraw, and he did not harden. He prayed for them from the cross, and he loved us while we counted him our enemy, and made us his friends.

I have lost my joy. Does that mean I have drifted into legalism? Not necessarily. Joy can be dimmed by grief, illness, depression, exhaustion or long trials, and those are not sins. But it is worth asking one honest question: has my confidence before God become tied to my performance? If you find that you feel accepted only on good weeks, that is very often where the joy has leaked away. Go back to the gospel itself. Read Galatians 2:20 and Romans 8:1 slowly and believe them about yourself. Joy grows where grace is believed, not where it is merely agreed with.

What if someone treats me as an enemy for telling them the truth? Check yourself first: were you right, and were you loving? If you were harsh, apologise for the harshness without withdrawing the truth. Then keep loving them. Do not cut them off, do not gossip about them, do not harden. Keep praying for them, and keep the door open. Paul did not stop writing to the Galatians; he wrote them this letter.

verseByVerse.quote: They make much of you, but for no good purpose. They want to shut you out, that you may make much of them. It is always good to be made much of for a good purpose, and not only when I am present with you,
verseByVerse.commentary:
They make much of you, but for no good purpose. Paul names the technique, and it has never gone out of use. The verb is zēloō: to court, to pay ardent attention to, as a suitor might. The Judaizers were not bullying the Galatians; they were flattering them, singling them out, making them feel worth the trouble of a long journey.

They want to shut you out. And then the second move, which is the point of the first: exclude the Galatians from Paul and the true fellowship, so that they would depend on the teachers and court them in return. The courting is bait; the shutting out is the hook: belonging that is always nearly his and never quite. And it works because of something in us. Every human heart is hungry to be noticed, chosen and approved, and whoever seems to feed that hunger can lead us almost anywhere. The only safe place for it is the one approval that cannot be withdrawn: God’s, given in Christ (3:26).

The anatomy of manipulation. That is the pattern of spiritual manipulation, and it does not require a heretic. It happens wherever a leader’s significance depends on being needed, and it can be entirely sincere. The signs are consistent: unusual attention early; a suggestion that you have been seen more clearly here than anywhere else; a group with an inside; a standard you are always approaching; a gentle discouragement from friendships or teaching outside the group; and a quiet impression that leaving would be a betrayal.

Two marks of healthy zeal. Paul does not conclude in verse 18 that all such attention is wrong. The first mark is purpose: what do they want you for? A teacher who wants Christ formed in you will be delighted when you grow past needing him. A teacher who wants you to make much of him will find your independence threatening, and will say so in spiritual language. The second is durability: not only when I am present. Paul is doing exactly that as he writes: absent, unpopular, and still labouring over them.

Courting for another. Paul uses the suitor’s language of himself too: I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ (2 Corinthians 11:2). The false teachers courted the Galatians for themselves; Paul courts them for Christ. A faithful minister is the friend of the bridegroom, not the bridegroom (John 3:29). And there is one whose zeal for us never switches off when we are out of the room. Christ does not want us to need him less as we grow. He wants us to need him more, because he is the only one whose love grows by being leaned on.

What it does not mean. It does not mean warm attention is always manipulative, or that a church that welcomes newcomers eagerly is suspect. Watch where the attention is leading: toward Christ and the wider body of his people, or toward one leader and one group.

I think I may be in a group like this. What should I do? Start by testing it against Scripture and against wise believers outside the group. Ask: am I free to read and hear other faithful teachers? Am I encouraged to have Christian friends elsewhere? Is my standing with God tied, openly or quietly, to my loyalty here? Would leaving be treated as sin? If the answers worry you, talk to a trusted pastor or mature Christian from another church. You do not owe a group your conscience; you owe that to Christ. And if there is abuse, spiritual or otherwise, it must never be tolerated or covered: seek help, and if a crime has been committed, report it.

How do I make sure I am not the one doing this? Ask what you want from the people you help. Are you glad when they grow, find other friends and teachers, and need you less? Do you speak well of other faithful churches and leaders? Do you keep loving people who disagree with you or move on? If you are a leader, invite others to examine your influence. The aim of all ministry is that people make much of Christ, not of us (John 3:30).

In everyday life. You need no one’s inner circle, because the Father has already made you his child (3:26). So look at your own zeal: is there someone you have been warm to only while they were useful to you? Send them a message this week that asks nothing back.

verseByVerse.quote: my little children, for whom I am again in the anguish of childbirth until Christ is formed in you! I wish I could be present with you now and change my tone, for I am perplexed about you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
My little children. The anger drops out of the letter, and what is left is a parent. Many early manuscripts read teknia, little children, which would be the only time Paul uses that tender word; others read tekna, children, the reading most modern editions print. Either way it comes at the point where he has the least reason to be tender.

In the anguish of childbirth. Elsewhere he calls himself the churches’ father (1 Corinthians 4:15). Here he is their mother in labour: ōdinō, the word for birth pangs. He went through it once to bring them to birth, and now a second time. It is a way of saying he is being torn.

Until Christ is formed in you! Not until they see he was right. The verb is morphoō, to take shape, from the root of conformed to the image of his Son (Romans 8:29): something taking its proper shape from the inside, like a child in the womb. The aim is not that they look like Paul, or keep the law, but that they look like Christ (2 Corinthians 3:18).

The metric of ministry. A congregation can be strong in attendance, giving and doctrinal precision while Christ is no more formed in them than he was a decade ago. Paul’s metric is brutal in its simplicity: do these people look more like Jesus than they did? A ministry that produces admirers, partisans, or well-informed critics of other churches, has produced something, but not this.

What does Christ formed in me actually look like? It looks like the fruit Paul names in the next chapter: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control (5:22–23). It looks like a growing humility that does not need to be noticed, a readiness to forgive, a love for the unlovely, courage in suffering, and a deepening delight in the Father. It does not happen by willpower. The Spirit forms Christ in us through the word, prayer, the Lord’s Supper, the fellowship of the church and the daily trials God sends. It is usually slow, often invisible to the person himself, and very often seen first by others.

Change my tone. He knows how the letter sounds. He is not withdrawing the anathemas, but he would give a great deal to be in the room, because a letter cannot modulate and a voice can.

For I am perplexed about you. Aporoumai: at a loss, without a way through. The apostle who has just settled the doctrine of justification does not know what to do about this particular set of people. That is a mercy to anyone praying for someone who has drifted: certainty about the truth and bewilderment about a person are not incompatible.

What it does not mean. It does not mean they needed to be born again a second time; the new birth happens once (John 3:3–8; 1 Peter 1:23). Paul’s labour now is for their growth.

I am praying for someone who has drifted, and I do not know what to do. Then you are where Paul was. You do not have to have a plan to keep loving. Keep praying specifically that Christ would be formed in them, not merely that they would return to church or agree with you. Keep the relationship warm. Say the truth when there is an opportunity, and say it with your face, in person, rather than in a long message if you can. And leave the outcome with God. Paul was at a loss, and God still had the Galatians in hand.

For worship. Out of the anguish of his soul the Servant shall see and be satisfied (Isaiah 53:11): Christ laboured on the cross to bring a people to birth, and he does not abandon them in the womb. He is forming his Son in us now, slowly, through every trial and every Sunday, and when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is (1 John 3:2).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–31 — Hagar and Sarah: Two Covenants
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul turns to the story of Abraham’s two sons, Ishmael by the slave woman Hagar, born in the ordinary way, and Isaac by the free woman Sarah, born by promise (vv. 21–23). He reads them as two covenants: Hagar stands for Sinai and the present Jerusalem, in slavery with her children; Sarah for the Jerusalem above, which is free and is our mother (vv. 24–27). Believers, like Isaac, are children of promise, and should expect the opposition Isaac met (vv. 28–29). Scripture says to cast out the slave woman and her son, and believers are children of the free woman (vv. 30–31).
verseByVerse.theology:
Typology, and Why the Two Covenants Cannot Share a House

Verse 24 is not allegory of the kind that dissolves history. Paul treats the two sons as facts, and says the history was designed by God to carry a meaning the coming of Christ has made visible (Luke 24:27).

Verses 24–25 give the test for the whole section: what a covenant produces shows what kind of covenant it is, when it is used as a way of salvation. And v. 30 shows why grace and merit cannot be mixed: add merit to grace and the result is merit, because once our performance is part of the ground, the whole weight rests on it. Paul casts out a system, not persons; he is in labour for the people who hold it, and Genesis itself shows God caring for Ishmael (Genesis 21:17–20).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Judaizers presented themselves as Abraham’s true heirs. Verse 22 shows that physical descent was never the mark, and v. 29 explains why religious men were persecuting a Gentile church: if a farmer who believed last month is as accepted as a man who has kept the law for forty years, the forty years bought nothing.

Now: Verse 23 touches most of us: the situation you have decided you must arrange yourself because God is taking too long is Hagar’s tent. And v. 29 warns us to watch what rises in us when someone is blessed without having earned it.

verseByVerse.quote: Tell me, you who desire to be under the law, do you not listen to the law? For it is written that Abraham had two sons, one by a slave woman and one by a free woman. But the son of the slave was born according to the flesh, while the son of the free woman was born through promise.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Tell me, you who desire to be under the law, do you not listen to the law? The sarcasm is exact, and the passage turns on it. You want the law? Then let us read it. And Paul is about to demonstrate that the Judaizers, the teachers urging the Galatians under the law, have been quoting a book they have not understood. Note the second use of the word: the law here means the Torah, the five books of Moses as a whole, not the commandments as a code. Paul is going to Genesis.

In the flow. Verse 21 begins the last argument of the letter’s doctrinal section, and it gathers up every thread so far: Abraham and his true children (3:6–9, 29), promise against law (3:15–18), the slave and the son (4:1–7), flesh against Spirit (3:3). It leads straight into 5:1: Christ has set us free for freedom.

For it is written that Abraham had two sons. Ishmael by the slave woman Hagar, Isaac by his free wife Sarah (Genesis 16; 21). Physical descent from Abraham cannot be the qualification, because Ishmael had it. He was Abraham’s son, circumcised by Abraham’s own hand (Genesis 17:23–25), and outside the covenant line. Blood was never the mechanism, and the family tree proves it before you have left Genesis.

One by a slave woman and one by a free woman. A child born to a slave was a slave; a child born to the free wife was the heir.

Born according to the flesh. Verse 23 gives the real distinction: how each son came to exist. Ishmael was produced by a plan. God had promised Abraham a son; ten years passed (Genesis 16:3); Sarah did the arithmetic on her own body, concluded that God needed help, and offered her slave (Genesis 16:1–4). It was legal, customary, and it worked. That is what according to the flesh means here: not immorality, but competence. Human capability doing what it can, on God’s behalf, because waiting had become unbearable.

Born through promise. Isaac was produced by nothing at all. Sarah was ninety and past every natural possibility, and she had laughed at the announcement (Genesis 18:10–14). There was a promise, and then, at the time God had said, there was a baby (Genesis 21:1–2). Is anything too hard for the LORD? That question is the question of the whole letter.

Children of promise in the Son of promise. Through Isaac shall your offspring be named (Genesis 21:12), and that offspring is Christ (3:16). So believers are children of promise like Isaac (4:28) because they are Christ’s (3:29). And the question asked at the tent door was answered again at Nazareth: nothing will be impossible with God (Luke 1:37).

Two ways of getting a result. What a capable person can arrange, and what only God can give. Everyone believes God can save; the live question is whether he needs the help. The Galatians were not planning to abandon Christ. They were proposing to assist him.

Hagar’s tent. Turn that on yourself, because the instinct is universal and it usually looks like responsibility. The thing you have decided you must arrange yourself because God is taking too long, the outcome you are engineering by means you would rather not examine: that is Hagar’s tent. It is usually not wickedness but Sarah with a calendar, right about the arithmetic and wrong about God.

So is it wrong to plan, or to work hard? No. Abraham’s fault was not that he acted but that he acted to secure by his own means what God had promised to give in his own way, and by a means God had not approved. Christians are told to work, plan, save, seek medical help and use every lawful means. The question is whether you are using means in faith, as God’s gifts, or in place of faith, because you have stopped believing he will keep his word. A good test is whether the plan requires you to bend God’s commands. Sarah’s plan did, and it filled the tent with grief for a generation (Genesis 16:4–6; 21:9–11).

For worship. Nobody arranged your new birth; nobody could have. The God who gave a son to a woman of ninety gave life to your dead heart, so that no one could mistake whose child you are. He gives life to the dead and calls into existence the things that do not exist (Romans 4:17), and every Christian is a laugh of joy in the tent of the impossible.
verseByVerse.note: Abraham’s son by the slave woman Hagar was Ishmael; his son by the free woman Sarah was Isaac, born by promise.

verseByVerse.quote: Now this may be interpreted allegorically: these women are two covenants. One is from Mount Sinai, bearing children for slavery; she is Hagar. Now Hagar is Mount Sinai in Arabia; she corresponds to the present Jerusalem, for she is in slavery with her children.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now this may be interpreted allegorically. This sentence troubles careful readers. The verb is allēgoreō: to speak another way, figuratively. In Paul’s century, Alexandrian interpreters, Philo above all, read the Old Testament in a way that dissolved the history: Abraham became the soul, Sarah virtue. If that is what Paul is doing, the door is open for anyone to make any text mean anything.

The history is his premise. But it is not what he is doing. He has just insisted that it is written that Abraham had two sons, and he treats the mothers and the manner of each birth as facts. He is saying that it happened, and that God so arranged it that it carries a meaning the coming of Christ has now made visible, as the risen Christ interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself (Luke 24:27). If God governs history, the pattern in a true story is not something a reader imposes; it is something the Author put there.

Where Christians differ: allegory in interpretation. Some use this passage to justify reading allegories into all of Scripture, finding hidden meanings unrelated to the plain sense. This commentary’s view: Paul’s method here is closer to typology, reading real people and events as patterns God built in to point forward to Christ, than to free allegory. He does not deny the history; he sees in it what God designed it to show (1 Corinthians 10:6, 11). Interpreters should first grasp the plain meaning of a text, and only find further meanings where Scripture itself warrants them. Paul, writing under inspiration, had that warrant; later interpreters must stay within what Scripture teaches.

These women are two covenants. Two arrangements by which people seek to stand before God, and two families they produce: at Sinai, a law to be kept; with Abraham, a promise to be believed (Genesis 15:18; Exodus 24:7–8). Feel what a first-century Jew would have felt: Hagar, the Egyptian slave who was sent away, is Sinai, where the law was given in fire.

Now Hagar is Mount Sinai in Arabia. Hagar’s descendants through Ishmael settled in Arabia (Genesis 25:12–18), where Sinai lies. But the deeper link is the pattern: a slave mother, a covenant that leads to slavery, children born into it.

The present Jerusalem. The actual city, the temple, the whole visible centre of the religion the Judaizers were selling, which had rejected Christ and clung to the law. In four clauses Paul puts the Jerusalem establishment on Hagar’s side of the family, and the Galatians on Sarah’s. A system that demands performance, used as a way of salvation, can only ever produce people in bondage, however holy the mountain it came from. You do not judge the tree by its address. Sinai thundered, and the people trembled at the foot of it and could not draw near. But Christ went up a different hill, outside the present Jerusalem, and bore the curse that Sinai pronounced. The law shows us the mountain we cannot climb; the gospel shows us the Son who climbed it for us.

Was the covenant at Sinai a bad thing, then? No. God gave it, and it was holy and good (Romans 7:12). It began with grace: “I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery” (Exodus 20:2). Its sacrifices pointed to Christ, and believing Israelites like David were justified by faith under it (Romans 4:6–8). But it was a covenant for a time of childhood (vv. 1–3): it kept Israel under strict rules, under the threat of curse, until Christ came (3:23–24). It could command but could not give the Spirit or a new heart (3:21; Jeremiah 31:31–33). So when people cling to Sinai after Christ has come, and treat its law as the way to be accepted by God, they are choosing slavery over sonship. Hagar stands for Sinai used in that way: the law cut off from the promise it was meant to serve.

Who frees the children of Sinai? Not Sinai. A covenant that bears children for slavery cannot also set them free; it has nothing to give them but its terms. The freedom Paul preaches comes from the Son, and he has said so a few sentences earlier: God sent forth his Son, born of woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons (4:4–5). Christ was born under the very law that held its children, kept it, and bore its curse, so that whoever trusts him, Jew or Gentile, is no longer a slave but a son.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Jewish people are rejected by God. The present Jerusalem means the system of law-keeping the false teachers offered, not the Jewish people as a race. Paul grieved for his own people with great sorrow and unceasing anguish (Romans 9:1–3). Any reading of this verse that feeds contempt for Jewish people has turned Paul’s own heart upside down.

How can I tell whether my church is a Hagar church or a Sarah church? Not by the strictness of its morals, because the free children of God love his law. Ask instead what people are trusting. Is the gospel of Christ’s finished work preached clearly and often, so that sinners leave knowing they are forgiven? Do people confess sins honestly, or only hide them? Are newcomers with messy pasts welcomed as fully as long-standing members? Is obedience urged as the fruit of grace, or as the price of acceptance? Free churches can be serious about holiness; what they are not is anxious about standing.

verseByVerse.quote: But the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother. For it is written, “Rejoice, O barren one who does not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who are not in labor! For the children of the desolate one will be more than those of the one who has a husband.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the Jerusalem above is free. The Galatians had been made to feel provincial, their membership depending on a committee far away in the real Jerusalem. Paul tells them their mother lives somewhere else: the heavenly Jerusalem, the city of God. Believers have already come to it (Hebrews 12:22); John sees her coming down out of heaven, prepared as a bride (Revelation 21:2). The believer’s citizenship is not pending. It is filed (Philippians 3:20).

And she is our mother. This is why the early church could call the church a mother: not because she gives grace of herself, but because God brings his children to birth within her through the word and Spirit, and feeds and raises them there.

Rejoice, O barren one. The quotation is Isaiah 54:1, the verse immediately after Isaiah 53, where the suffering servant, whom the New Testament names as Jesus (Acts 8:32–35), makes many to be accounted righteous. The barren woman is told to sing because of what the servant has just done. Her fruitfulness is purchased. The Servant was crushed, and the empty tent filled, and is filling still, with children from every tribe and tongue and people and nation.

In its own setting. In Isaiah the barren one is Zion in exile, emptied of her children. God tells her to start singing before there is anything visible to sing about, because the children are coming.

The children of the desolate one. Paul sees this fulfilled first in Sarah, decades with an empty tent while Hagar had a son; and then in the church, this small, mostly Gentile movement that would out-populate the establishment that despised it. It has, in thousands of languages.

The God of barren women. Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel, Hannah, Elizabeth: the line of promise runs straight through barren women, so that when the child finally comes nobody can mistake where he came from. The barren has borne seven, sang Hannah (1 Samuel 2:5). He waits until there is nothing left to explain it, and then he fills the tent.

A word for a particular reader. Some woman reading Galatians 4 is literally barren, and has been told to rejoice by people who meant well, and it landed like a stone. The text is not asking her to pretend. Isaiah’s command to sing is addressed to a woman whose grief is real and whose situation has not yet changed, and it is grounded not in optimism but in what God has promised to do. Scripture never asks anyone to feel that a loss is not a loss. It does say that the emptiness he leaves in a life for a while is not a verdict on it.

Does this promise that God will give me children? No, not in the sense of a guarantee of a pregnancy. Isaiah 54 is a promise to God’s people as a whole, fulfilled in the gathering of the church, not a pledge to every childless couple. God does sometimes give children after long barrenness, and it is right to pray for them. But many faithful believers never have children, and they are not less blessed or less fruitful. In Christ, the childless are given spiritual sons and daughters, a name better than sons and daughters (Isaiah 56:4–5), and a family in the church that is as real as any household. Your fruitfulness in God’s kingdom does not depend on your womb.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the church replaces Israel entirely. Jewish believers are part of the Jerusalem above too, from Peter and Paul to the present day. Christians differ on God’s purposes for the Jewish people as a nation (Romans 11:25–29), but agree that there is one family of Abraham, and that no one enters it except through Christ.

In everyday life. When you feel small, provincial, or excluded from the people who seem to matter in Christian circles, remember your address, and live this week as a citizen of the free city above: unafraid of the committees, generous, glad.

verseByVerse.quote: Now you, brothers, like Isaac, are children of promise. But just as at that time he who was born according to the flesh persecuted him who was born according to the Spirit, so also it is now.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Like Isaac. Before the hard verse comes, the assurance: not candidates, not probationers, but Isaac, the miracle child nobody could have produced.

How do I know which son I am? A reader will not simply accept the compliment, and he is right not to. Both sons were Abraham’s. Both lived in the same tent. Ishmael was circumcised and Isaac was circumcised, and for fourteen years Ishmael was the only son in that tent, so nobody watching could have told you which line the promise was attached to. Paul has already given the test, twice, and it is not a matter of intensity. Ishmael was not less sincere than Isaac and may well have worked harder. The difference is where each son came from. So ask what you are actually resting on when you are honest, and the answer usually surfaces fastest at the two extremes. After a good stretch, prayer flowing, temper holding, a real usefulness to somebody, does your confidence before God quietly rise? And after a bad one, does it fall? If it moves with your performance, you have been measuring the wrong thing, whatever you believe on paper; that confidence is Hagar’s, because it was produced by you. Most believers find their confidence moves a little; the answer is not despair but to rest again on Christ.

You are being told your name. The test is not, have I enough faith? That sends a man back inside himself to look for a quality he will never be able to weigh. Isaac did not qualify by being a better baby. If you are resting on what Christ has done, you are not being told to work up more assurance. You are being told your name.

Just as at that time. The reference is Genesis 21:9. On the day Isaac was weaned Abraham threw a feast, and Sarah saw Ishmael laughing, a play on Isaac’s own name, Yitzchaq, he laughs. Ishmael was most likely mocking the child at the party held in his honour. Paul calls it persecution: the older brother, produced by human arrangement, could not bear the child who was pure gift. Born according to the Spirit: Isaac’s birth by God’s power, as every believer’s new birth is. The child of promise was mocked at his own feast, and centuries later the true Son of promise was mocked at his: they clothed him in purple, bowed to him in jest, spat on him and laughed. The flesh has always hated the gift. But the mockers could not stop the inheritance from passing to the heir, and they cannot stop it now.

So also it is now. The people persecuting the Galatian churches were not pagans. They were religious men with a claim to Abraham, and what they could not tolerate was a family they had not qualified for.

The persecutor who was stopped. Paul knew this from the inside: he had been violently persecuting the church of God (1:13), until the risen Christ asked, Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? (Acts 9:4). The hostility of religious flesh toward the children of the Spirit is aimed, in the end, at Christ himself (John 15:18, 20), and he counts every blow as struck at him.

Why grace provokes rage. A man who has spent his life earning his standing has an enormous investment, and free grace writes it off. If the Gentile who believed last month is as accepted as the Pharisee who has kept the calendar for forty years, then the forty years bought nothing. Nobody hears that calmly. The elder brother in the parable is furious at exactly this, and he never once says an untrue thing about himself (Luke 15:29–30).

A comfort and a warning. A comfort: hostility from religious people is not evidence that you have gone wrong; it begins at a child’s birthday party in Genesis. And a warning, the more useful one. Watch what rises in you when someone is blessed without having earned it: the convert with the disgraceful history who is radiant, the newcomer given the opportunity you waited years for. That flicker is the flesh recognising the child of promise and resenting him for it.

What does persecution from religious people look like today? It is rarely violent in most Western churches, though in some places it is. More often it is mockery, suspicion and exclusion: being called careless about holiness because you preach free grace; being treated as second-class because you do not keep a group’s extra rules; being shut out of fellowship for questioning a leader. Do not exaggerate ordinary disagreement into persecution, and do not assume every critic is an Ishmael; sometimes your critics are right. But when you are opposed for trusting Christ alone, recognise the old pattern and take heart.

verseByVerse.quote: But what does the Scripture say? “Cast out the slave woman and her son, for the son of the slave woman shall not inherit with the son of the free woman.” So, brothers, we are not children of the slave but of the free woman.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But what does the Scripture say? Paul has been arguing; now he stops and lets the text pronounce. Scripture settles it. And the sentence he chooses is the hardest in the chapter.

Cast out the slave woman. It is Genesis 21:10, and in Genesis it is Sarah who says it, apparently in anger, and the thing is very displeasing to Abraham (Genesis 21:11). What makes it Scripture rather than a domestic quarrel is verse 12, where God tells Abraham to do as Sarah says: through Isaac shall your offspring be named. The line of promise must not be confused with the line of human arrangement.

What is to be cast out? Read what Paul does with it. He is not issuing instructions about persons; he applies it to the two covenants he has been contrasting for ten verses. The thing that cannot stay is the system: law-keeping as the ground of acceptance, sitting alongside the gospel as a supplementary option. Law-religion and grace cannot share the inheritance. The Galatians were trying to keep both mothers in the house. Paul says the arrangement is impossible, and not because grace is intolerant. Because the two produce different children, and one of them has no share in the estate. So the Galatians should cast out the false teachers’ message, and refuse its teachers the authority to shape the church.

Not a mixture but a failure. Add merit to grace and you do not get a moderate position; you get merit, because the moment my performance is part of the ground, the whole weight has shifted onto it. Otherwise grace would no longer be grace (Romans 11:6). A little law as the basis of standing is like a little water in petrol. It is not a mixture. It is a failure.

The son remains for ever. Jesus laid down the same household law: the slave does not remain in the house for ever; the son remains for ever. So if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed (John 8:34–36). Those he frees remain in the Father’s house as long as he does. And consider how it was done. The only Son who ever had that standing by right laid it down, was counted with the slaves, and was cast out to suffer outside the gate (Hebrews 13:12), so that the children of the slave woman could be brought into the house as heirs. Sarah’s son kept the inheritance because Ishmael was sent away. Ours was kept because the true Son was.

What it does not mean. It does not mean cruelty to people. Paul casts out a doctrine; he spends the surrounding verses in labour pains for the people who hold it. Anyone who quotes verse 30 to justify being hard with a person has read the sentence and missed the chapter. And Genesis itself handles Ishmael tenderly: God hears the boy crying in the desert and is with him as he grows (Genesis 21:17–20). Scripture is more tender than our use of it.

Does this mean my church should expel people who hold wrong views? Not on the strength of this verse alone. Paul’s target is a false gospel that adds works to Christ for justification, which he has already called accursed (1:8–9). A church must not let such teaching be taught from its pulpit, and teachers who persist in it after patient correction must not be given authority. Church discipline exists for that (Titus 3:10). But most disagreements among Christians are not about the ground of salvation, and they are to be borne with in love. And even those who are put out of fellowship are to be prayed for and pursued, with the aim of their restoration (2 Thessalonians 3:14–15).

Not children of the slave. The chapter lands on an identity, not a warning, and the pronoun is we: Paul puts himself in the sentence with them. Chapter 5 is built on this line: for freedom Christ has set us free (5:1). He is telling them what they are.

How do I cast out the slave woman in my own heart? By refusing, every day, to let your performance become the ground of your standing with God. When you have a good day, do not let it make you feel more accepted; thank God for the grace that helped you. When you have a bad day, do not let it make you feel less accepted; confess it, and rest again on Christ. Throw out the inner ledger. Then obey, gladly, because the free son loves his Father’s house and his Father’s ways.

For worship. The heir of all things has made us fellow heirs. Scripture says of the slave’s son, cast him out; the Son says of everyone the Father gives him, whoever comes to me I will never cast out (John 6:37). No one can snatch from the Father’s hand a child he has brought in (John 10:28–29). The door of the Father’s house has closed behind us, not in front of us.
