5.title: For Freedom Christ Has Set Us Free: The Spirit and the Flesh
5.overview:
In chapter 5 the letter turns from argument to life. Having argued for freedom from the law as a way of being justified, Paul shows that this freedom produces not moral chaos but something better than law-keeping ever could, and he answers two questions: what does freedom look like in practice, and if not the law, what shapes a Christian’s behaviour?

Freedom is not licence (v. 13). The Judaizers feared lawlessness; Paul’s answer is not to bring the law back but to walk by the Spirit. The whole law is fulfilled in love of neighbour (v. 14), and the Spirit grows that love in believers. The heart of the chapter sets the works of the flesh beside the fruit of the Spirit (vv. 19–23): many works, which human nature produces and which tear a community apart, against one fruit, a single character that is the character of Christ, grown by the Spirit in those who stay close to him.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 1 sums up four chapters: freedom is the goal, not a stage on the way to a stricter religion, so believers must stand firm and not take up the yoke of slavery again, the yoke Peter said no one could bear (Acts 15:10), when Jesus offers his own easy yoke (Matthew 11:29–30).

Verses 2–6 are the warning. Whoever accepts circumcision as what completes his standing has changed systems: Christ is of no advantage to him, he is obligated to keep the whole law, and he has fallen away from grace. But believers wait by faith, through the Spirit, for the hope of righteousness, and what counts is faith working through love.

Then the appeal (vv. 7–12). Someone cut in on them as they ran. This teaching did not come from the God who called them, and a little of it changes the whole. Yet Paul is confident in the Lord about them, leaves the troubler to God’s judgment, and refuses any gospel that removes the offence of the cross.
verseByVerse.theology:
Freedom as the Goal of Redemption, and What Falling from Grace Means

Gospel freedom is freedom from performance-based religion, the liberty to live as sons rather than as slaves calculating wages. It is not lawlessness: the law’s moral demands are fulfilled from within by those who walk by the Spirit, rather than imposed from outside on those who must earn their standing.

Verse 4 describes a change of position, not of conduct. To fall from grace here is to step off the ground of grace onto the ground of law, not to disgrace oneself. And because Paul writes v. 10 a few sentences later, confident about the same people, v. 4 is best read as the warning that keeps them from the thing it describes.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Circumcision was offered to the Galatians as an upgrade, a fuller belonging. Verses 2–3 show it was an exchange. Verse 12 would have struck hard locally, since the mother goddess, whose chief shrine was at Pessinus in Galatia, was served by priests who castrated themselves.

Now: Standing firm (v. 1) usually means refusing to answer the question where do I stand with God today by reaching for the last few days. And v. 8 gives a test for any new teaching: does it come to you the way the God who called you came to you?

verseByVerse.quote: For freedom Christ has set us free; stand firm therefore, and do not submit again to a yoke of slavery.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Galatians 5 turns from argument to practice. Stand firm in freedom, because to accept circumcision as necessary is to fall from grace (vv. 1–12); use freedom to serve one another in love (vv. 13–15); and walk by the Spirit, who wars against the flesh and bears his fruit (vv. 16–26). The chapter is the portrait of a freed people, drawn from the face of their Liberator.

For freedom Christ has set us free. Four chapters of argument are compressed into the line the letter is remembered by. Why say freedom twice? Because freedom is what it is for. It is not a stage on the way to something else, nor a probationary liberty, nor a transfer to a stricter and more mature religion. Christ released his people because he wanted them free.

Free from what, and free for what? Free from the law as a way of righteousness, from its curse (3:13), from the guardians and the elementary principles (4:1–9), from sin’s slavery, and from the endless anxious question of whether you have done enough. And free for God: to call him Father, to obey him from the heart, to love your neighbour without calculating. That needs saying, because a great many Christians treat grace as the doorway and law as the corridor beyond it. They will tell you cheerfully that they were saved by grace, and then describe a daily life in which everything depends on their performance. Paul says the door and the corridor are made of the same thing: the grace that brought you in is the same grace that carries you on, every day until the end: as you received Christ Jesus the Lord, so walk in him (Colossians 2:6).

Stand firm therefore. Stand fast, as a soldier holds his position. Freedom is not a resting state. Left alone, a free man drifts back toward slavery, because slavery is restful in a way that liberty is not. A slave is told what to do and knows exactly where he stands. Freedom asks you to live without a scoreboard, and that can feel harder than obedience.

A yoke of slavery. A yoke was the wooden frame laid across the shoulders of working animals: a picture of burden and servitude. The rabbis called the law’s yoke a glad discipline; Peter, at the Jerusalem council, called it a yoke that neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear (Acts 15:10). And Jesus also offers a yoke: take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart, and you will find rest for your souls; for my yoke is easy, and my burden is light (Matthew 11:29–30). So the question is never whether a man will wear a yoke. It is whose.

Again. The verb is passive: do not let yourselves be subjected. Nobody was going to force the Galatians; they were going to agree, for reasons that felt like devotion. And again is the sharpest word in the sentence, because these were Gentiles who had never been under Moses in their lives. Paul means that a return to law-keeping would land them back where their paganism had them: performing, appeasing, never sure.

What standing firm looks like. On a Wednesday, standing firm mostly looks like refusing to answer one question the way your instincts want to answer it. The question is, where do I stand with God today? The instinctive answer reaches for the last few days: how you prayed, how you spoke to your wife, whether you did the thing you promised yourself you would stop doing. Standing firm is declining to answer it that way. Not because the week does not matter; it matters a great deal. But it is not the ground you are standing on, and the day you let it become the ground, the yoke is back on your shoulders and nobody had to put it there.

Is it legalism to keep personal rules, like not drinking or fasting on Fridays? Not in itself. A Christian may freely adopt a rule for wisdom’s sake: to avoid a temptation, to discipline the body, to serve a weaker brother (Romans 14:21; 1 Corinthians 9:27). It becomes a yoke of slavery in two ways: when you think keeping it makes you more acceptable to God, and when you bind it on other Christians as though God had commanded it. So keep your rule if it helps you, hold it loosely, never use it to measure others, and never let it whisper that you are more pleasing to God than the brother who does not keep it.
verseByVerse.note: A yoke was the wooden frame joining working animals — a picture of burdensome obligation.

verseByVerse.quote: Look: I, Paul, say to you that if you accept circumcision, Christ will be of no advantage to you. I testify again to every man who accepts circumcision that he is obligated to keep the whole law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Look: I, Paul, say to you. He puts his name in the sentence, and the whole weight of his apostleship (chapters 1–2) on what comes next.

Of no advantage. Not less advantage. None. Yet circumcision is a small thing: a rite God himself commanded, which Paul says counts for nothing either way (v. 6). The issue is what it is being asked to do. If a man accepts circumcision as the thing that completes his standing with God, he has not added a little security to Christ. He has changed systems. And in the system he has entered, Christ is not an asset, because that system does not deal in gifts. It deals in obligations, and you cannot have Christ as a partial Saviour.

But Paul circumcised Timothy. A fair objection, and Paul’s opponents were evidently raising it (v. 11). Paul circumcised Timothy (Acts 16:3), yet refused to let Titus be circumcised (2:3). Because the two cases are opposite in everything that matters. Titus was a test case: the demand was made in Jerusalem, as a condition, to prove that a Gentile could not be fully accepted otherwise, and Paul did not yield even for a moment. Timothy’s mother was Jewish, so to the synagogues of the region he would have counted as a Jew left uncircumcised, and that would have shut the door of every building Paul wanted to preach in. Nobody claimed it justified him. It was a matter of access, not of standing.

The principle. One question governed Paul in each case: is anyone claiming this is necessary? When nobody is, he is flexible to the point of inconvenience; the moment somebody says you must, he will not move an inch. The same principle governs many secondary practices in church life.

May Christians circumcise their sons today, for health or family reasons? Yes. Neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts for anything (v. 6). Paul himself had Timothy circumcised for the sake of his witness among Jews (Acts 16:3). What is forbidden is circumcision as a requirement for being accepted by God. A Jewish Christian parent may circumcise his son as a mark of his heritage; no one may make it a condition of salvation.

What would circumcision be today? Anything added to Christ as a condition of being right with God. Nobody in your church is likely to demand circumcision, but plenty of things play its part: a particular experience you must have had, a style of worship, a political position, a level of Bible knowledge, a list of things good Christians do not do, a baptism in the right church, or a feeling of being sufficiently sorry. Any of these can be a good thing or a matter of conviction. The moment it becomes Christ and something, it becomes Christ of no advantage. Ask of any teaching: does it leave Christ standing alone as my whole righteousness?

Obligated to keep the whole law. Verse 3 closes the escape route. The Judaizers were selling one item, and Paul says there is no such thing: circumcision signs you up to the whole law (James 2:10). Take hold of a corner of the law and you have taken hold of all of it, for life, without a single failure. Nobody mentioned that in the sales pitch, and no one has ever kept it.

In everyday life. Finish this sentence honestly: I am right with God because Christ died and rose for me, and because I... If anything comes after the and, cross it out. Then live today out of the first half alone, and do your good works as a thank you, not as a down payment.

verseByVerse.quote: You are severed from Christ, you who would be justified by the law; you have fallen away from grace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Severed from Christ. This verse frightens people, and the reader most likely to be holding it is not a Judaizer but a Christian who has had a bad year. So begin with what the sentence actually says.

Not a scandal. In ordinary speech, to have fallen from grace means to have disgraced yourself: a scandal, a moral collapse, a public fall. The people Paul addresses have not fallen into sin; they have become more religious, not less. They are keeping a calendar and considering a rite, and they are doing it in order to please God more thoroughly. To fall from grace is to leave the sphere of grace for the sphere of works.

Two changes of position. Both halves of the sentence describe a change of position, not of behaviour. Severed (katargeō) means rendered inoperative, disconnected from any benefit. And Paul says who it applies to in the same breath: you who would be justified by the law. Justification is acquittal: guilt removed and the believer counted right with God, though not made sinless on the spot (Romans 4:5). The only question is on what ground the verdict is given, and Paul allows only one. And fallen away means falling out of grace as out of a place: you have stepped off the ground of grace onto the ground of law, and grace is where Christ does his work.

The lifeboat. Think of a man in a lifeboat who decides to swim alongside it, still holding the rope. He has not stopped believing in the boat; he has stopped being in it. Paul is not telling the Galatians that God has thrown them out. He is telling them what law-standing does: it does not add to Christ’s work, it replaces it, and there is no arrangement in which a man is partly justified by each.

Hold it beside verse 10. Six verses later, to the same people, Paul says: I have confidence in the Lord that you will take no other view. So verse 4 is not a verdict passed on the Galatians; it is the warning that will keep them from the thing described, and it works by being heard.

Where Christians differ: can a believer fall from grace? Some take this verse to mean true believers can lose their salvation: Arminian Christians read it that way, holding that the Galatians were real believers who could forfeit their salvation by trusting in the law, and they are right that the warning is real and must not be blunted. This commentary’s view: Paul is describing the meaning and consequence of seeking justification by law: it is a rejection of grace and Christ. Those who persist in it show they never truly rested on Christ (1 John 2:19). True believers may be confused and tempted, as the Galatians were, but God keeps his own (Philippians 1:6; John 10:28–29), and warnings like this one are among his means of keeping them. Those whom he justified he also glorified (Romans 8:30). Falling from grace here means abandoning the principle of grace, not a true believer being lost. That is why Paul can write verse 4 and verse 10 in the same breath.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that sinning makes you fall from grace. Grace is for sinners. Where sin increased, grace abounded all the more (Romans 5:20).

I am afraid this describes me. Does it? Ask what the verse actually describes: a person who is seeking to be justified by his own law-keeping and is at peace with that arrangement. Now ask whether that is you. If you are afraid because you know your record will not carry you, that fear is not the condition Paul is describing; it is the exact opposite of it. Nobody standing on his own performance is troubled by the news that performance will not do. A warning against a cliff is not a report that you have gone over it, and the people who read it most anxiously are almost always the ones furthest from the edge.

How would I know if I were trying to be justified by the law? Watch where your confidence goes when you think of standing before God. If you find yourself listing what you have done, how long you have been a Christian, how much you give, what you avoid, you are reaching for the rope instead of the boat. If you find yourself saying, nothing in my hands I bring, simply to the cross I cling, you are in grace. Most Christians drift between the two in a single week. The remedy is not to examine yourself harder but to look at Christ longer.

Grace has a name. Grace is not a policy in heaven but Christ himself, given for us. Paul can say severed from Christ and fallen away from grace in one breath because they are the same loss: the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation (Titus 2:11), and it appeared in a person. The boat in the picture is the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me (2:20), and his is the righteousness Paul wanted, not his own but that which comes through faith in Christ (Philippians 3:9). So the way back is not more effort but less: stop asking whether you have done enough, look at what he has done, and stand there.

verseByVerse.quote: For through the Spirit, by faith, we ourselves eagerly wait for the hope of righteousness. For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts for anything, but only faith working through love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For through the Spirit, by faith. Paul has just said you to those seeking justification by law; now he says an emphatic we ourselves, drawing a line down the middle of the room and inviting the Galatians back over it.

The hope of righteousness. Eagerly wait (apekdechometha) is to wait for a thing certainly coming and not here yet: a striking word to use of righteousness, when Paul has spent three chapters insisting the believer is justified already. The hope of righteousness is the final verdict of acquittal at the judgment, the full and public revelation of our righteousness in Christ, and the day when we are finally and actually like him.

Righteous now, and waiting. Both are true, and holding them together is the whole balance of the Christian life. Believers are already justified (Romans 5:1), with nothing outstanding. They wait confidently for that verdict to be publicly declared, and for the state that matches it, when the man you want to be and the man you are have at last become the same man. Every believer lives in the gap between those two, and the discomfort is not a sign that anything has gone wrong.

The hope has a face. The righteousness we wait for is not an abstract quality but a person. Christ Jesus became to us righteousness (1 Corinthians 1:30), and the day the verdict is published is the day he appears: when Christ who is your life appears, then you also will appear with him in glory (Colossians 3:4). So the waiting is eager rather than anxious: the believer is not waiting to find out whether his record will pass, but for the one who has already passed it for him, and when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is (1 John 3:2).

The legalist cannot wait. Waiting requires that the outcome be secure without your involvement, and a man whose standing depends on his own progress cannot afford to wait for anything; he has to be getting somewhere, visibly, or the whole structure wobbles. The gospel produces patient people because it has already settled the question they would otherwise spend their lives trying to answer.

Neither circumcision nor uncircumcision. After four chapters fighting circumcision, you might expect Paul to say that being uncircumcised is what counts. He says neither does. Ethnic and religious markers are irrelevant to standing with God. The moment you make your uncircumcision a badge, you are playing the same game with the pieces reversed.

Faith working through love. Four words fought over for centuries. The verb is energeō, at work: faith is the living thing, and love is faith at work. True faith is never idle; it shows itself in love. Faith alone justifies, but the faith that justifies is never alone. A faith that produces no love is not a faith that needs supplementing. It is a report of something that was never there.

Where Christians differ: faith working through love. Roman Catholic teaching has used this phrase to argue that we are justified by faith formed by love, so that love is part of the ground of justification; both sides agree that living faith always loves. This commentary’s view: Paul says what counts is faith, and describes that faith as one that works through love. Love is the fruit of justifying faith, not part of its ground, and the grammar agrees: love is not what qualifies faith, it is what faith does. We are justified by faith alone, receiving Christ’s righteousness; the faith that receives Christ then works through love (Ephesians 2:8–10; James 2:17; the Westminster Confession 11.2; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 11.2).

If love is the evidence, how much love is enough? That is the wrong question, and it is the question the Judaizers, with their law-keeping conditions, taught people to ask. Love is not the entrance fee; it is the sign of life. A newborn baby breathes weakly, but it breathes, and the doctor does not ask whether it breathes enough to be human. Look for direction, not quantity: is there a love for God and for his people that was not there before, and is it growing, however slowly? If it is, it is the Spirit’s work. If you are troubled by how little you love, bring that trouble to Christ, whose love for you does not depend on yours for him, and ask him to enlarge your heart.

In everyday life. Think of the one person in your home, work or church whom you find hardest to love. Do one concrete thing for their good this week, without telling anyone. That is not a way of earning God’s favour; it is faith, which already has God’s favour, getting to work.

verseByVerse.quote: You were running well. Who hindered you from obeying the truth? This persuasion is not from him who calls you. A little leaven leavens the whole lump.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You were running well. The metaphor is the stadium: Paul is a coach watching a runner who was going to finish, and something happened.

Who hindered you from obeying the truth? The verb is enkoptō: to hinder, to block the way; in a race it is a runner cutting in across another’s lane. Someone tripped them up. So Paul is not describing a runner who got tired or lost heart. Somebody stepped in front of him. And obeying the truth means believing and living the gospel: for Paul the truth is something you do as well as something you hold.

Who got in front of you? That is a more useful diagnosis than it first appears, because Christians who have gone backwards usually blame themselves for a failure of stamina, and it is often not that at all. Somebody cut in. A teacher, a book, a friend with strong opinions, a season under a ministry that made the gospel conditional. The question Paul asks is worth asking honestly of any cooled faith: not, why did I run out of energy?, but, who got in front of me, and when? Very often there is a date.

This persuasion is not from him who calls you. Verse 8 is quiet and decisive: God, who called them by grace, is not the source of this new teaching. And he identifies God carefully: as him who calls you, present tense, still calling. You know the voice that called you, and this is not it.

A test for ordinary believers. Not, is it strict? God is often strict. But does this teaching come to you the way he came to you? He came with a gift, to someone with nothing to offer, and the effect was relief. When a teaching arrives and its effect is that you feel measured, watched, and slightly behind, you may not be able to refute it. You can still recognise that it is not the voice that called you. My sheep hear my voice, Jesus said (John 10:27).

A little leaven leavens the whole lump. Then verse 9, a proverb. A pinch of sour dough goes into a large batch, and in time the whole mass has changed. Two things follow. First, quantity is irrelevant. The Judaizers were asking for one concession, and Paul’s point is that a gospel with a small condition attached is not mostly the gospel; given time, it is a different loaf entirely. Second, the change is invisible while it is happening. Nobody in a church that is losing the gospel can feel it going. The sermons and the language are unchanged; what alters first is the atmosphere: the quiet arrival of measurement into a room that used to be full of relief.

Leaven and the Lamb. Paul uses the same proverb in 1 Corinthians 5:6, and there he gives at once the reason leaven has no place in the church: Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed (1 Corinthians 5:7). At Passover Israel cleared every crumb of leaven from their houses and ate the lamb with unleavened bread, as a people leaving slavery (Exodus 12:15–20). A gospel with a condition added is old leaven carried back into the house where the Lamb has died, and the issue is not fussiness about doctrine but loyalty to the one who was sacrificed.

How do I tell whether a teaching is leaven or just a different emphasis? Ask what it does to the gospel of free justification in Christ. Christians differ honestly on baptism, church government, the end times and much else, and those differences, important as they are, need not touch the heart. Leaven is different: it changes what makes a person right with God, or adds a condition to Christ, or quietly moves the weight from his work to yours. Ask: does this leave me resting wholly on Christ? Does it make grace more amazing or less? Does it fit with the plain teaching of Scripture, read as a whole? If a teaching makes Christ smaller and you larger, it is leaven, however small it looks.
verseByVerse.note: Leaven (yeast) spreads through the whole lump of dough.

verseByVerse.quote: I have confidence in the Lord that you will take no other view, and the one who is troubling you will bear the penalty, whoever he is. But if I, brothers, still preach circumcision, why am I still being persecuted? In that case the offense of the cross has been removed. I wish those who unsettle you would emasculate themselves!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Confidence in the Lord. After the leaven, a surprise. He has called them foolish, bewitched, severed from Christ, and now he says he is confident about them, in the Lord: not in their good sense, nor in his own arguments. Paul trusts that God will bring them back.

How to hold on to someone who is drifting. You can be confident in the person, which is optimism and collapses on contact with facts, or you can write them off. Paul does neither. He tells them the worst honestly and then declares his expectation that God will keep them, which is the only ground on which anyone has ever been kept, including him.

Whoever he is. A particular man, or each one of them: God will judge the false teacher, however important. Paul does not organise a campaign against him; he leaves him to God.

But if I, brothers, still preach circumcision, why am I still being persecuted? Verse 11 lets slip what was being said about Paul. Somebody in Galatia had been claiming that Paul himself taught circumcision when it suited him (perhaps pointing to Timothy, or to his past as a circumcising Pharisee), and therefore that the Galatians were only being asked to do what the apostle really wanted. Paul’s answer is not a denial but a piece of evidence: look at my life. Nobody stones a man for preaching what everybody already accepts. If so, why is he still persecuted by those who demand it? The scars are the argument.

The offense of the cross. And then the phrase that explains everything. The word is skandalon, a stumbling block. What offends is not the suffering; the world has always admired a martyr. It is what the cross says about the person looking at it: that he could not be saved by any other means, that his religion and his decency contributed nothing, that he had to be rescued like a criminal. Add any requirement and the offence drains away, because now there is something for the man to do. A religion you can contribute to is a religion the world will tolerate. A gospel nobody is annoyed by has usually been adjusted.

The stone in Zion. Paul applies Isaiah’s stone to Christ: behold, I am laying in Zion a stone of stumbling, and a rock of offense; and whoever believes in him will not be put to shame (Romans 9:33; compare 1 Peter 2:6–8). So the offence of the cross is finally the offence of a person. The Messiah Israel expected would not hang on a tree under God’s curse (3:13; Deuteronomy 21:23), yet this one did, and he did it in the sinner’s place. The stone men trip over is the same stone on which a believer stands and is never put to shame.

What is the offence of the cross today? Much the same as then, though it wears modern clothes. People are offended to be told that they are sinners who cannot save themselves; that decent, religious and kind people need a Saviour as much as criminals do; that there is only one way to God, through a crucified Jew; and that their good works earn nothing. People will happily admire Jesus as a teacher or example. What they resist is being told they needed him to die for them. Do not soften those points to be liked. Explain them gently, with tears if need be, but leave the offence where God put it, because it is the same message that saves.

I wish those who unsettle you would emasculate themselves! Verse 12 reads as a crude outburst until you know the region. Across Asia Minor, with its chief shrine at Pessinus in Galatia itself, the mother goddess Cybele was served by priests who castrated themselves in ecstatic worship. So Paul is not merely being coarse. He is saying: you want to cut flesh to be accepted by God? Then you already know what that religion looks like, because it is on your own doorstep. If the knife is the mechanism, why stop where Moses stopped? It shows the Galatians that the road they are on ends somewhere they have already seen.

Is strong language ever right for me? Rarely, and with great care. Paul was an apostle writing under inspiration about wolves who were destroying a flock he had founded, and even here his target is the teachers, not the confused sheep. Elsewhere Scripture tells us to let no corrupting talk come out of our mouths (Ephesians 4:29) and to correct opponents with gentleness (2 Timothy 2:25). If you find you enjoy biting words, that is a sign to stop. Keep your strongest language for the dangers that most threaten souls, and even then speak it with sorrow, never with relish, and never against the people who are being misled.
verseByVerse.note: Paul’s bitter wish may allude to the priests of the goddess Cybele in that region, who castrated themselves.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Galatians were called to freedom, but they must not use it as an opening for the flesh; through love they are to serve one another (v. 13). The whole law is fulfilled in one command, to love your neighbour as yourself (v. 14). If they bite and devour one another, they will be consumed by each other (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology:
Love as the Fulfilment of the Law

For the believer the law’s moral demands are not abolished but fulfilled, from a different source. The law commands from outside; love, produced by the Spirit, moves from within: the law written on the heart (Jeremiah 31:33): not a different law, but the same law, obeyed by a heart that loves the God who gave everything, not as the price of his favour.

Verse 13 also answers the charge, as old as the gospel, that free grace leads to licence. Paul admits the danger and still refuses to answer licence with law. And v. 15 shows how a religion of performance destroys a congregation: once standing is earned, every other believer becomes a measurement.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Galatians were living out v. 15 while arguing about how to be holy, and vv. 13–14 name the one thing that binds a church as rules never can.

Now: A church that makes the Christian life mainly about visible markers produces pride in those who meet the standard, shame in those who do not, and division. The cure v. 13 offers is not a new rule but service, given concretely to the person you still disagree with.

verseByVerse.quote: For you were called to freedom, brothers. Only do not use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh, but through love serve one another. For the whole law is fulfilled in one word: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
For you were called to freedom, brothers. Paul now faces the objection waiting since verse 1: if people are genuinely free, what is to stop them doing as they like?

An opportunity for the flesh. He does not dodge it. Aphormē was a military base of operations. The flesh, sinful human nature, can occupy your liberty. And the reasoning it offers is always theologically impeccable. I am not under law. God has forgiven this already. Grace is greater than my sin. Every one of those sentences is true, and all three have been used to excuse things that wrecked a family.

No fence, but love. Paul’s answer to that objection, which every preacher of grace meets (Romans 6:1), is not a fence. Having demolished law as the ground of standing, he will not smuggle it back as the ground of behaviour. His answer to the flesh is love.

Serve one another. The verb is deliberately shocking: douleuete, be slaves to one another. Paul has torn the yoke off their shoulders, and the first thing he tells them to do with their freedom is to put themselves at each other’s disposal. True freedom is freedom to love.

Free lord, dutiful servant. Luther put the paradox exactly: a Christian is a perfectly free lord of all, subject to none, and a perfectly dutiful servant of all, subject to all. The two are not in tension, because the slavery Paul has been fighting is slavery to a system in order to be accepted, and this is bondage to a person because you already are. One is how you try to get standing. The other is what standing does.

Fulfilled in one word. Verse 14 quotes Leviticus 19:18 (compare Romans 13:8–10), though the believer is not under the law. The resolution is in the verb: not summarised but fulfilled, brought to its intended completion. The law was never an arbitrary list; every commandment in it was describing what love looks like when it meets a particular situation. Do not steal is love meeting your neighbour’s property. Do not bear false witness is love meeting his reputation. So a man who genuinely loves is doing what the law was written to produce, not to be justified, but as its fruit, as a man who loves his wife does not need a rule against reading her letters.

A higher standard, not a lower one. So the standard is higher and not lower. A code can be satisfied; you can reach the end of a list. As yourself has no end to reach. Nobody has ever gone to bed having loved his neighbour as much as he instinctively looks after himself.

Fulfilled first in him. Before love fulfils the law in us, it fulfilled it in Christ. He came not to abolish the law but to fulfil it (Matthew 5:17), and he is the one man who ever loved his neighbour as himself, and then more than himself: he loved his Father with all his heart, and his enemies all the way to the cross (Romans 5:8). That fulfilment reaches us through him: God condemned sin in the flesh in his Son, so that the righteous requirement of the law might be fulfilled in us, who walk according to the Spirit (Romans 8:3–4). Our love is not a new way of earning. It is his obedience working itself out in his people.

If love fulfils the law, can a kind person fulfil it without Christ? Not in the way the law means. Many unbelievers are kinder than many Christians, and that is a real gift of God’s common goodness. But the law’s first command is to love God with all your heart (Matthew 22:37–40), and its second asks for love as yourself, every day, from the heart, with no gaps. Nobody has managed even the second, which is why the kind person needs Christ as much as the cruel one does. And this frees the religious person too: the love the law asks for is not something either of us generates. Christ fulfilled it for us, and the Spirit grows it in us (v. 22).

So does the law still bind the believer? If you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the law (v. 18) means not under it as a covenant of works, a curse or the ground of our standing. It does not mean that God’s moral will has lapsed. The law still describes what love does: this is the love of God, that we keep his commandments (1 John 5:3). Love fulfils the law; it does not abolish it. The Spirit-led Christian does not need the law to make him acceptable, but he is glad of it as a description of the life the Spirit is producing.

What it does not mean. It does not mean love replaces the commandments, so that we decide what love means. Love is defined by the commandments (Romans 13:9). A person who says, I am doing the loving thing, while breaking God’s commands about marriage, honesty or life, has redefined love to suit himself.

Does loving my neighbour as myself mean I must first learn to love myself? No. The command assumes that we already care for ourselves: we feed ourselves, protect ourselves, think about our own interests without being told to (Ephesians 5:29). It takes that instinct as the measure and turns it outward. The cure for a crushed sense of self is not self-love but being loved by God, which frees you to stop looking inward at all. And who is my neighbour? Jesus answered that with a Samaritan: whoever is in front of you and in need, even if he is not your kind (Luke 10:29–37).

In everyday life. Pick a specific person and a specific service: the washing-up nobody wants to do, the visit you keep postponing, the hour given to a lonely neighbour. Do it as one set free, not as one paying a debt. When your love falls short, as it will, Christ’s perfect love stands in your place, and your poor service is accepted for his sake.

parallels.desc: you shall love your neighbour as yourself

verseByVerse.quote: But if you bite and devour one another, watch out that you are not consumed by one another.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Bite and devour. The three verbs come from animals and escalate: a snap, then eating, then nothing left. Paul is describing it in a church.

An argument about holiness. The Galatian congregations were apparently already tearing each other apart over how to be holy. That is not an irony but a mechanism, and still a common way for a good church to destroy itself.

How it works. Once standing before God is tied to performance, every other believer in the room becomes a measurement. If he keeps more than I do, he is a threat, and I must find the flaw that explains him. If he keeps less, he is a reassurance, and I need him to stay where he is. Neither of those is love, and both feel like discernment. Add a genuine doctrinal disagreement, and it all gains a righteous vocabulary, so that people who are defending their own standing believe they are contending for the truth.

Consumed by one another. He does not say the strong will eat the weak. He says everyone loses. The party that prevails is left holding a smaller, colder, more suspicious congregation than the one it was fighting for.

One for whom Christ died. Paul gives the deepest reason against devouring a brother in another letter: do not destroy the one for whom Christ died (Romans 14:15; compare 1 Corinthians 8:11–12). The believer across the room is someone the Son of God loved enough to die for. Every bite in a church fight lands on a body that belongs to Christ.

What do you want to be true? Two practical things follow. The first is a test for a disagreement you are currently inside: ask what you want to be true about the other person. If you find you would be disappointed to discover he was right, or that his motives were good, then whatever the merits of your case, you are biting. The verse does not ask whether your position is correct. Paul obviously thought his was.

The cure is service. Second, Paul does not answer biting with a rule; he has just said, through love serve one another. The antidote to devouring a brother is serving him: deliberately, in some concrete way, while you still disagree with him. It is very hard to keep eating a man you are carrying something for. Pressing anger produces strife (Proverbs 30:33), and quarrels come from the passions at war within you (James 4:1–2); service starves them.

What it does not mean. It does not mean truth does not matter. Paul fights hard for it in this letter. It means believers must not attack each other with cruelty. You can contend for the faith without devouring the brother who is confused about it.

My church is already in a fight. What should I do? First, refuse to add to it: no gossip, no forwarding of messages, no recruiting to a side, no conversations about people that you would not have with them present. Second, if you have a grievance, take it directly and privately to the person concerned, and then if needed to the elders (Matthew 18:15–17). Third, pray for those you disagree with, by name, asking God to bless them. Fourth, look for a way to serve someone on the other side. And if the issue is a real matter of the gospel, speak plainly but without contempt. A church can survive disagreement; it rarely survives malice.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–26 — The Flesh and the Spirit
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul tells the Galatians to walk by the Spirit, and they will not carry out the desires of the flesh, for the two are at war within them; those led by the Spirit are not under the law (vv. 16–18). The works of the flesh are plain, and those who live by them will not inherit the kingdom of God (vv. 19–21). The Spirit grows a very different harvest, against which there is no law (vv. 22–23). Those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh, so they are to keep in step with the Spirit, without conceit, provoking or envy (vv. 24–26).
verseByVerse.theology:
Putting the Flesh to Death, and Why the Fight Is Evidence of Life

The Christian life has two sides: putting the flesh to death, which v. 24 states as already done to every believer, and coming alive to God, which v. 25 calls keeping in step with the Spirit. Neither is self-powered. The first applies what happened to the old self in Christ’s death (2:20); the second is the Spirit’s fruit.

The tension between v. 17 and v. 24 is resolved by the image of crucifixion, which was slow: the flesh in a believer is mortally wounded and its outcome settled, but it is still loud, and will be until the body dies. Verse 21 needs the same care: the ache that makes a tender conscience afraid of that verse is evidence that it is not describing him.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Galatians needed to see that the law and moral chaos were not the only two options, and vv. 16–18 give the third. The middle of Paul’s list (v. 20) described their own congregations. And in v. 25, keep in step is built on the same root as the elementary principles that had them in bondage (4:3, 9): Paul does not tell them to stop marching, but tells them who sets the pace now.

Now: Walking by the Spirit (v. 16) is concrete rather than mystical: asking for his help before the difficult conversation rather than after it, staying in the word where he speaks, and taking the small next step of obedience you would rather not have noticed.

verseByVerse.quote: But I say, walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh. For the desires of the flesh are against the Spirit, and the desires of the Spirit are against the flesh, for these are opposed to each other, to keep you from doing the things you want to do. But if you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But I say, walk by the Spirit. Here is Paul’s whole answer to both legalism and licence, and it is neither a law nor a technique. Walk is a present imperative, go on walking: the ordinary word for daily conduct, step by step. Not soar, not fight, not achieve: walk. By the Spirit means depending on him, following his lead, relying on his power.

You will not gratify. This is a promise, not a command. The Greek double negative means you will certainly not carry out the flesh’s desires; it does not say the desires will stop. And the order here is the whole strategy of Christian holiness. He does not say, stop gratifying the flesh and then you will be able to walk by the Spirit. He says walk, and the other will follow. Sin is displaced far more often than it is defeated by direct assault, because a man staring at his temptation and gritting his teeth is still looking at it.

What the flesh is. Flesh here means human nature in its fallen state, set against God: the mind that does not submit to God’s law, and cannot (Romans 8:7). It is not the body as such: several of the works of the flesh in vv. 19–21, like envy and rivalry, have nothing to do with the body.

Against the Spirit. Verse 17 is honest about the cost. This is a settled war within every believer, and it should be said plainly, because young Christians often assume the conflict is evidence that something went wrong at their conversion. It is the reverse. Before conversion there was no war of this kind; conscience might protest (Romans 2:15), but the flesh had the field. The fight itself is a sign of life: there is now something in you that wants what God wants, and it will not be quiet.

Opposed to each other. Paul does not mean the believer is helpless, but that neither side gets its way unopposed. You cannot drift into holiness, and you cannot sin with a quiet heart either; and verse 16 has already promised which side prevails when we walk by the Spirit.

What walking by the Spirit looks like. It is not a mystical state or waiting for a feeling. In practice it means: asking him for help rather than relying on willpower (Luke 11:13); filling the mind with his word, since he leads through what he has written (Colossians 3:16); saying no to the flesh at the first stirring, not after a long negotiation (Romans 8:13); saying yes to the next step of obedience he shows you, even small ones; and staying close to God’s people and the means of grace (the word, prayer and the Lord’s Supper), where he works. Walking is step by step: no single great experience settles it, but daily, ordinary dependence does.

Led by the Spirit. Led is passive, as in Romans 8:14. The Judaizers offered a code to be kept; Paul offers a person to be followed. Those led by the Spirit are not under the law’s condemnation, nor under it as a system of control; they fulfil it from within. A code can only stand outside you and tell you what to do; the Spirit is inside, and he produces the life.

The Spirit who led the Son. The Spirit who leads us is the Spirit of God’s Son, sent into our hearts (4:6), and he has led this way before. Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, was led by the Spirit in the wilderness for forty days, tempted by the devil (Luke 4:1–2). Where Adam and Israel gave way to their desires, he refused every one. The same Spirit now leads Christ’s brothers through the same war. He leads us behind a captain who has already won the fight, and makes us like him on the way.

Does being led by the Spirit mean following inner voices and impressions? Not in the sense many people mean. In Romans 8:14 and here, being led by the Spirit is about the direction of a life, the Spirit leading God’s children away from the flesh and toward holiness, not a stream of private messages about which job to take. The Spirit speaks in Scripture, which he inspired and which is complete and sufficient (2 Timothy 3:16–17). He does work in our hearts: convicting, comforting, bringing his word to mind, giving wisdom. But an impression is never to be treated as a new word from God, and anything that contradicts Scripture is not his leading. Test every prompting by the Bible. Christians whose churches expect prophetic words today see some of this differently, and they are brothers and sisters; they too agree that every such word must be tested by Scripture (1 Thessalonians 5:20–21).

Where Christians differ: sinless perfection. Some, especially in parts of the holiness tradition, teach that believers can reach a state where the flesh is eradicated and they no longer sin, and they are moved by a right hunger for holiness. This commentary’s view: Paul describes an ongoing war between flesh and Spirit in the believer. The Spirit gives real victory, and believers grow in holiness, but the flesh is not destroyed until glory (Romans 7:14–25; 1 John 1:8; the Westminster Confession 13.2; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 13.2). The Christian life is a fight, not a state of sinless rest.
verseByVerse.note: “Flesh” here means human nature in its fallen state, set against God.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the works of the flesh are evident: sexual immorality, impurity, sensuality, idolatry, sorcery, enmity, strife, jealousy, fits of anger, rivalries, dissensions, divisions, envy, drunkenness, orgies, and things like these. I warn you, as I warned you before, that those who do such things will not inherit the kingdom of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the works of the flesh are evident. Works is the word Paul has used all through the letter for works of the law, and the echo is deliberate. Law-keeping and licence look like opposites, and Paul files them under the same heading, because both are things a man produces out of his own resources. Only the products differ. Fifteen are listed, in four groups. Some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, add adultery at the start and murders after envy; the earliest do not, so most modern Bibles omit them.

Sexual immorality, impurity, sensuality. Sexual immorality (porneia) is the broad word for all sex outside marriage. Impurity (akatharsia) is moral uncleanness. Sensuality (aselgeia) is indulgence that has stopped caring who sees.

Idolatry, sorcery. Then religion goes wrong. Sorcery translates pharmakeia (hence pharmacy): potions, spells and drugs used to bend outcomes. Both belong on a list of fleshly works because both are attempts to manage the divine: an idol is a god you can locate, and a spell is a result you can arrange.

Enmity, strife, jealousy. Slow down at the long middle: eight sins of relationships, the largest group: enmity (hostility), strife (quarrelling), jealousy, fits of anger (outbursts of rage), rivalries (selfish ambition), dissensions (splits), divisions (factions, haireseis), envy. Every one thrives in a church meeting as easily as in a tavern; these were tearing the Galatian churches apart (v. 15), and Paul has put the sins of the respectable at the centre of his list. A congregation that would be horrified by verse 19 will often carry verse 20 as its ordinary weather.

Drunkenness, orgies, and things like these. Last come sins of excess: orgies (kōmoi) were the drunken processions that ended pagan festivals. And the list is not complete. Paul is not writing a legal code but a portrait, and nobody can plead that his particular version is not itemised.

Will not inherit the kingdom. Few passages disturb tender consciences more. So read the verb carefully: do is prassō, practise, in the present tense: those whose lives are characterised by these things, who have made their peace with them. Not the believer who falls and repents, but the one who continues in them without repentance (1 Corinthians 6:9–11). There is a world of difference between a man who falls into a ditch and a man who lives in it, and Scripture never confuses them.

The morning after. The question is not whether you sinned, but whether the sin still grieves you and you take it to Christ. A man in whom the Spirit lives cannot sin comfortably. The very ache that makes you afraid of this verse is the evidence the verse is not about you, and the blood of Jesus cleanses the one who brings it to him.

Heirs through the Son. The key word is inherit. In this letter nobody earns an inheritance; it comes by being a son, and sonship comes through Christ (4:4–7). The works of the flesh are the life of someone who has never been adopted, and the warning is that such a life has no share in the estate. But the same Son who won the inheritance gives his people the Spirit who cries Abba, Father in their hearts (4:6), and that Spirit makes war on every item on this list.

I keep falling into the same sin, a sexual one. Am I one of those who practise it? The question to ask is not whether you have fallen again, but which side you are on in the fight. Are you at peace with it, defending it, planning for it? Or do you hate it, confess it, and keep fighting it, even after many defeats? The second is not the life Paul condemns; it is the war of verse 17. But do not settle for endless defeat. Bring it into the light with a mature Christian friend or pastor (James 5:16). Remove what feeds it: devices, places, habits. Ask for help, practical and spiritual. And each time you fall, go straight back to Christ, whose blood cleanses from all sin (1 John 1:7, 9).

Is it not harsh to shut people out of God’s kingdom for envy or drunkenness? Only if we think of the kingdom as a club with a fee. The kingdom of God is the place where God is king and love reigns completely. A heart that is set on these things, and will not let them go, does not want that kingdom; it wants itself, and heaven would be unbearable to it. And the list will not let the religious person feel safe either, because jealousy, rivalry and factions sit beside drunkenness and orgies. The holy God takes every one of these seriously enough to judge it, and seriously enough to have borne it himself in his Son. No one who comes to Christ is turned away (John 6:37), and the list in Corinthians ends with such were some of you.

Is it sorcery to take medicine? No. The word described magic, potions and drugs used to manipulate spiritual powers, often with occult practices attached. Medicine used to heal is a gift of God; Paul told Timothy to take a little wine for his stomach (1 Timothy 5:23), and Luke was a physician. What the verse condemns today includes occult practices like fortune-telling, spells and seeking spirits, and the misuse of drugs to escape or to alter the mind in the way drunkenness does.
verseByVerse.note: “Sorcery” translates a word that also covered magic potions and drugs.

verseByVerse.quote: But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control; against such things there is no law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the fruit of the Spirit. The flesh has works; the Spirit has fruit. Works are manufactured; fruit is grown, and no apple was ever produced by an apple tree straining. Fruit grows naturally from life; the Spirit produces it as we abide in Christ (John 15:4–5).

One fruit, not nine. The singular matters: not nine badges to collect, but one fruit with nine facets, a single character, which is finally the character of Christ himself, being formed in a person (4:19). You do not choose patience this year and gentleness next.

Is love. Love heads the list, as it must, since verse 14 has just said the whole law is fulfilled in it. Agapē seeks another’s good at its own cost. It comes first and is the root of the rest (1 Corinthians 13): joy is love rejoicing, peace is love resting, patience is love waiting, and so on down the list.

Joy, peace. Joy (chara) is gladness in God, and the New Testament’s joy is not the same thing as cheerfulness of temperament; it survives circumstances that ruin cheerfulness, because its ground is outside them. Peace (eirēnē) is wholeness: first peace with God, and then, as a consequence, the inward rest of a man who has stopped negotiating his standing, and harmony with others.

Patience, kindness, goodness. Patience is makrothymia, long-tempered: a long fuse with people. It is the word used of God’s forbearance with us. Kindness (chrēstotēs) is gracious tenderness, not mere politeness but active usefulness to somebody. Goodness (agathōsynē) is moral substance and generosity, the quality of a man who is the same when nobody is checking.

Faithfulness, gentleness, self-control. Faithfulness (pistis) is reliability and loyalty: being where you said you would be, keeping your word when it costs. Gentleness is prautēs, meekness, and it is not weakness; in Greek it could be used of a powerful horse that had been broken to the bridle, so it is strength under control. And self-control (enkrateia) comes last, striking on this list, since every self-help programme in the world sells it. Paul says it is a fruit. You do not generate it. You receive it, and then you use it.

Against such things there is no law. A dry piece of understatement, and it lands the whole argument of the chapter. The Judaizers feared grace would produce lawlessness. Paul says: look at what the Spirit produces, and find me the legislature that would prohibit any of it. The law was always aiming at this, and the Spirit is producing it without the law’s help.

How is the fruit of the Spirit different from the gifts of the Spirit? The fruit is character, the same in every believer and growing for a lifetime. The gifts are abilities for service, distributed differently, as the Spirit apportions to each one individually as he wills (1 Corinthians 12:11). The fruit matters more. Paul says that without love the greatest gifts are nothing (1 Corinthians 13:2), and Jesus warns of people who prophesied and cast out demons in his name and were never his (Matthew 7:22–23). A church should prize holiness above gifting.

I see almost none of this in myself. Have I got the Spirit at all? This list is often used to wound, so three things should be said. First, fruit is slow, and it is seasonal, and nobody digs up a tree in March to check. Second, you are the worst-placed person in the world to assess it: ask the people who live with you, who will almost always report growth the man himself cannot see. And third, look at what the sentence does not say. It does not say the fruit of the diligent Christian. It says the fruit of the Spirit, and he is not slow, and he is not uncertain of the outcome, and the growing was never your department.

If I cannot produce the fruit, what do I actually do? You stay connected to the vine, and you cooperate with the gardener. Abide in Christ by trusting him and staying in his word (John 15:7). Pray specifically for the fruit you lack. Put yourself where growth happens: the preaching of the word, the Lord’s Supper, the fellowship of believers. Pull up weeds when you see them, by confessing and turning from sin. And when an opportunity comes to exercise patience or kindness, take it, trusting the Spirit to give what he asks. Effort is not excluded; it is the effort of a branch staying in the vine, not of a branch trying to grow apples by itself.

For worship. Read the nine words again and you will see a face. Love that went to the cross; joy set before him that carried him through it; peace he left to his friends on the night he was betrayed; patience with slow disciples; kindness to lepers and children; goodness that no one could convict of sin; faithfulness to his Father to the end; gentleness that would not break a bruised reed; self-control at his arrest and before Pilate, when twelve legions of angels were a word away. The Spirit is making us like him. What God began in Christ he is growing in us, and one day the harvest will be complete, and the Son will be the firstborn among many brothers.
verseByVerse.note: “Fruit” is singular: one harvest with many flavours.

verseByVerse.quote: And those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And those who belong to Christ Jesus. That is, all true believers. Not unusually consecrated Christians: everyone who is his.

Have crucified the flesh. The tense is the key: have crucified, a past action, complete. Paul states what happened to every Christian, as a fact before it is a duty. United to Christ in his death, believers have put the flesh to death (2:20; Romans 6:6). At conversion they turned decisively against their sinful nature.

If it is dead, what has been fighting? This raises the obvious difficulty, and it is worth putting bluntly. Seven verses earlier Paul described a war going on inside the believer that keeps him from doing what he wants. Now he says the flesh has been crucified. If it is dead, what exactly has been fighting? The answer is in the image itself, and it is one of the most useful things in the chapter. Crucifixion was not a quick death. That was the point of it: the method was meant to be slow: a man nailed to a beam could take hours or even days to die, and for the whole of that time he was mortally wounded, fixed in place, going nowhere, and still perfectly capable of shouting at people. Crucifixion was slow, painful and final. He was finished. He was not yet silent.

The noise of a dying man. That is the flesh in a believer: mortally wounded, its authority broken, its outcome settled, but audible until the day the body dies. So the voice you hear on a bad Thursday is real, and it is loud, and it is not evidence that nothing happened to you. It is the noise of something that has been executed and has not yet stopped.

When did this happen? Paul has already told us: I have been crucified with Christ (2:20). It happened at the cross, and it became yours when you were united to him by faith. Which is why the sentence begins where it does: those who belong to Christ Jesus.

Relief in the order. If crucifying the flesh were your project, every failure would mean starting again. Because it is Christ’s finished work applied to you, your failures are the noise of a dying man rather than the recovery of a victorious one. You are refusing to take orders from something that is already condemned. And so believers continue to put it to death daily (Romans 8:13; Colossians 3:5): not to make the execution happen, but because it has.

How do I put the flesh to death in practice? Starve it and refuse it. Starve it by cutting off what feeds it: if a certain website, friendship, habit or late-night hour regularly leads you into sin, remove it, however drastic that seems (Matthew 5:29–30; Romans 13:14). Refuse it by saying no at the first stirring, and saying it in Christ’s name: this is not who I am now. Replace it with the opposite good: generosity for greed, thanksgiving for complaining, service for envy. And do it all by the Spirit (Romans 8:13), in prayer, in the company of other believers, and in the confidence that the flesh has already lost.

In everyday life. When the old voice shouts today, answer it out loud if you need to: you were nailed to the cross with Christ; I do not take orders from you. Then do the next good thing.

verseByVerse.quote: If we live by the Spirit, let us also keep in step with the Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If we live by the Spirit. The if is not a doubt. The sentence takes the thing as true: since we live by the Spirit, as we do. The Spirit gave every believer new birth and a new heart that wants God (John 3:5–6; Ezekiel 36:26). The shape of all New Testament ethics follows: this is what you are, therefore be it.

Keep in step. In verse 16 the word was walk. Here it is stoichōmen: to keep rank, march in line, match the step of the man beside you. Follow the Spirit’s lead step by step, in daily obedience, as soldiers follow the one ahead.

The word turned round. That verb is built on the same root as stoicheia, the word Paul used twice in chapter 4 for the elementary principles that had the Galatians in bondage (4:3, 9). The Galatians had marched to a calendar and a code before. Paul does not tell them to stop marching. He tells them who sets the pace now.

Where the Spirit marches. Keeping in step with the Spirit always brings a man to the same place, because the Spirit’s whole work is to glorify Christ: he will take what is mine and declare it to you, Jesus said (John 16:14). The new march is set by the Spirit of the Son who bought us out of the old (4:4–6).

Ahead or behind. Keep in step names two ways of getting it wrong. You can march ahead of him, driving a ministry or a decision at a pace nothing has been given to sustain, and calling the exhaustion faithfulness. Or you can lag behind: hearing the small thing you should do, agreeing with it, and not doing it, until the agreeing has quietly become a substitute for the doing. Neither looks like rebellion, and the correction is the same: find where he actually is, and be there. He sets the pace at something a real person can sustain over a whole life, which is exactly what the law never did.

How do I know where the Spirit is leading in a decision, like a job or a move? Begin with what he has already said. Scripture settles the moral boundaries: if an option requires sin, it is not his leading. Within those boundaries, the Spirit leads by giving wisdom, so ask for it (James 1:5), think carefully, weigh your gifts and responsibilities, consider how each option affects your love for God, your family and your church, and seek counsel from mature believers (Proverbs 15:22). Then decide, and trust God’s providence with the outcome. You do not need a sign or an inner voice. Keeping in step is mostly about the next obedient step, and a wise decision made in faith is a step in step.
verseByVerse.note: “Keep in step” is a military word for marching in line.

verseByVerse.quote: Let us not become conceited, provoking one another, envying one another.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let us not become conceited. A small verse that brings the whole soaring argument down onto how you feel about the Christian three seats away, and leads into chapter 6. Conceited translates kenodoxoi: empty-glory, a reputation held up by air, often pride in spiritual achievements. And the moment a man’s significance depends on something that hollow, he cannot leave other people alone, because the only way to maintain a comparative standing is comparatively.

Provoking one another. Two symptoms follow, the same disease at different altitudes. Provoking is challenging, as to a fight. It is what the man ahead does: needling, making sure the gap is felt.

Envying one another. Envying is what the man behind does: resenting, watching, quietly hoping for a stumble. They look like opposites and they are identical: both are a person whose eyes are fixed on another believer rather than on Christ, and whose sense of himself is being calculated from the difference. The Spirit frees us from both.

The flicker. Think of the believer whose ministry, family or reputation is flourishing most visibly in your circle, and what happens in you when good news about him is announced. A flicker of something before the congratulation catches up is verse 26 with your name on it, and Paul puts it directly after the fruit of the Spirit for that reason: envy cannot coexist with love, joy and peace, because it needs somebody else to have less. The cure is not to try harder to be pleased but to look somewhere else. Empty glory is only attractive while it is the best glory in view. Set beside the real thing, the Son of God who had glory in full, laid it down, took the form of a slave and was executed for people who were arguing about rank (Philippians 2:3–7), the competition in the third row loses its grip. He must increase, but I must decrease (John 3:30).

Is it wrong to admire another Christian, or want to be like them? No. Paul himself says, be imitators of me, as I am of Christ (1 Corinthians 11:1), and Hebrews tells us to remember our leaders and imitate their faith (Hebrews 13:7). Admiration thanks God for another’s gifts and wants to grow in the same direction; envy resents them for having what you lack and is secretly glad when they stumble. The difference shows when they succeed: admiration rejoices, envy aches. If you notice the ache, confess it, and then thank God aloud for the very thing you envied. That is how the Spirit turns envy into love.

In everyday life. Pick the person you most often compare yourself with, and pray for their blessing by name, specifically, for the thing you most envy or most look down on.
