6.title: Boasting Only in the Cross: The New Creation and the Community of Grace
6.overview:
Galatians 6 shows what the freedom of the gospel looks like in a church. Freedom produces love, and love takes concrete shape: the church restores the fallen gently, carries burdens, supports its teachers, sows to the Spirit and does not grow weary of doing good.

Then Paul takes the pen himself (vv. 11–18). The false teachers want a good showing in the flesh and a way round persecution; Paul will boast only in the cross, through which the world has been crucified to him and he to the world. What counts is not circumcision or uncircumcision but a new creation.

The letter ends as it began, with grace. He closes by commending them to it, the only ground on which anyone stands before God.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul puts six chapters of doctrine to work on a brother caught in any transgression: he is to be restored, the word for mending a net or setting a bone, in a spirit of gentleness, by people who keep watch on themselves (v. 1). Verse 2 calls this bearing one another’s burdens and so fulfilling the law of Christ. Verses 3–5 explain why restoration goes wrong: self-deception, a verdict reached by comparison, and forgetting that each will carry his own load on the day of account.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Church as a Community of Restoration

The church is a communion of saints, committed to mutual care, discipline and restoration, and verse 1 puts the letter’s teaching on justification into practice. We deal gently with a failing brother because we know we stand only by grace; the man who forgets his own proneness to sin will be a prosecutor, and the man who remembers it will be a restorer. Gentleness without truth becomes sentimentality, and truth without gentleness wounds further.

Verses 2 and 5 keep the balance: others are to help carry what is crushing a man, but his own obedience, repentance and answer at the last day nobody can carry for him.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Galatian congregations were biting and devouring one another (5:15). Some took freedom as licence and others answered with condemnation; verse 1 corrects both, and v. 3 names what was fuelling the second: men who thought they were something.

Now: A warm and orthodox church can still carry nothing, because burden-bearing is voluntary and its absence goes unnoticed. And v. 4 asks whether our sense of doing well or badly comes from our own work or from comparing ourselves with someone else.

verseByVerse.quote: Brothers, if anyone is caught in any transgression, you who are spiritual should restore him in a spirit of gentleness. Keep watch on yourself, lest you too be tempted.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Galatians 6 shows what walking by the Spirit looks like in the church, and then sums up the letter: restore the fallen gently and carry one another’s burdens (vv. 1–5); support your teachers, and do not grow weary of sowing to the Spirit (vv. 6–10); and boast only in the cross, since what counts is a new creation (vv. 11–18). The letter that began with grace ends with grace, and the last thing it holds up is a cross.

Caught in any transgression. Paul puts five chapters of doctrine to work on the hardest situation in ordinary church life: a Christian who has fallen. The verb is passive: overtaken, caught out, perhaps ambushed by sin before he realised. That does not make the sin smaller; Paul calls it a transgression, and any sin will do. It does change the posture you approach him in. You are looking at a casualty, not a defector.

You who are spiritual. Not an elite tier of believers: Paul has just spent a chapter saying every Christian lives by the Spirit and should keep in step with him (5:16, 25). The spiritual are those actually walking in step today. But there is an edge in it, because the Galatians were full of people who thought themselves advanced, and Paul is quietly saying: if you are so spiritual, here is the job.

Restore him. Restore (katartizō) is used of mending torn nets (Matthew 4:21) and of setting a broken bone. Nobody sets a bone by shouting at it. You get close, cause only as much pain as the job needs, and the entire object is a limb that works again. A bonesetter who enjoyed the pain would be unfit for the work.

In a spirit of gentleness. The word appeared four verses ago in the fruit of the Spirit (5:23). Gentleness is not softness about the sin; it is strength under control, the strength of a man who could crush and chooses to heal.

Keep watch on yourself. Suddenly singular, in a sentence full of plurals: Paul speaks to the restorer alone. You could fall too. Let anyone who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall (1 Corinthians 10:12).

The only restorer who never fell. The gentleness asked for here is Christ’s own. He called himself gentle and lowly in heart (Matthew 11:29). He is the one restorer who never needed to keep watch on himself, because he was tempted in every respect as we are, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15). His sinlessness did not make him hard with the fallen. He restored Peter by a charcoal fire, after three denials, with three questions and no lecture (John 21:15–17). When we go to a fallen brother, we go as men who were picked up by him, and we handle the brother as he handled us.

The real danger. The danger is not the obvious one. The temptation in a restoration is rarely to commit the same sin. It is to enjoy the position: to find that being the one who is well is unexpectedly pleasant, to relay the details as a prayer request, to feel a quiet firmness of ground under you that you did not have last week. That is a worse condition than the one you came to mend, and it is invisible to the man in it.

The practical shape of it. Go, rather than discuss him. Go having asked honestly whether you would want this conversation conducted on you the way you are about to conduct it, and having confessed to God the sin in yourself that is most like his. Say the true thing plainly, because gentleness that will not name the sin is not gentleness but cowardice wearing its coat. And go knowing that the only thing separating you from him is grace you did not generate. A man who has grasped this letter cannot be a prosecutor; he has read the charge sheet with his own name on it.

And if the person will not be restored? Then the gentleness does not give way to indifference. Jesus lays out the steps: go privately, then with one or two others, then to the church (Matthew 18:15–17). Where someone who calls himself a believer persists in serious sin without repentance, the church must act (1 Corinthians 5:11–13), always with the aim of bringing him back.

What if the sin is abuse, or a crime? Then gentleness toward the sinner must never mean danger for the victim. Restoration in this verse is about a person’s relationship with God and the church; it does not cancel the duty to protect the vulnerable or to report a crime to the authorities, whom God has appointed to punish wrongdoing (Romans 13:1–4). Abuse is never to be hushed up, minimised or handled privately to protect a reputation, and no victim should be pressed to reconcile with an abuser or to stay in danger. The church can pray for a repentant offender and seek his good, while keeping him well away from those he harmed and from positions of trust.

Does being restored mean being given back the position he had? Not necessarily. Restoration means being brought back to repentance, forgiveness and fellowship: welcomed at the Lord’s Table, loved, no longer treated as an outsider. That should be full and warm. But trust, and especially leadership, is a separate matter. Scripture sets qualifications for elders, including being above reproach (1 Timothy 3:2), and a man who has gravely fallen may be fully forgiven and still rightly not hold office again, or only after long proof. Forgiveness is a gift; trust is rebuilt.

verseByVerse.quote: Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Bear one another’s burdens. Go on carrying the barē, the weights that press a man down: not minor inconveniences but what is genuinely too much for one person. A marriage that is failing, a diagnosis, a son who has stopped speaking to his parents, the particular sin from the verse before that a man cannot get free of on his own.

The law of Christ. After five chapters saying the believer is not under law, Paul uses the word positively and attaches Christ’s name to it, not smuggling the old system back in, nor writing a new code. The whole law is fulfilled in loving your neighbour as yourself (5:14), and the Lord himself gave it as a new commandment: that you love one another, just as I have loved you (John 13:34; compare 1 Corinthians 9:21). It is Christ’s law of love, defined not by a list but by a life, and the standard is no longer only as you love yourself, but as I have loved you, which is a good deal more expensive.

Why his name is on it. Christ did not merely legislate burden-bearing. He is the one who bore the burden nobody else could lift: surely he has borne our griefs and carried our sorrows (Isaiah 53:4). When a Christian takes the weight of another man’s failure onto his own shoulders, he is doing, in miniature and at infinite distance, the thing that was done for him at Calvary.

Whose weight are you under? That makes the practical question quite specific, and it is worth answering rather than admiring. Whose weight are you actually under at the moment? Not who do you pray for: praying matters greatly, but it can be done entirely in your own house. Whose burden has cost you a Saturday, or money you had other plans for, or a friendship that got harder because you told the truth inside it? A church can be doctrinally immaculate, warm on a Sunday, and carrying nothing at all, because burden-bearing is invisible and voluntary and nobody ever notices its absence.

It will not be reciprocal. In a healthy church it evens out over years, but not on any given Tuesday, and the man who keeps accounts will not last. You carry, and sometimes you are carried, and the ledger between you was closed at the cross.

I am the one with the burden, and I find it hard to ask for help. What should I do? Ask anyway, because the command assumes there will be burdens to carry, and someone has to let them be carried. Pride often hides as independence: I do not want to be a nuisance. But refusing help denies others the chance to obey Christ, and leaves you crushed under a weight God never meant you to carry alone. Start small: tell one trusted believer the truth about what is happening. Say plainly what would help: a meal, a lift, someone to sit with you, someone to pray with you weekly. And if your burden is a sin you cannot break, tell a mature Christian; confession to one another is a means of healing (James 5:16).

verseByVerse.quote: For if anyone thinks he is something, when he is nothing, he deceives himself. But let each one test his own work, and then his reason to boast will be in himself alone and not in his neighbor. For each will have to bear his own load.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He deceives himself. Three verses that look like scattered proverbs make one argument: restoration goes wrong through self-assessment. Pride prevents burden-bearing, and the proud man deceives himself, leading his own mind astray. This is the peculiar quality of spiritual pride: it is the one sin that blinds you specifically to itself. A man knows when he has lost his temper. Nobody has ever thought, this morning I am inflated.

When he is nothing. That sounds crushing until you remember what the letter has established. Paul has called these people sons and heirs of God; he means you are nothing on your own account, and something only in Christ. Paul could say of himself, by the grace of God I am what I am (1 Corinthians 15:10), and he once asked the proud Corinthians to name one thing they had not been given (1 Corinthians 4:7). Every gift worth having came through the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me (2:20). A man who forgets that has mistaken a delivery for an achievement, and taken the credit for a parcel paid for with blood.

Test his own work. The remedy is to assay, as metal is put in the fire to find what it actually is, and the object is his own work, not others’. The Galatians were measuring themselves against one another, which is why the chapter before ends with provoking and envying (5:26).

Not in his neighbor. Paul is not endorsing self-congratulation but locating the measurement. A man who has assayed his own work has a real, if modest, sense of what God has actually given him to do and whether he is doing it, and any satisfaction comes from God’s work in his own life. A man who has measured himself against his neighbour has nothing at all, because his verdict depends entirely on who happens to be standing next to him, and it will change when the neighbour changes.

Arithmetic on other people. When you last felt good, or a failure, about your Christian life, was it arithmetic performed on other people? God has not asked you to carry their pack, or to weigh yours against it; the quieter question is what he has given you to do today, and whether his grace is enough for it.

His own load. This looks like a contradiction of verse 2. Two things resolve it. First, the words differ, though not to be pressed too hard: verse 2’s barē is a weight a man cannot carry alone; verse 5’s phortion is a ship’s cargo or a soldier’s pack, the normal load each must carry. It is the very word the Lord uses when he says my burden is light (Matthew 11:30). Second, the tense. Verse 2 is a present imperative about now; verse 5 is a future: will have to bear. Paul is probably looking ahead to the day when each of us gives his own account (Romans 14:12), and no one else can stand in the queue for us.

Two errors. So the two verses divide the world sensibly. What is crushing you, others are commanded to help carry. What is properly yours, your own obedience, your own repentance, your own answer at the last day, nobody can carry, and it is not a kindness to pretend otherwise. There is the Christian who will not let anyone near a weight that is breaking him, and calls it strength. And there is the Christian who has quietly transferred his own pack to his church, his counsellor or his spouse, and calls it fellowship.

How do I actually test my own work? Hold it up to God’s word and God’s calling, not to other people. Ask: what has God given me to do, in my family, my work, my church, my neighbourhood? Am I doing it faithfully, with love, as for the Lord (Colossians 3:23)? Where have I been lazy, proud or unkind? Where has God plainly helped me grow? Write the answers down if it helps, and talk them over with a wise friend who will be honest. Then thank God for the good, confess the bad, and get on with the next task. The aim is not a score but faithfulness.
verseByVerse.note: A “burden” in verse 2 is a crushing weight; a “load” in verse 5 is one’s own pack.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 6 turns to money: those taught are to share all good things with the one who teaches, and the verb comes from the word for fellowship. Paul instructs congregations to give, not teachers to raise support.

Verses 7–8 warn that God is not mocked. What is sown is reaped, more than was sown and later than it was sown, and the delay deceives people. From the flesh comes corruption; from the Spirit, eternal life, not as wages but as the growth of a life already given. Verses 9–10 assume weariness and answer it with one condition, if we do not give up, and then turn outward: do good to everyone, and especially to the household of faith, while there is time.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Harvest as the Motive of Present Faithfulness

Verses 7–9 read present obedience in the light of a future harvest. The harvest is secured by grace, not earned, but the reaping is real and certain, and knowing it keeps the believer at work. Verse 8 describes a direction of life: what a person sows shows which field he lives in, and one indwelt by the Spirit sows to the Spirit as a living tree puts out leaves.

Verse 6 grounds the support of gospel ministry in something older than church order: the Levites had no land and Israel was to provide for them, and Paul elsewhere quotes the Lord’s saying that the labourer deserves his wages (1 Corinthians 9:11; 1 Timothy 5:17–18).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Galatians were weary, and drifting toward the Judaizers’ more comfortable programme would have ended the trouble. Verse 9 is aimed there: the harvest is coming, do not walk off the field.

Now: Sowing is small, repeated and unremarkable, so v. 8 seldom alarms anyone into faithfulness. Verse 9 is for people at the end of their strength, and Paul gives them not a forecast but a fact: sowing is followed by reaping, and the season is God’s.

verseByVerse.quote: Let the one who is taught the word share all good things with the one who teaches.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let the one who is taught the word. Then money, without preliminaries. Taught is katēcheō (hence catechism).

Share all good things. Share is the family of koinōnia, the New Testament’s word for the deepest communion of the church, used here of supporting the teacher. Money is fellowship in its most testable form. And all good things is broad: money, food, hospitality, encouragement.

What the teacher hands you. What a faithful teacher hands his hearers week by week is Christ. The Galatians had once had Jesus Christ publicly portrayed as crucified before their eyes (3:1). A congregation that shares its bread with the man who brings it that word is not paying for a service. It is answering, in a small and practical way, the riches it has been given.

Who is instructed. Paul does not tell teachers to raise support; he tells congregations to give it. A man who must ask for his own living will find it very hard to say the unwelcome thing, and this letter exists because somebody said an extremely unwelcome thing.

Not a novelty. The principle is stated more fully elsewhere: if we have sown spiritual things among you, is it too much if we reap material things from you? (1 Corinthians 9:11, 14). And the labourer deserves his wages (1 Timothy 5:17–18). Nor is it new: the Levites had no land, and Israel was told to provide for them and welcome them at its feasts (Deuteronomy 12:19; 14:27).

Why here? Because it is the first thing Paul thinks of after burden-bearing, and because of what comes next. Verse 7 begins, do not be deceived: God is not mocked, and the sowing and reaping that follows probably has, as its nearest setting, what a congregation does with its money. Few things in church life are a more exact readout of what people actually believe.

Paul’s own freedom. Paul himself made tents in Corinth rather than be a burden, and made it his boast to preach free of charge (1 Corinthians 9:15–18). So paid ministry is not the only faithful shape, but the congregation may not use the apostle’s freedom as an excuse. He chose to go without. He never once said the teacher was not owed.

What decides your giving? Then the searching part, which is what makes this more than church administration. Ask what your giving is actually being decided by. Many Christians give from what is left, which means the teaching of the word is funded by the residue of a lifestyle that was designed without reference to it. Paul’s word is share: not tip, not subsidise, not fund from surplus. It assumes a common life in which what one has is available to the other, and that is a considerably more disturbing idea than a percentage.

What it does not mean. It does not mean teachers should demand support or preach for money. Elders are to be not greedy for gain (1 Peter 5:2), and a teacher who makes money the point has disqualified himself.

Does this mean I must give a tenth? The New Testament does not lay down a fixed percentage for Christians; it calls for giving that is regular, proportionate, generous and cheerful (1 Corinthians 16:2; 2 Corinthians 9:6–7). Christians differ on whether the tithe still binds, and many find it a wise starting place. Whatever your view, the question is not how little you can give but how gladly you can share. Begin by giving first, not last, from each pay; support your own church and those who teach you; and let your giving grow as God provides. Christ, though he was rich, became poor for your sake (2 Corinthians 8:9).

In everyday life. Do something this week for the one who teaches you, beyond money: a note of thanks for one specific thing you learned, a meal, a promise to pray for him by name.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not be deceived: God is not mocked, for whatever one sows, that will he also reap. For the one who sows to his own flesh will from the flesh reap corruption, but the one who sows to the Spirit will from the Spirit reap eternal life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God is not mocked. The tone hardens without warning. The verb comes from the word for the nose: to sneer. The sense is not chiefly that he takes offence but that nobody gets away with it. You may treat him as a system to be worked around; the treatment simply does not succeed.

Whatever one sows. The picture is a farmer, and the principle runs through Scripture (Job 4:8; Proverbs 22:8; Hosea 8:7). It carries three certainties. You reap what you sow: no farmer has ever been surprised by the species of his own crop. You reap more than you sow, and that cuts both ways. And you reap later than you sow, which is the certainty that deceives people, because the gap between the sowing and the harvest is long enough to make a man think the connection is not real.

The gap. That gap is what verse 7 is aimed at. Nobody sneers at God while the harvest is coming in. The sneer happens in month four, when nothing has visibly followed and the whole warning seems overwrought. Paul’s answer is that the ground is keeping the account whether or not anyone is watching. And the ground is not a machine; it is the moral order of a holy God, before whom no creature is hidden and to whom we must give account (Hebrews 4:13). To sneer at that order is to treat the Holy One as a fool, and he is not.

Sows to his own flesh. Sowing to the flesh is investing your life, time, money and energy in sinful desires (5:19–21). The harvest is phthora, corruption, ending in ruin and eternal destruction. The flesh pays out less often in catastrophe than in decomposition: a marriage that goes quietly hollow, an appetite that needs more each year to do the same work, a conscience that stops registering, a man in his sixties who cannot say what he built. Nothing dramatic happened; it simply went off. And at the end, the decay is not merely of a life but of a soul.

Sows to the Spirit. Sowing to the Spirit is investing in what pleases the Spirit: prayer, Scripture, worship, love, service. The harvest is eternal life. And here a guard is needed, because the sentence can be read as wages for services rendered, which would contradict the entire letter.

Where Christians differ: is eternal life earned by sowing? Some take this verse to mean salvation is a reward for good living. This commentary’s view: Eternal life is God’s free gift in Christ (Romans 6:23), received by faith (the whole message of Galatians). But the life of faith shows itself in sowing to the Spirit, and that life leads to its harvest. Sowing to the Spirit is not the root of salvation but its fruit and its path (Romans 2:6–7; 8:13). Those who sow persistently to the flesh, without repentance, show they do not have the Spirit.

A direction of life. Nothing you sow can purchase eternal life, which is the life of the risen Christ: God gave us eternal life, and this life is in his Son (1 John 5:11). The Spirit who joins us to Christ is the one who brings that life to harvest. So verse 8 describes a direction of life: a person indwelt by the Spirit of Christ sows to the Spirit for the same reason a living tree puts out leaves, and the harvest is not his wages but the full growth of Christ’s life in him. This is not aimed at the believer who falls and gets up and fights again. The war between flesh and Spirit (5:17) is itself a sign that the Spirit is there; the one in danger is the one who has stopped fighting and no longer cares.

Small seeds. Sowing is small, repeated and unremarkable, and nobody has ever sown a field in one afternoon. This morning’s twenty minutes with the Bible open, the apology you made instead of the point you were entitled to make: none of it felt like anything. That is what seed is like in the hand. We seldom connect our spiritual dullness to anything because we look for a cause the size of the effect, and there never is one. There is a field, and there is what has been going into it for years, and the Spirit who raised Jesus lives in you and makes the seed grow.

Is this karma? No. Karma is an impersonal law of cause and effect that no one can escape. Here a personal God is speaking, who forgives, and who laid the penalty of his people’s sin on Christ. But forgiveness does not always remove the earthly consequences of sin. David was forgiven, The LORD also has put away your sin, and yet the child died (2 Samuel 12:13–14); and the Lord disciplines the one he loves (Hebrews 12:6). Nor does every hardship mean a person is reaping a particular sin; Job and the man born blind (John 9:3) show otherwise. A parent who has lost a child should never read that loss as God’s payment for their sin: David’s case was named by a prophet, and yours has not been. What this verse warns against is thinking we can sow to the flesh and escape the harvest.

I sowed to the flesh for years. Is it too late? No, not if you are turning to Christ now. The harvest of eternal life does not depend on the length of your sowing but on the grace of the one who gives it: the thief on the cross sowed nothing and was with Christ in paradise that day (Luke 23:43). God can restore the years the swarming locust has eaten (Joel 2:25). Some earthly consequences may remain, and you should face them honestly, putting right what you can. But Christ has borne the eternal harvest of your sin on the cross. From today, begin to sow to the Spirit, in small seeds, and trust God with the crop.

For worship. The one who sowed most perfectly to the Spirit reaped what we had sown. Christ planted nothing but righteousness, and was handed the harvest of our corruption on the cross, so that his perfect obedience is counted as ours and our patchy sowing is accepted for his sake. Then he went into the ground like seed and came up as the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep (1 Corinthians 15:20). God is not mocked, and God is not stingy: he gives eternal life as a gift to those who could never have grown it.

verseByVerse.quote: And let us not grow weary of doing good, for in due season we will reap, if we do not give up. So then, as we have opportunity, let us do good to everyone, and especially to those who are of the household of faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let us not grow weary. The us matters. Paul has mostly been saying you, and here, as in 5:25–26, he puts himself inside the exhortation, which means the apostle knew what it was to be tired of doing good. He assumes weariness. The verb means losing heart, going slack (as in 2 Corinthians 4:1): a warning not against wickedness but against a very ordinary exhaustion, the state of a Christian worn out from carrying burdens, restoring the fallen and giving away money.

In due season. At its own proper time, God’s appointed season. No farmer resents June for not being September. He works a field that shows him nothing for months, because the timetable was never his to set, and he knows the difference between nothing is happening and nothing is visible.

If we do not give up. The one condition, and it is not achievement. Give up is to faint, to go limp. Paul does not say we shall reap if we sow enough, or well, but if we do not stop. The risk is not failure but abandonment: walking off the field after years of work, three weeks before something comes up.

Consider him. The letter to the Hebrews uses the same verb for going limp and gives the remedy: consider him who endured from sinners such hostility against himself, so that you may not grow weary or fainthearted (Hebrews 12:3). Jesus did good for some three years in the face of rejection, and at the end his field looked like a cross, a borrowed tomb and eleven frightened men. He did not give up. For the joy that was set before him he endured the cross (Hebrews 12:2), and the harvest of that sowing has been coming in ever since. A tired Christian keeps going not by staring at his own furrow, but by looking at his Lord’s.

The people this verse belongs to. This verse belongs to particular people, most likely reading it at the end of their strength, and the God who never grows weary gives power to the faint (Isaiah 40:28–29). The mother who has prayed for a son for twenty-two years and has stopped expecting the phone to ring. The man who teaches eight children in a back room while the church around him talks about growth. The wife who has been gentle with a hard husband for a decade with nothing whatever to show for it. The pastor in a small town who has buried more people than he has baptised. Paul’s answer to every one of them is a fact about the universe God made: sowing is followed by reaping, and the season is his.

As we have opportunity. Verse 10 turns the weariness outward. Opportunity is the same word as the season in verse 9: the sowing season is now. As we have opportunity does not mean when it is convenient, but while there is still time.

Do good to everyone. The word everyone forbids the church that has turned inward and does its good only where it will be appreciated by people who share its views.

The household of faith. Fellow believers come first, as one cares first for one’s own family. Especially forbids a general benevolence toward mankind as a substitute for helping the believer two streets away whose boiler has failed; family first, not family only. And a household does not run an application process. The claim on you is not that the person deserves it. It is that he is kin.

I am exhausted. Is resting the same as giving up? No. Giving up is abandoning the field; resting is what keeps you in it. God built rest into creation, Jesus took his tired disciples away to a desolate place to rest a while (Mark 6:31), and Elijah under the broom tree was given sleep and food before he was given a task (1 Kings 19:5–8). If you are worn out, you may need to sleep, to share the work, to say no to something good, or to ask for help. None of that is unfaithfulness. What Paul warns against is losing heart: concluding that doing good is pointless and walking away. Rest, and then go back to sowing.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–18 — The Cross and the New Creation
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In v. 11 Paul takes the pen and writes the closing paragraph himself, in large letters. He exposes motive: the men pressing circumcision want a good showing, a way round persecution and converts to boast about (vv. 12–13). Paul will boast only in the cross, by which the world is crucified to him and he to the world (v. 14). What counts is a new creation, not circumcision or uncircumcision, and peace and mercy rest on all who walk by that rule, and on the Israel of God (vv. 15–16). He closes the case with the scars he bears for Jesus, and ends where he began, with grace, calling them brothers (vv. 17–18).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Cross as the Permanent Centre, and the Israel of God

Paul’s boast in v. 14 sums up the letter. The cross, where the law’s curse was borne and the new creation began, is not only the entrance to the Christian life but its permanent centre. This is Luther’s theology of the cross against a theology of glory: God’s ways are read from below, through shame and suffering, not from above through human notions of power and success.

On v. 16 much turns on the small word kai, which can mean and or even. Read as even, those who walk by this rule, Jew and Gentile together, are the Israel of God; this fits the letter’s argument best (3:29; 4:26). Read as and, a second group is in view, most naturally believing Jews, a reading held by serious readers who expect a future for ethnic Israel on the strength of Romans 11. Either way, no one enters that number by ancestry or by a mark.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Judaizers wanted social safety, and vv. 12–13 name it without charity: circumcising the Gentiles satisfied the synagogue and left Rome uninterested. Verse 17 answers it with the marks Paul carried from his sufferings, among them the stoning at Lystra in Galatia itself (Acts 14:19).

Now: The test v. 13 puts to a softened conviction is not whether the reason is defensible but what the adjustment costs you. And v. 17 honours anyone whose faithfulness has cost them something unglamorous: Paul called his scars the marks of Jesus.

verseByVerse.quote: See with what large letters I am writing to you with my own hand. It is those who want to make a good showing in the flesh who would force you to be circumcised, and only in order that they may not be persecuted for the cross of Christ. For even those who are circumcised do not themselves keep the law, but they desire to have you circumcised that they may boast in your flesh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With my own hand. Paul takes the pen off his secretary. Letters in that world were normally dictated, with the author adding a line at the end in his own hand as a signature (2 Thessalonians 3:17); here he takes over for the whole closing paragraph, and he writes big. Possibly his eyes were poor (4:15); chiefly it is emphasis, the ancient bold type. What follows is the whole letter compressed, and he does not want it missed.

A good showing in the flesh. The first thing he writes large is not doctrine but motive. Make a good showing is literally to present a fine face in public.

That they may not be persecuted. Then Paul names what they are actually buying with the Galatians’ circumcision: escape from persecution by non-Christian Jews. This is a diagnosis, not an insult. Judaism had a measure of tolerance under Rome, and circumcised Jews who followed a Messiah could shelter under it; uncircumcised Gentiles worshipping a crucified Jew could not, and Jewish Christians seen to dissolve the boundary paid for it at home. If Gentile converts were circumcised, Christianity looked like a Jewish sect, and the offence of the cross disappeared (5:11).

A reasonable committee. So the Judaizers were not, on Paul’s diagnosis, chiefly theologians, but men under pressure. Get the Gentiles circumcised and the whole problem goes away: the synagogue is satisfied, Rome is uninterested, and nobody has to be beaten. It is a solution any reasonable committee might reach.

Do not themselves keep the law. Circumcision obligates a man to the entire code (5:3), and the men selling it are not keeping it either. So this was never a serious attempt at law-righteousness. It was a way of belonging safely, dressed in Scripture.

Boast in your flesh. Then the second motive, and it is uglier. Converts as trophies: something done to another man’s body that can be counted and reported. Every generation of ministry has its version: the number, the person who has become a credential.

What does the adjustment cost you? That puts a question to anyone who has ever softened a Christian conviction and given a theological reason for it. The test is not whether your reason is defensible; the Judaizers had excellent reasons, and one of them was avoiding a beating. The test is what the adjustment costs you. Every change these men proposed made their lives easier, and the flesh has never once recommended a course of action that would get its owner persecuted. Paul’s alternative is a cross, which is exactly what the whole manoeuvre was designed to avoid.

Get behind me. The Lord met this reasoning in his own disciples. When he first spoke of his cross, Peter took him aside and rebuked him: far be it from you, Lord; this shall never happen to you. Jesus answered, get behind me, Satan, for you are not setting your mind on the things of God, but on the things of man (Matthew 16:22–23). A way of following the Messiah that avoids the cross is the temptation Jesus refused most sharply, and he refused it for us. The Judaizers wanted to keep the name of Christ and lose his cross; he took up the cross so that we might bear his name.

Is it wrong to avoid persecution if I can? Not in itself. Jesus told his disciples to flee from one town to the next when persecuted (Matthew 10:23), Paul escaped Damascus in a basket and appealed to his rights as a Roman citizen, and we are to pray for peaceful lives (1 Timothy 2:1–2). Wisdom, tact and lawful protection are good. What is wrong is avoiding persecution by changing the message: dropping the parts of the gospel that offend, keeping quiet about Christ when silence is denial, or bending God’s commands to fit in. Ask whether you are avoiding trouble or avoiding Christ. The first may be wise; the second is the Judaizers’ path.

What it does not mean. It does not mean all Jewish Christians were insincere. Paul speaks of these particular teachers. Many Jewish believers, like Peter, James and Barnabas, shared his gospel and suffered for it.
verseByVerse.note: Paul dictated his letters, then took the pen himself to finish; his large letters may reflect poor eyesight or simply emphasis.

verseByVerse.quote: But far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, by which the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Far be it from me to boast. They boast in flesh; Paul boasts in a gallows. The opening phrase is mē genoito, as at 2:17 and 3:21: may it never be. Any other boast is unthinkable.

Three crucifixions. This is the letter’s third: the old self under condemnation died with Christ (2:20); the flesh’s rule inside is broken (5:24); and here the world’s hold from outside is broken. One cross deals with guilt, with the flesh and with the world, and that is why it is the only thing left to boast in.

How strange it sounded. The cross was not yet jewellery. It was Rome’s public death for slaves and rebels, so shameful that polite writers avoided the word. Cicero said the very name of the cross should be far from the body of a Roman citizen, and from his thoughts, eyes and ears. And a Pharisee knew Deuteronomy 21:23 (3:13): a hanged man is cursed by God. To boast in a crucifixion was, in Jewish terms, blasphemy, and in Roman terms, disgusting.

The only boast. Not his conversion, his missionary record, his learning, his visions or his suffering. One thing, and it is something done for him rather than by him. Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord (1 Corinthians 1:31).

The world has been crucified to me. A double death. The world is the whole system of values, status and religion opposed to God, religious achievement included. Through the cross it is dead to Paul. What it holds out, standing, security, the approval you were raised to want, is not all evil, but its offers have lost their power. It cannot buy him any more, because he has seen the one thing it had no answer for.

And I to the world. Paul is dead to the world too: it no longer has a claim on him, and he has lost his standing in its eyes. This is the harder half, the one the false teachers were desperate to avoid. A man dead to the world is no longer being ranked, which is precisely why he was free to write this letter and they were not. Isaac Watts’s hymn When I Survey the Wondrous Cross is built on this verse: forbid it, Lord, that I should boast, save in the death of Christ my God.

What it looks like with a mortgage. It is not withdrawal; Paul had a trade and cared enormously about money for the poor. It means the world can still take things from you but can no longer set your price. Ask what would happen if the reputation you have built quietly collapsed, not through sin, just through being overlooked or misunderstood. If the answer is that you would lose something painful but survivable, the crucifixion has been done. If the answer is that you would not know who you were, the world is still very much alive. That is not a reason to despair but to look again at the cross; the world loosens its grip slowly.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul hated the created world or other people. God so loved the world that he gave his only Son (John 3:16), and everything created by God is good, to be received with thanksgiving (1 Timothy 4:4).

How do I boast in the cross in practice? Make it the first thing you say about yourself when you stand before God: not what you have done, but what Christ did. When you are praised, quietly give the credit to his grace. When you are accused, run to the cross rather than to your record. When you speak of your faith to others, talk about Jesus crucified and risen, not mainly about your experience or your church. Sing the hymns that look at the cross, and look at it yourself each day, slowly, until its glory crowds out the smaller glories you are tempted to chase.

For worship. The Son of God, hanging on a beam outside a city, stripped, mocked, numbered with criminals, bearing a curse that belonged to other people; and there is not a throne in the history of the world that has ever been so completely a throne as that. There the love of God was shown at full strength, the justice of God was satisfied in full, the powers were disarmed and put to open shame (Colossians 2:15), and the Lamb who was slain was found worthy (Revelation 5:12). The universe has one boast in it, and it is a man on a cross.

verseByVerse.quote: For neither circumcision counts for anything, nor uncircumcision, but a new creation. And as for all who walk by this rule, peace and mercy be upon them, and upon the Israel of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Neither circumcision nor uncircumcision. The verdict that ends the argument. Paul finishes the same sentence three ways: in 5:6 what counts is faith working through love; in 1 Corinthians 7:19 it is keeping the commandments of God; here, a new creation. Three answers, one thing: the question is never the mark on the body but whether God has done something.

A new creation. What counts is regeneration, not ritual. Kainē ktisis is new in kind, not merely recent: Paul is reaching for Genesis 1, and for Isaiah’s promise of new heavens and a new earth (Isaiah 65:17). The gospel produces not a reformed version of the old thing but the age to come arriving early in a person: the life God will one day give the whole renewed world has already begun in everyone joined to the risen Christ. Jesus called it being born again, and Paul the washing of regeneration: a heart that was dead to God made alive by God himself (John 3:3–8; Titus 3:5). If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation (2 Corinthians 5:17). The Judaizers were proposing an alteration to somebody who had already been raised: the difference between renovating a house and being born.

I do not feel like a new creation. Am I one? Being a new creation is first something God declares and does, not something you feel. The new creation has begun in you if you have been united to Christ by faith: God has given you a new heart, his Spirit lives in you, and you belong to the age to come. But the old body, the old memories, many old habits and the remaining flesh are still there, which is why it does not always feel new. Look for the marks: a new love for Christ, a new hatred of sin, new desires to please God, a new family in the church. These may be small. A newborn does not feel like a person either, but he is one, and he will grow.

This rule. Rule is kanōn, a measuring rod. The rule is what he has just said: not circumcision, not uncircumcision, but new creation, the rule of grace alone.

Peace and mercy be upon them. A blessing, echoing Psalm 125:5 and 128:6: peace be upon Israel. Paul’s greetings put peace last; here it comes first, with mercy beside it, as though at the end of a letter this severe he wants the last word on the Galatians to be that they will be dealt with kindly.

The Israel of God. The most argued-over phrase in the letter. Much turns on the small word kai, which can mean and or even. Read it as even the Israel of God, and the phrase caps the sentence: those who walk by this rule, Jew and Gentile together in Christ, are the Israel of God. Read it as simply and, and a second group is in view, most naturally Jewish believers, the believing remnant, singled out for a particular blessing at the end of a letter that has been hard on their nation’s badge.

Where Christians differ: who is the Israel of God? Some take the Israel of God to be ethnic Israel, or believing Jews, distinct from Gentile believers. Others take it as the whole church. The reading of kai as and, with believing Jews in view, is held by serious readers who love this book, including many who expect a future for ethnic Israel on the strength of Romans 11 and who honour the Scriptures as fully as anyone. This commentary’s view: In context, Paul has spent the whole letter arguing that all believers, Jew and Gentile, are Abraham’s offspring and heirs (3:7, 29), that the Jerusalem above is our mother (4:26), and that ethnic markers count for nothing. It would be strange to end by separating believing Jews as a special group. The Israel of God is best understood as the whole people of God in Christ, the true Israel (Romans 2:28–29; Philippians 3:3). This does not cancel God’s purposes for ethnic Israel (Romans 11), but describes the church as the fulfilment of Israel.

What everyone agrees on. Whoever the Israel of God is, peace and mercy rest on them, and no one gets into that number by ancestry or by a mark. The Galatians had been told they were second-tier members of God’s people; Paul’s final blessing lays peace and mercy on everyone walking by this rule, and does not check anybody’s papers on the way past.
verseByVerse.note: Interpreters differ over whether “the Israel of God” means believing Jews or the whole church, Jew and Gentile together. The more persuasive reading is the whole church (compare 3:29).

verseByVerse.quote: From now on let no one cause me trouble, for I bear on my body the marks of Jesus. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit, brothers. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
From now on let no one cause me trouble. It sounds abrupt, almost weary: Paul has said all he needs to, and the case is closed. After six chapters of argument, he simply shows the scars.

The marks of Jesus. The marks are stigmata: a brand on a slave, soldier or temple servant to show whose he was. Paul’s were almost certainly the scars of beatings and stoning. The false teachers wanted a mark cut into Gentile flesh to prove ownership and belonging. Paul says: I have marks. Put there by people trying to stop me (2 Corinthians 11:24–25), some perhaps at Lystra, in Galatia, where hearers of this letter may have watched him dragged out and left for dead (Acts 14:19). Those are his credentials, and they settle the question of whose he is far more conclusively than circumcision ever could.

Marks that are honoured. That matters for anyone whose faithfulness has cost them something visible and unglamorous: a career that went nowhere because of a conviction, a family that cooled, a body worn out in a small work nobody counted. Those marks are not evidence of a failure to manage life well. Paul called his the marks of Jesus, and expected them to be honoured.

Where Christians differ: the stigmata. Some medieval saints, such as Francis of Assisi, were said to receive the stigmata: wounds like Christ’s, miraculously appearing on their hands and feet, seen as a sign of special holiness. This commentary’s view: Paul’s marks were the ordinary scars of persecution suffered for preaching Christ, not miraculous wounds. Scripture nowhere teaches miraculous stigmata or treats them as a sign of holiness. The true marks of belonging to Christ are faith, love, holiness and willingness to suffer for him.

I have never suffered for Christ like this. Am I a lesser Christian? No. Your standing with God rests on Christ’s wounds, not yours, and God assigns different paths to different servants. Many Christians in quiet places live long lives without beatings or prison, and they are not second-class. But every believer bears some marks: the cost of honesty at work, the friend lost over your faith, the self-denial nobody sees, the patience in a hard marriage, the ridicule for your convictions. Do not despise those small marks, and do not go looking for dramatic ones. Be faithful where you are, pray for those who suffer more (Hebrews 13:3), and be ready if the cost rises.

With your spirit, brothers. After all the sharp words, the Greek sentence ends, just before the Amen, with brothers. The man who pronounced an anathema, a solemn curse, on the false gospel in the first chapter (1:8–9) signs off calling them family.

Grace at both ends. The letter that began with grace (1:3, 6) ends with grace, and everything between the two is an argument that nothing may be added to it. The letter closes where it opened, because there is nowhere else for a Christian to stand.

In everyday life. Before you sleep tonight, say the last verse of Galatians over yourself and over the people you love.

For worship. So the last thing Galatians does is hold up its subject one more time: a Son sent in the fullness of time, born of a woman, born under the law; who kept every clause of it and was made a curse on a tree, so that the blessing of Abraham could reach a farmer in Lystra with no ancestry and nothing to bring; who bought slaves out of the market, put his Spirit in their hearts and taught them to say Father. He bears marks too, in his hands, his feet and his side, the price of everything this letter defends. Nothing was cheapened. Everything was paid. And from first to last it was grace.
verseByVerse.note: The “marks” were the scars left by beatings and stoning — like the brands on a slave showing whom he belonged to.

6.text: <sup>1</sup>Brothers, if anyone is caught in any transgression, you who are spiritual should restore him in a spirit of gentleness. Keep watch on yourself, lest you too be tempted.<sup>2</sup>Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ.<sup>3</sup>For if anyone thinks he is something, when he is nothing, he deceives himself.<sup>4</sup>But let each one test his own work, and then his reason to boast will be in himself alone and not in his neighbor.<sup>5</sup>For each will have to bear his own load.<sup>6</sup>Let the one who is taught the word share all good things with the one who teaches.<sup>7</sup>Do not be deceived: God is not mocked, for whatever one sows, that will he also reap.<sup>8</sup>For the one who sows to his own flesh will from the flesh reap corruption, but the one who sows to the Spirit will from the Spirit reap eternal life.<sup>9</sup>And let us not grow weary of doing good, for in due season we will reap, if we do not give up.<sup>10</sup>So then, as we have opportunity, let us do good to everyone, and especially to those who are of the household of faith.<sup>11</sup>See with what large letters I am writing to you with my own hand.<sup>12</sup>It is those who want to make a good showing in the flesh who would force you to be circumcised, and only in order that they may not be persecuted for the cross of Christ.<sup>13</sup>For even those who are circumcised do not themselves keep the law, but they desire to have you circumcised that they may boast in your flesh.<sup>14</sup>But far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, by which the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.<sup>15</sup>For neither circumcision counts for anything, nor uncircumcision, but a new creation.<sup>16</sup>And as for all who walk by this rule, peace and mercy be upon them, and upon the Israel of God.<sup>17</sup>From now on let no one cause me trouble, for I bear on my body the marks of Jesus.<sup>18</sup>The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit, brothers. Amen.
